67.x: Devagupta of Malwa killed Grahavarman and held Rajyashri at Kannauj.
67.tq: Use the wrong-ruler-for-the-deed trap with closely associated contemporary rulers.
xs: **Devagupta of Malwa** killed Grahavarman and held Rajyashri at Kannauj — option **(3)** is correct.
**Shashanka** of Gauda killed **Rajyavardhana**, not Grahavarman.
**Bhaskaravarman** of Kamarupa was Harsha's **ally**; **Pulakesin II** defeated Harsha.
xa: Harsha freed his sister **Rajyashri**.
Shashanka's capital was **Karnasuvarna**; he cut the **Bodhi tree** at Gaya.
Alliance: Harsha + **Bhaskaravarman** vs **Shashanka**.

67.s: The Vardhana dynasty of Thanesar, to which Harsha belonged, is also named after its founder. Who was he?
67.x: The line is called the Pushyabhuti dynasty after its founder Pushyabhuti (BPSC 2022 key); its rulers were once Gupta feudatories. Grahavarman was a Maukhari, Vindhyashakti founded the Vakatakas, and Bhaskaravarman ruled Kamarupa.
67.tq: Pushyabhuti = Vardhana line of Thanesar
xs: The line is named after its founder **Pushyabhuti** — option **(1)** is correct (BPSC 2022 key).
**Grahavarman** was a **Maukhari**; **Vindhyashakti** founded the **Vakatakas**; **Bhaskaravarman** ruled **Kamarupa**.
xa: The Pushyabhutis were once **Gupta feudatories**.
Some notes name **Naravardhana** (late **5th/early 6th c.**) as founder.
Some call **Prabhakaravardhana** the founder — he was the first great ruler.

67.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the political result of Harsha's conflict with Dhruvasena II of Valabhi?
o: Dhruvasena II defeated Harsha and annexed Kannauj.
Dhruvasena II succeeded Sasanka in Gauda.
Dhruvasena II became Harsha's vassal and married Harsha's daughter.
Dhruvasena II became the ruler of Kamarupa under Harsha's protection.
67.x: Dhruvasena II of Valabhi was made a vassal of Harsha and married Harsha's daughter.
67.tq: Identify the specific result of a campaign instead of confusing it with Harsha's other conquests.
xs: **Dhruvasena II** became Harsha's **vassal** and married **Harsha's daughter** — option **(3)** is correct.
Dhruvasena II (Dhruvabhata) ruled **Valabhi** (Maitrakas) and became Harsha's **son-in-law**.
**Gauda** was Sasanka's; **Kamarupa** was Bhaskaravarman's — not Dhruvasena's.
xa: ⚠ **Bhaskaravarman** = ally; **Dhruvasena II** = vassal and son-in-law; **Pulakesin II** = defeated Harsha.
After Shashanka's death Harsha took **Magadha** and Gauda.
**Nepal** and **Kashmir** accepted Harsha's overlordship / sent tribute.

67.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Kingdom or ruler)
a. Maukharis
b. Gauda
c. Kamarupa
d. Valabhi

List-II (Association)
i. Bhaskaravarman
 ii. Dhruvasena II
 iii. Grahavarman
 iv. Sasanka

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
67.x: The Maukharis were associated with Grahavarman, Gauda with Sasanka, Kamarupa with Bhaskaravarman and Valabhi with Dhruvasena II.
67.tq: Begin with the distinctive Kamarupa–Bhaskaravarman pair and complete the matching.
xs: Correct code: **a–iii, b–iv, c–i, d–ii** — option **(1)**.
**Maukharis** — **Grahavarman**; **Gauda** — **Sasanka**.
**Kamarupa** — **Bhaskaravarman**; **Valabhi** — **Dhruvasena II**.
xa: Sasanka's capital = **Karnasuvarna**.
Bhaskaravarman was Harsha's **ally** (BPSC 2024).
Grahavarman was killed by **Devagupta of Malwa**.

67.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Harsha allied with Bhaskaravarman against Shashanka.
2. Shashanka's capital was Karnasuvarna.
3. Bhaskaravarman ruled Gauda (Bengal).
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
67.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: Bhaskaravarman ruled Kamarupa (Assam); Gauda was Shashanka's kingdom. So A is incomplete and C and D include statement 3.
67.tq: Kamarupa = Bhaskaravarman (ally); Gauda = Shashanka (rival, Karnasuvarna).
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: Harsha allied with **Bhaskaravarman** against **Shashanka** — correct.
Statement 2: Shashanka's capital was **Karnasuvarna** — correct.
Statement 3: **Bhaskaravarman** ruled **Kamarupa (Assam)**, not Gauda — wrong.
xa: **Gauda (Bengal)** was Sasanka's kingdom.
After Sasanka's death Harsha took **Magadha** and Gauda.
Sasanka **killed Rajyavardhana**.

67.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Harsha's relations with neighbouring regions:
1. Nepal and Kashmir acknowledged his overlordship or sent tribute.
2. Kamarupa acknowledged his authority.
3. Pulakesin II of Badami was defeated and made a vassal by Harsha.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
67.x: Nepal, Kashmir and Kamarupa acknowledged Harsha's authority or sent tribute. Pulakesin II defeated Harsha on the Narmada and was not made his vassal.
67.tq: Use the reversed-result trap in the Harsha–Pulakesin conflict.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: **Nepal** and **Kashmir** accepted overlordship / sent tribute — correct.
Statement 2: **Kamarupa** acknowledged Harsha — correct.
Statement 3: **Pulakesin II** **defeated Harsha** — he was never his vassal — wrong.
xa: Pulakesin's victory is recorded in the **Aihole inscription**; he took the title **Paramesvara**.
**Valabhi** (Dhruvasena II) was a vassal.
Harsha's empire: Rajasthan, Punjab, UP, Bihar, Orissa.

67.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the nature of Harshacharita?
o: A Sanskrit romantic comedy by Harsha
A hymn to the Sun composed by Mayura
67.x: Harshacharita, written by Banabhatta, is a semi-historical biography of Harsha and an important literary source for his reign.
67.tq: Distinguish a work about the ruler from works written by the ruler.
xs: **Harshacharita** is a **semi-historical biography** of Harsha — option **(1)** is correct.
It was written by court poet **Banabhatta** and is the chief literary source for the reign.
**Ratnavali / Priyadarshika** are romantic comedies, **Nagananda** a Buddhist play — all by Harsha; the Sun hymn is **Mayura**'s.
xa: Bana also wrote **Kadambari**, completed by son **Bhushanabhatta**.
"Not written by Harsha" = **Harshacharita** (APPSC G2 2025).
Bana's village: **Pritikuta** on the **Sona** river.

67.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
67.x: Nagananda is a Buddhist-themed play centred on self-sacrifice. Ratnavali and Priyadarshika are romantic comedies, while Harshacharita is Banabhatta's biography of Harsha.
67.tq: Match each work with its literary nature before eliminating swapped descriptions.
xs: **Nagananda — Buddhist theme of self-sacrifice** is correct — option **(1)**.
**Harshacharita** is Bana's **biography**, not a comedy.
**Kadambari** is a **prose romance**, not a hymn; **Ratnavali** is Harsha's **romantic comedy**, not a biography.
xa: Harsha's three dramas: **Ratnavali**, **Priyadarshika**, **Nagananda**.
**Mayura** wrote **Suryashataka** (hymn to the Sun).
**Matanga Divakara** was also a court poet of Harsha.

67.s: Who completed Banabhatta's Kadambari?
67.x: Kadambari, a prose romance begun by Banabhatta, was completed by his son Bhushanabhatta.
67.tq: Use the author–work–successor relationship rather than confusing court poets.
xs: **Bhushanabhatta**, Bana's son, completed **Kadambari** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Mayura** and **Matanga Divakara** were other court poets; **Silabhadra** headed **Nalanda**.
xa: Kadambari is among the world's **earliest Sanskrit novels** (APPSC G1 2018).
Bana also wrote **Harshacharita**.
Bana was Harsha's **Asthana Kavi**.

67.s:
Consider the following statements regarding sources for the reign of Harsha:
1. The Madhuban plate is useful for establishing chronology.
2. The Sonpat seal is an inscriptional source for Harsha's reign.
3. The Banskhera inscription bears Harsha's signature.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
67.x: The Madhuban plate, Sonpat seal and Banskhera inscription are all sources for Harsha's reign; the Banskhera record is noted for bearing Harsha's signature.
67.tq: Check each source independently before selecting the combined code.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: the **Madhuban plate** (land grant) is used for **chronology** — correct.
Statement 2: the **Sonpat seal** is an epigraphic source — correct.
Statement 3: the **Banskhera** inscription bears **Harsha's signature** — correct.
xa: The **Aihole** inscription (Chalukya) records Harsha's defeat on the **Narmada**.
Literary source: **Harshacharita**; foreign account: **Si-Yu-Ki**.
Hiuen Tsang visited Harsha's court in **631 CE**.

67.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Source)
A. Harshacharita
B. Si-Yu-Ki
C. Banskhera inscription
D. Madhuban plate

List-II (Type or feature)
1. Foreign account
2. Epigraphic land grant and chronology
3. Literary Sanskrit biography
4. Epigraphic record bearing Harsha's signature

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
67.x: Harshacharita is a literary Sanskrit biography, Si-Yu-Ki is a foreign account, Banskhera bears Harsha's signature and the Madhuban plate is an epigraphic land-grant record useful for chronology.
67.tq: Start with the distinctive Banskhera and Madhuban clues, then complete the source classification.
xs: Correct code: **A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2** — option **(1)**.
**Harshacharita** — literary Sanskrit biography; **Si-Yu-Ki** — foreign account (Hiuen Tsang).
**Banskhera** — bears **Harsha's signature**; **Madhuban plate** — land grant and **chronology**.
xa: The **Sonpat seal** is another epigraphic source.
The **Aihole** inscription records the defeat on the Narmada.
Si-Yu-Ki = "**Records of the Western World**".

67.s: Which of the following is an epigraphic source associated with the defeat of Harsha on the Narmada?
67.x: The Aihole inscription is a Chalukyan epigraphic source recording Pulakesin II's victory over Harsha on the Narmada.
67.tq: Link the historical event to the source category and political issuer.
xs: The **Aihole inscription** of **Pulakesin II** records Harsha's defeat on the **Narmada** — option **(3)** is correct.
**Madhuban plate** = land grant / chronology; **Harshacharita** = Bana's biography; **Si-Yu-Ki** = Hiuen Tsang's account.
xa: The Aihole inscription is of **634 CE**; the war is placed c. **618-619 CE**.
Pulakesin took the title **Paramesvara**.
The **Banskhera** inscription bears Harsha's signature.

67.s: Which one of the following works was NOT written by Harshavardhana?
67.x: Harshacharita, the semi-historical biography of Harsha, was written by his court poet Banabhatta (APPSC G2 2025). Ratnavali and Priyadarshika (romantic comedies) and Nagananda (a Buddhist play on self-sacrifice) are the three Sanskrit dramas written by Harsha himself.
67.tq: Harsha wrote 3 plays; Bana wrote Harshacharita and Kadambari
xs: **Harshacharita** was not written by Harsha — option **(4)** is the answer (APPSC G2 2025).
It was written by his court poet **Banabhatta**.
**Ratnavali**, **Priyadarshika** (romantic comedies) and **Nagananda** (Buddhist play) are Harsha's own.
xa: Bana also wrote **Kadambari**.
Bana is paired with **Harsha**, not the Guptas or Kanishka.
**Mayura** wrote **Suryashataka**.

67.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Matanga Divakara — Court poet of Harsha
67.x: Vakpatiraja was associated with Yashovarman of Kannauj, not Harsha's court. Banabhatta, Mayura and Matanga Divakara were associated with Harsha's court.
67.tq: Find the swapped patron–poet association.
xs: **Vakpatiraja — court poet of Harsha** is wrong — option **(1)** is the answer.
**Vakpatiraja** belonged to **Yashovarman** of Kannauj.
**Matanga Divakara**, **Mayura** (Suryashataka) and **Banabhatta** (Harshacharita) were Harsha's court poets.
xa: **Padmagupta** is another distractor — he belongs to the **Paramaras**.
Bana was Harsha's **Asthana Kavi**.
Bana's village: **Pritikuta** on the **Sona**.

67.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the Kannauj assembly from the Prayag assembly?
o: Kannauj was held every five years for charity, whereas Prayag honoured Hiuen Tsang.
Prayag was a one-time debate attended only by Buddhist scholars.
Kannauj honoured Hiuen Tsang and promoted Mahayana, whereas Prayag was associated with charity.
Both assemblies were held at the confluence of the Ganga and Yamuna.
67.x: The Kannauj assembly honoured Hiuen Tsang and propagated Mahayana, while the Prayag assembly was primarily a charitable gathering held periodically.
67.tq: Split the alternatives by purpose and frequency before considering location.
xs: **Kannauj** honoured **Hiuen Tsang** and spread **Mahayana**; **Prayag** was for **charity** — option **(3)** is correct.
Kannauj was a **one-time** assembly (**643 CE**); Prayag was held **every five years**.
Only Prayag was at the **Ganga-Yamuna confluence**; Prayag had representatives of **all religions**.
xa: Kannauj attendance: **20 kings**, 1000 Nalanda scholars, 3000 Brahmins and Jains.
At Prayag, Harsha gave away his **whole treasury**, keeping only personal clothes.
Prayag is called the **Moksha Parishad**.

67.s: The Kannauj assembly convened by Harshavardhana was held in
67.x: The Kannauj assembly is dated to 643 CE.
67.tq: Distinguish the assembly year from Hiuen Tsang’s court date and Harsha’s other chronological markers.
xs: The Kannauj assembly was held in **643 CE** — option **(3)** is correct.
**605** = Yashomati's sati; **631** = Hiuen Tsang at Harsha's court; **647** = Harsha's death.
xa: It honoured **Hiuen Tsang** and propagated **Mahayana**.
It lasted **23 days** (some notes: 21-day debate) and saw an **assassination attempt** on Harsha.
⚠ **Kannauj** = 643, one-time; **Prayag** = every five years, charity.

67.s:
Consider the following statements about the Kannauj assembly:
1. It was held to honour Hiuen Tsang and propagate Mahayana doctrine.
2. It lasted for 23 days according to the stated APP account.
3. It ended without any disturbance or attempt on Harsha’s life.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
67.x: The assembly honoured Hiuen Tsang, propagated Mahayana and lasted 23 days in the stated account. It was followed by violence, arson and an attempt on Harsha’s life, so statement 3 is false.
67.tq: Identify the negative event that reverses an otherwise correct account of the assembly.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: it honoured **Hiuen Tsang** and propagated **Mahayana** — correct.
Statement 2: it lasted **23 days** — correct.
Statement 3: there was **violence, arson** and an **assassination attempt** on Harsha — wrong.
xa: Attendance: **20 kings** (some notes: kings of **18 countries**).
Also 1000 **Nalanda** scholars and 3000 Hinayanists/Mahayanists.
Figures on the Kannauj assembly **differ across sources**.

67.s:
With reference to the Prayag assembly, consider the following statements:
1. It was held every five years.
2. Harsha gave away his treasury and retained only his personal clothes.
3. Hiuen Tsang attended the sixth such assembly.
4. It represented only Mahayana Buddhists.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
67.x: The Prayag assembly was held every five years, Harsha distributed his treasury while retaining only his clothes, and Hiuen Tsang attended the sixth assembly. Representatives of all religions attended, so statement 4 is false.
67.tq: Reject the exclusivist word ‘only’ when the assembly included representatives of all religions.
xs: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 1, 2 and 3 only**.
Statement 1: held **every five years** — correct; Statement 2: Harsha gave away his **whole treasury**, keeping only **personal clothes** — correct.
Statement 3: Hiuen Tsang attended the **sixth** such assembly — correct.
Statement 4: **representatives of all religions** attended — wrong.
xa: Prayag eclecticism: **Buddha, Sun and Shiva** worshipped on successive days.
⚠ **Kannauj** (643) = one-time Mahayana debate.
Prayag = **Moksha Parishad**, at the **Ganga-Yamuna** confluence.

67.s: Which sequence correctly represents the stages of Harsha's religious life?
67.x: Harsha was initially a devout Saiva, later followed Hinayana Buddhism and was subsequently converted to Mahayana Buddhism.
67.tq: Arrange the stages in the stated order rather than selecting a later permanent label.
xs: Harsha moved **Saivism → Hinayana Buddhism → Mahayana Buddhism** — option **(2)** is correct.
He was converted to **Mahayana** by **Hiuen Tsang**.
xa: Influences: sister **Rajyashri** and **Xuanzang**.
Pro-Buddhist measures: **banned animal food**; built thousands of **stupas**.
Harsha, like **Ashoka**, turned to Buddhism and patronised **Nalanda**.

67.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Harsha's religious policy:
1. He banned animal food.
2. He punished the killing of living beings.
3. He completely withdrew patronage from Brahmanical scholars.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
67.x: Harsha adopted pro-Buddhist measures such as banning animal food and punishing the killing of living beings. However, he remained tolerant and continued patronising Brahmanical scholars.
67.tq: Spot the absolute statement that conflicts with the ruler's recorded religious tolerance.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statements 1 and 2: Harsha **banned animal food** and **punished killing of living beings** — correct.
Statement 3: he **kept patronising Brahmanical scholars** — wrong.
xa: He built thousands of **stupas**, rest houses and monasteries at Buddhist sites.
At Prayag, Buddha, **Sun** and **Shiva** were worshipped on successive days.
Hiuen Tsang: Buddhism **declining**, Brahmanism rising.

67.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the fourfold division of revenue during Harsha's reign?
o: Public servants, traders, peasants and Buddhist monks
King's use, merchants, artisans and temples
King's use, public servants, scholars and religious activities
67.x: The four parts were assigned to the king's own use or state administration, public servants, scholars and religious activities including charity to Brahmanas and Buddhist monks.
67.tq: Match each item in a classification with its proper category.
xs: Revenue went to the **king's use**, **public servants**, **scholars** and **religious activities** — option **(3)** is correct.
This fourfold division comes from **Hiuen Tsang**.
Another version: state administration, government employees, scholars, charity to **Brahmanas and Buddhist monks**.
xa: Land tax = **one-sixth** of produce.
Officials were paid in **land grants** → feudal trend.
Hiuen Tsang: taxation **light**, burden not heavy.

67.s: The land revenue during Harsha's reign was generally fixed at what proportion of the produce?
67.x: Land revenue was one-sixth of the produce.
67.tq: Use the exact fraction and distinguish it from nearby traditional rates.
xs: Land tax was **one-sixth** of the produce — option **(1)** is correct.
Hiuen Tsang found taxation **light**; subjects were free from oppression by officials.
xa: Revenue was divided into **four parts**.
Officials' pay: **land grants** rather than cash.
Punishments were harsh — **four ordeals**: water, fire, weighing, poison.

67.s: Which of the following best explains the feudal trend in Harsha's administration?
o: Land revenue was entirely remitted to cultivators.
Officials were paid through land grants instead of cash and feudatories sent tribute.
All officials were selected by village assemblies and paid in bullion.
Feudatories were abolished and taxes were collected only by Buddhist monasteries.
67.x: Officials were commonly remunerated through land grants rather than cash, while samantas acknowledged Harsha's authority by sending tribute. These features indicate a feudal trend.
67.tq: Apply the definition of a feudal tendency to administrative facts.
xs: Officials were paid by **land grants instead of cash** and **feudatories sent tribute** — option **(2)** is correct.
Land grants as pay = the **feudal trend**.
**Samantas** sent tribute — Valabhi (vassal), Kamarupa (ally), Nepal and Kashmir.
xa: Officials: **Avanti** (war and peace), **Simhanada** (commander-in-chief), **Kuntala** (cavalry).
⚠ **Skandagupta** here = Harsha's **elephant-force** officer, not the Gupta king.
The basic unit of administration was the **village**.

67.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Avanti — War and peace
2. Simhanada — Commander-in-chief
3. Kuntala — Cavalry
4. Skandagupta — Elephant force
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
67.x: All four pairs are correctly matched. Avanti dealt with war and peace, Simhanada was commander-in-chief, Kuntala headed the cavalry and Skandagupta was associated with the elephant force.
67.tq: Start from the sure official–department pairs and verify the complete combination.
xs: All four pairs are correctly matched — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
**Avanti** — war and peace; **Simhanada** — commander-in-chief.
**Kuntala** — cavalry; **Skandagupta** — elephant force (officials named in **Harshacharita**).
xa: ⚠ **Skandagupta** here = Harsha's elephant-force officer, **not the Gupta king**.
Officials' pay = **land grants** rather than cash.
Hiuen Tsang glorified Harsha's **powerful army**.

67.s: Which of the following statements about Harsha's punishments is NOT correct?
o: The four ordeals included water, fire, weighing and poison.
Prisoners were always released after a short period in custody.
The system included ordeals as a method of determining guilt.
The penal system could be harsh, with prisoners left to languish in dungeons.
67.x: Prisoners could be left to languish in dungeons; they were not always released after a short period. The four ordeals were water, fire, weighing and poison.
67.tq: Find the absolute statement that reverses the described severity of punishment.
xs: "Prisoners were always released after a short period" is wrong — option **(2)** is the answer.
Prisoners were **left to languish in dungeons**.
The **four ordeals** — **water, fire, weighing, poison** — were used, so options 1, 3 and 4 are correct.
xa: Hiuen Tsang recorded the same ordeals.
He found the kingdom well-governed with no revolts, yet was **robbed twice**.
Basic administrative unit: the **village**.

67.s:
With reference to Nalanda during the reign of Harsha, consider the following statements:
1. It was founded in the Gupta period by Kumaragupta I.
2. Its head was Silabhadra.
3. It functioned as a centre primarily associated with Mahayana Buddhism.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
67.x: Nalanda was founded by Kumaragupta I in the Gupta period, was headed by Silabhadra in Harsha's time, and was an important Mahayana centre.
67.tq: Reject the tempting substitution of Harsha or Hiuen Tsang for the founder or head.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: Nalanda was founded by Gupta ruler **Kumaragupta I** — correct.
Statement 2: its head in Harsha's time was **Silabhadra** (APPSC G1 2022) — correct.
Statement 3: it was a **Mahayana** centre — correct.
xa: ⚠ Trap: the head was **not Harsha**, not Hiuen Tsang, not Kumarajiva.
**Valabhi** = the **Hinayana** centre.
Earlier head: **Dharmapala of Kanchipuram**; other panditas **Dingnaga, Sthiramati**.

67.s: Which one of the following statements about Nalanda is correct?
o: Teaching was conducted mainly in Prakrit and debate was discouraged.
It had a difficult entrance examination and Sanskrit was the medium of instruction.
Students were required to pay tuition and arrange their own accommodation.
Admission was unrestricted and there was no entrance examination.
67.x: Nalanda had a difficult entrance examination, used Sanskrit as the medium of instruction and encouraged debate over lectures. Students received free boarding.
67.tq: Apply the institutional features to identify the precise description.
xs: Nalanda had a **tough entrance exam** and **Sanskrit** as medium — option **(2)** is correct.
Debate was preferred over lecture — so option 1 is wrong.
Boarding and training were **free** — so option 3 is wrong.
xa: About **10,000 students** and a large staff.
"Nalanda" means **giver of knowledge**.
Harsha built a **multi-storied monastery** there (UPSC).

67.s:
Consider the following statements about Nalanda:
1. It provided free boarding for about 10,000 students.
2. Hiuen Tsang studied there and later taught there.
3. Harsha built a multi-storied monastery at Nalanda.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
67.x: Nalanda accommodated about 10,000 students with free boarding; Hiuen Tsang studied and taught there; and Harsha built a multi-storied monastery at the institution.
67.tq: Combine the student, traveller and patron facts without confusing patronage with foundation.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: **10,000 students** with **free** boarding — correct.
Statement 2: **Hiuen Tsang** studied and later taught there — correct.
Statement 3: Harsha built a **multi-storied monastery** (UPSC) — correct.
xa: Harsha was a major **patron**, not the founder — founder was **Kumaragupta I**.
Head in Harsha's time: **Silabhadra**.
Some notes give Hiuen Tsang **nine years** at Nalanda.

67.s: Hiuen Tsang, who visited India during the reign of Harshavardhana, was popularly known as the
67.x: Hiuen Tsang was a Chinese Buddhist monk popularly called the ‘Prince of Pilgrims’; some accounts also refer to him as the ‘King of Travelers’.
67.tq: Use the distinctive title as a direct name-recall clue.
xs: Hiuen Tsang was called the **"Prince of Pilgrims"** — option **(2)** is correct.
Some notes also call him the "**King of Travelers**".
xa: He was at Harsha's court in **631 AD**, coming via **Central Asia/Afghanistan**.
His work: **Si-Yu-Ki** ("Records of the Western World").
He praised **Harsha**, **Pulakesin II** and **Narasimhavarman**.

67.s:
Consider the following statements regarding places described by Hiuen Tsang:
1. Bhinmal was described as a Gurjara capital.
2. The Sun temple of Multan was mentioned in his account.
3. Pataliputra had retained its position as the premier city of northern India.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
67.x: Bhinmal was described as a Gurjara capital and the Sun temple of Multan was mentioned. Hiuen Tsang observed that Kannauj, not Pataliputra, had become the premier city.
67.tq: Reject the reversed comparison in statement 3.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: **Bhinmal (Pi-lo-mo-lo)** = **Gurjara capital** — correct.
Statement 2: he described the **Sun temple of Multan** — correct.
Statement 3: **Kannauj** had **replaced Pataliputra** as the premier city — wrong.
xa: The Multan Sun temple was also described by **Abu Zaid, Al-Masudi, Alberuni**.
Harsha's capital shift: **Thanesar → Kannauj**.

67.s:
According to Hiuen Tsang, consider the following statements about Harsha's kingdom:
1. The tax burden was not heavy and subjects were free from oppression by officials.
2. The kingdom was well governed with no revolts, yet he himself was robbed twice.
3. Trade and towns were expanding rapidly.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
67.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: he saw signs of decline of trade and the rise of a self-sufficient agrarian economy. So A is incomplete and C and D include statement 3.
67.tq: Hiuen Tsang: light tax, good order (but robbed twice), declining trade.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: tax burden **not heavy**; subjects free from oppression — correct.
Statement 2: **well-governed**, no revolts, yet he was **robbed twice** — correct.
Statement 3: he saw **decline of trade** and a self-sufficient **agrarian** economy — wrong.
xa: Caste was **rigid**; **untouchables/outcastes** are mentioned.
Punishment by ordeals of **water, fire, weighing, poison**.
He glorified Harsha's **powerful army**.

67.s: Which one of the following was NOT an observation attributed to Hiuen Tsang?
o: Brahmanism was rising while Buddhism was declining.
The position of women had declined, though women were not treated as inferior.
The caste system was rigid and untouchables were mentioned.
Jainism was specifically described as the principal rising religion.
67.x: Hiuen Tsang mentioned rigid caste distinctions, untouchables, the declining position of women and the rise of Brahmanism. He did not mention Jainism in this observation.
67.tq: Find the single statement outside the recorded set of observations.
xs: Jainism as the "principal rising religion" is not his observation — option **(4)** is the answer.
Hiuen Tsang **does not mention Jainism**.
He did record: Buddhism **declining**, Brahmanism **rising**; women's position declined; caste **rigid**, untouchables mentioned.
xa: Women's status declined, though they were **not treated as inferior**.
Economy: signs of **decline of trade**.
Taxation: **light**, burden not heavy.

67.s:
Hiuen Tsang praised which of the following rulers?
1. Harshavardhana
2. Pulakesin II
3. Narasimhavarman
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
67.x: Hiuen Tsang praised Harsha, Pulakesin II of the Chalukyas and Narasimhavarman of the Pallavas.
67.tq: Test a complete set of names while avoiding a single-ruler assumption.
xs: Hiuen Tsang praised all three — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
He praised **Harsha**, **Pulakesin II** (Chalukya) and **Narasimhavarman** (Pallava).
xa: **Pulakesin II** stopped Harsha at the **Narmada** (c. **618-619 CE**).
Hiuen Tsang confirms that defeat, also recorded in the **Aihole inscription**.
He visited Andhra in **639-640 CE**, under **Kubja Vishnuvardhana**.

67.s: In Hiuen Tsang's account, Andhra was referred to as An-to-lo and its capital was identified as which place?
67.x: Hiuen Tsang referred to Andhra as An-to-lo and identified Vengi as its capital.
67.tq: Separate the regional name and capital from nearby Buddhist centres.
xs: Hiuen Tsang called Andhra "**An-to-lo**" with its capital at **Vengi** — option **(4)** is correct.
**Amaravati** and **Nagarjunakonda** were **decaying**; **Sriparvata vihara** lacked patronage.
xa: **Vengi** had about **20 viharas**.
**Dhanyakataka**: **20 Mahasanghika viharas**, about **1,000 monks** studying the **Abhidhamma Pitaka**.
Visit: **639-640 CE**, under Eastern Chalukya **Kubja Vishnuvardhana**.

67.s:
Which statement about the Buddhist establishments of Vengi is correct?
1. Vengi town had about 20 viharas.
2. Dhanyakataka had about 20 Mahasanghika viharas.
3. Amaravati and Nagarjunakonda were described as flourishing without decline.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
67.x: Vengi had about 20 viharas and Dhanyakataka had about 20 Mahasanghika viharas. Amaravati and Nagarjunakonda were described as decaying, so statement 3 is false.
67.tq: Use the negative condition in the third statement to eliminate an otherwise attractive all-inclusive option.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(3) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: **Vengi** had about **20 viharas** — correct.
Statement 2: **Dhanyakataka** had **20 Mahasanghika viharas** — correct.
Statement 3: **Amaravati** and **Nagarjunakonda** were **decaying** — wrong.
xa: Dhanyakataka had about **1,000 monks** studying the **Abhidhamma Pitaka**.
**Sriparvata vihara** lacked patronage.
Elephants roamed the forests of **Srikakulam**.

67.s: Which of the following statements about Buddhist sites in Andhra, as described by Hiuen Tsang, is NOT correct?
o: Amaravati and Nagarjunakonda were in a state of decay.
Sriparvata vihara suffered from lack of patronage.
Some monasteries had degenerated into brothels.
All monasteries continued to receive strong royal patronage.
67.x: The account records decline at Amaravati and Nagarjunakonda, degeneration of some monasteries and lack of patronage at Sriparvata. It does not describe universal strong royal patronage.
67.tq: Reject the extreme universal statement against several specific signs of decline.
xs: "All monasteries received strong royal patronage" is wrong — option **(4)** is the answer.
**Amaravati** and **Nagarjunakonda** were **decaying**; **Sriparvata vihara** lacked patronage.
Some monasteries had **degenerated into brothels**.
xa: His account is the **main evidence for decline of Buddhism** in Andhra.
Some notes blame **Shaiva propaganda** and **Kumarila Bhatta**.
Andhra = "**An-to-lo**", capital **Vengi**.

67.s: According to the tradition recorded by Hiuen Tsang, which was the correct sequence of Buddha's visits in Andhra?
67.x: The tradition recorded by Hiuen Tsang stated that Buddha first visited Salihundam and then Dharanikota, identified with Dhanyakataka.
67.tq: Use the first-and-second sequence clue to distinguish the correct tradition.
xs: Tradition: Buddha first visited **Salihundam**, then **Dharanikota** — option **(2)** is correct.
**Dharanikota** is identified with **Dhanyakataka**.
xa: Dhanyakataka had **20 Mahasanghika viharas** and about **1,000 monks**.
Hiuen Tsang reached Andhra in **639-640 CE**.
Elephants roamed the forests of **Srikakulam**.

67.s: Harshavardhana is regarded as the last great Buddhist patron-king of northern India before the rise of which political order?
67.x: Harshavardhana is remembered as the last great Buddhist patron-king of northern India before the emergence of Rajput states.

o: Indra Varma founded the Vishnukundins as a feudatory of Harshavardhana.
Indra Varma, the founder of the Vishnukundins, began as a Vakataka vassal.
Indra Varma founded the Vishnukundin kingdom after serving as a Gupta governor.
Indra Varma was the founder of the Pallava dynasty.
67.x: Indra Varma, regarded as the founder of the Vishnukundins, initially served as a Vakataka vassal.

67.s:

xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.

Statements 2 and 3: some notes blame **Shaiva propaganda** and **Kumarila Bhatta** — correct.

67.s:

67.x: The Maukhari dynasty originated at Gaya in Bihar, where its earliest inscriptions are found. The family later ruled from Kannauj.

B. Harivarma

Sharvavarma was a Maukhari ruler. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #144 · pp 250-252]

The Maukhari line ran **Harivarma** → Adityavarma → **Ishvaravarma** → **Sharvavarma** → **Grahavarma**.
So of the four listed: Harivarma, Ishvaravarma, Sharvavarma, Grahavarma.
xa: The Maukharis **originated** in **Gaya** and ruled from **Kannauj**.
**Grahavarman** married Harsha's sister **Rajyashri**.

67.s:

Harsha held a religious assembly at Kannauj. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #144 · pp 250-252]
xs: Statements **I and II** are correct — option **(3) I and II only**.
I and II: the **Kannauj Assembly**, presided over by **Harshavardhana**, was attended by **rulers of 20 countries**, **Brahmins**, **Shramanas** and courtiers.
III is wrong: the **Prayagraj Sangam** hosted the **Mahamoksha Council**, held **every fifth year**.

n: Kalidasa was a court poet or scholar of Chandragupta II. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 112-113]
Harisena wrote the Prayaga Prashasti. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 112-113]
Hastimalla was a Kannada poet. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 112-113]
Hastimalla was a Kannada playwright. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 112-113]
Kshemeshvara was associated with Kashmir. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 112-113]
Kshemeshvara was an 11th-century Sanskrit poet. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 112-113]
xs: The correct match is **a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i** — option **(1)**.
**Kalidasa** → court poet of **Chandragupta II**; **Harisena** → **Prayaga Prashasti**.
**Hastimalla** → **Kannada poet and playwright** (Hoysala rulers); **Kshemendra** → **11th-century Sanskrit poet** of **Kashmir** (notes: Kshemeshvara, **Dasavatar Charita**).
xa: Kalidasa's works include **Kumarasambhavam**, **Raghuvansham**, **Meghadutam**.
**Mahendravarman I** — Pallava ruler-scholar, **Mattavilasa Prahasana**.
**Vishakhadatta** — **Devi-Chandraguptam**.
**Bharavi** — **Kiratarjuniyam**.

67.s: Which work is associated with Kautilya, also known as Chanakya?
67.x: Kautilya (Chanakya), minister of Chandragupta Maurya, wrote the Arthashastra on statecraft. Mahabhashya is Patanjali's, Aryabhatiya is Aryabhatta's and Ashtadhyayi is Panini's.
67.tq: Link each work to its author.
n: Kautilya is also known as Chanakya. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 113-115]
Kautilya wrote the Arthashastra. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 113-115]
Kautilya was a political thinker. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 113-115]
Kautilya was associated with the Mauryan context. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 113-115]
xs: **Kautilya (Chanakya)** wrote the **Arthashastra** — option **(3)**.
He was a **political thinker** of the **Mauryan context**.
**Mahabhashya** is **Patanjali**'s, **Aryabhatiya** is **Aryabhatta**'s and **Ashtadhyayi** is **Panini**'s.
xa: Panini was a **grammarian**; Patanjali a **grammarian and philosopher**.
**Varahamihira** — **Brihatsamhita**.
**Bhaskaracharya II** (**12th century**) — **Siddhantasiromani**, **Lilavati**.

67.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

67.tq: Link each scholar to his work.
n: Panini wrote the Ashtadhyayi. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 113-115]
Patanjali wrote the Mahabhashya. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 113-115]
Aryabhatta wrote the Aryabhatiya. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 113-115]
Varahamihira wrote the Brihatsamhita. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 113-115]

**Aryabhatta** → **Aryabhatiya**; **Varahamihira** → **Brihatsamhita**.
xa: **Kautilya (Chanakya)** → **Arthashastra**.
**Bhaskaracharya II** → **Siddhantasiromani** and **Lilavati**.
Aryabhatta was a **mathematician and astronomer** of ancient India.

67.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Scholar)
a. Kalidasa
b. Harisena
c. Banabhatta
d. Vishakhadatta

List-II (Work or contribution)
i. Prayaga Prashasti
ii. Devi-Chandraguptam
iii. Harshacharita and Kadambari
iv. Abhijnanashakuntalam and Meghadutam
67.x: Kalidasa wrote Abhijnanashakuntalam and Meghadutam, Harisena the Prayaga Prashasti, Banabhatta Harshacharita and Kadambari, and Vishakhadatta Devi-Chandraguptam, giving a-iv, b-i, c-iii, d-ii.
67.tq: Link each scholar to his work.
n: Kalidasa wrote Abhijnanashakuntalam. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 113-115]
Kalidasa wrote Meghadutam. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 113-115]
Harisena composed the Prayaga Prashasti. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 113-115]
Banabhatta wrote Harshacharita. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 113-115]
Banabhatta wrote Kadambari. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 113-115]
Vishakhadatta wrote Devi-Chandraguptam. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 113-115]
xs: The correct match is **a-iv, b-i, c-iii, d-ii** — option **(3)**.
**Kalidasa** → **Abhijnanashakuntalam and Meghadutam**; **Harisena** → **Prayaga Prashasti**.
**Banabhatta** → **Harshacharita and Kadambari**; **Vishakhadatta** → **Devi-Chandraguptam**.
xa: **Kadambari** is among the world's **earliest Sanskrit novels**, completed by Bana's son **Bhushanabhatta**.
Kalidasa was a court poet of **Chandragupta II**; Harisena of **Samudragupta**.
⚠ **Harsha** wrote Ratnavali, Priyadarshika, Nagananda; **Bana** wrote Harshacharita, Kadambari.
**Dandin** — **Dashakumaracharita**.

67.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Dandin wrote Dashakumaracharita.
II. Bharavi wrote Kiratarjuniyam.
III. Sudraka wrote Mrichchhakatikam.
IV. Rajasekhara wrote Mattavilasa Prahasana.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
67.x: I, II and III are correct: Dandin wrote Dashakumaracharita, Bharavi Kiratarjuniyam and Sudraka Mrichchhakatikam. IV is false because Mattavilasa Prahasana is by the Pallava king Mahendravarman I.
67.tq: Check each statement separately.
n: Dandin wrote Dashakumaracharita. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 113-115]
Bharavi wrote Kiratarjuniyam. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 113-115]
Sudraka wrote Mrichchhakatikam. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 113-115]
Mahendravarman I wrote Mattavilasa Prahasana. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 113-115]
xs: Statements **I, II and III** are correct — option **(3)**.
**Dandin** → **Dashakumaracharita**; **Bharavi** → **Kiratarjuniyam**; **Sudraka** → **Mrichchhakatikam**.
IV is wrong: **Mattavilasa Prahasana** is by the Pallava **Mahendravarman I**; **Rajasekhara** wrote **Karpuramanjari**, **Kavyamimamsa**, **Viddhasalabhanjika**.
xa: Rajasekhara was court scholar of the **Gurjara-Pratiharas**.
**Vishakhadatta** — **Devi-Chandraguptam**.
**Bhavabhuti** — **Uttararamacharitam**, under **Yashovarman**.
**Hastimalla** — **Kannada** poet under the **Hoysalas**.

67.s:
Consider the following statements about Rajasekhara:
I. He was a court scholar of the Gurjara-Pratiharas.
II. He was associated with Mahendrapala-I and Mahipala-I.
III. He wrote Kavyamimamsa.
IV. He wrote Tarikh-i-Subuktigin.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
67.x: I, II and III are correct: Rajasekhara was a court scholar of the Gurjara-Pratiharas Mahendrapala I and Mahipala I and wrote Kavyamimamsa. IV is false because Tarikh-i-Subuktigin is by Baihaqi.
67.tq: Check each statement separately.
n: Rajasekhara was a court scholar. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 113-115]
Rajasekhara was associated with the Gurjara-Pratihara rulers. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 113-115]
Rajasekhara was associated with Mahendrapala-I. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 113-115]
Rajasekhara was associated with Mahipala-I. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 113-115]
Rajasekhara wrote Kavyamimamsa. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 113-115]
Baihaqi wrote Tarikh-i-Subuktigin. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 113-115]
xs: Statements **I, II and III** are correct — option **(2)**.
I and II: **Rajasekhara** was a **court scholar** of the **Gurjara-Pratiharas** **Mahendrapala-I** and **Mahipala-I**.
III: he wrote **Kavyamimamsa** (also **Karpuramanjari**, **Viddhasalabhanjika**).
IV is wrong: **Tarikh-i-Subuktigin** is not among Rajasekhara's works.
xa: **Bhavabhuti** and **Vakpatiraja** served **Yashovarman** of Kannauj.
**Padmagupta** was linked with the **Paramaras**.
**Kshemeshvara** — **11th-century** Sanskrit poet of **Kashmir**.

67.s:

b. Rajasekhara

67.x: Kalidasa wrote Kumarasambhavam, Rajasekhara Viddhasalabhanjika, Bhavabhuti Mahaviracharitam and Vishakhadatta Mudrarakshasa, giving a-iv, b-iii, c-i, d-ii.
67.tq: Pair each dramatist with his signature play.
n: Kalidasa wrote Kumarasambhavam. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 113-115]
Kalidasa wrote Malavikagnimitram. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 113-115]
Rajasekhara wrote Viddhasalabhanjika. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 113-115]
Bhavabhuti wrote Mahaviracharitam. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 113-115]

**Kalidasa** → **Kumarasambhavam**; **Rajasekhara** → **Viddhasalabhanjika**.
**Bhavabhuti** → **Mahaviracharitam**; **Vishakhadatta** → **Mudrarakshasa**.
xa: Bhavabhuti also wrote **Malatimadhava** and **Uttararamacharitam**.
Rajasekhara also wrote **Karpuramanjari** and **Kavyamimamsa**.

Kalidasa also wrote **Raghuvansham** and **Malavikagnimitram**.

68.s: After the reign of Harsha, control of Kannauj was coveted mainly because it represented which of the following?
o: Exclusive control over the Deccan trade routes
The permanent seat of the Rashtrakuta capital
The religious authority of the Pala monasteries
The title of Samrat of North India and imperial sovereignty
68.x: After Harsha, Kannauj became a symbol of imperial sovereignty and was associated with the title of Samrat of North India.
68.tq: Connect the political symbolism of a city with the motive for competing over it.
xs: After Harsha, Kannauj meant **imperial sovereignty** and the title of **Samrat of North India** — option **(4)** is correct.
**Manyakheta**, not Kannauj, was the Rashtrakuta capital — so option 2 is wrong.
xa: Economic pull: **Gangetic-Doab agrarian wealth** and Arabian Sea trade via **Gujarat**.
Kannauj's primacy began under **Harsha** (Hiuen Tsang: Pataliputra lost its place).
Old names: **Mahodaya**, **Kanyakubja**.

68.s:
Which economic factors increased the importance of Kannauj in the tripartite struggle?
1. The agrarian wealth of the Gangetic Doab
2. Access to Arabian Sea trade through Gujarat
3. The possibility of bypassing the Arab-held Indus delta
4. Direct control over the Kaveri delta
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
68.x: Kannauj commanded the agrarian wealth of the Gangetic Doab and access to Arabian Sea trade through Gujarat, thereby bypassing the Arab-held Indus delta. The Kaveri delta was not a factor in Kannauj's importance.
68.tq: Separate the economic features of the Gangetic region from a geographically distant distractor.
xs: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 1, 2 and 3 only**.
Statement 1: **Gangetic-Doab agrarian wealth** — correct.
Statements 2 and 3: access to **Arabian Sea trade via Gujarat**, bypassing the **Arab-held Indus delta** — correct.
Statement 4: the **Kaveri delta** is not among the factors in the notes — wrong.
xa: Political value: the title of **Samrat** of North India.
The struggle lasted nearly **two centuries**, **8th-10th c.**
Outcome: shift of power to **regional kingdoms**.

68.s:
Consider the following statements about the powers in the tripartite struggle for Kannauj:
1. The Gurjara-Pratiharas were based in Rajasthan-Gujarat and Avanti, and later at Kannauj.
2. The Rashtrakuta capital was Manyakheta (Malkhed) in the Deccan.
3. Mihira Bhoja was a Pala ruler of Gauda.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
68.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: Mihira Bhoja was a Gurjara-Pratihara ruler who held Kannauj in the later phase; the Pala rulers were Dharmapala, Devapala and Mahipala I. So A is incomplete and C and D include statement 3.
68.tq: Bhoja = Pratihara; Pala names end in -pala.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: **Gurjara-Pratiharas** = Rajasthan-Gujarat / **Avanti**, later Kannauj — correct.
Statement 2: Rashtrakuta capital = **Manyakheta (Malkhed)** — correct.
Statement 3: **Mihira Bhoja** was a **Pratihara**; the Palas were **Dharmapala, Devapala, Mahipala I** — wrong.
xa: Pala base: **Gauda (Bengal)** and **Magadha (Bihar)**.
Rashtrakuta rulers: **Dhruva, Govinda III**, Amoghavarsha, **Indra III**.
Pratihara rulers: **Vatsaraja, Nagabhata II, Mihira Bhoja**, Mahendrapala I.

68.s:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
A. Rise of Pala ruler Gopala
B. Reign of Pallava Mahendravarman I
C. Reign of Pratihara Bhoja
D. Reign of Chola Parantaka I
68.x: The correct sequence is Pallava Mahendravarman I, Pala Gopala, Pratihara Bhoja and Chola Parantaka I.
68.tq: Place the early Pallava ruler first and the later Chola ruler last before ordering the middle items.
xs: Order: **Mahendravarman I → Gopala → Bhoja → Parantaka I** — option **(1) B, A, C, D** (UPSC 2020).
Pallava **Mahendravarman I** comes first, then Pala **Gopala**.
Pratihara **Bhoja** follows, then Chola **Parantaka I**.
xa: **Mihira Bhoja** held Kannauj with **Mahendrapala I** in the late **9th c.**
The **Gwalior prashasti** is of **Mihira Bhoja**.
**Cholas** and **Pallavas** were not part of the tripartite struggle.

68.s: Which of the following sets contains only dynasties listed as non-participants in the struggle for Kannauj?
68.x: Cholas, Pallavas and Kalyani Chalukyas were listed among the dynasties that did not participate. Palas, Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas were the contending powers.
68.tq: Check every member of the set rather than relying on one familiar dynasty.
xs: **Cholas, Pallavas and Kalyani Chalukyas** are all non-participants — option **(2)** is correct.
Every other set includes a contender — **Palas**, **Pratiharas** or **Rashtrakutas**.
Non-participants also include **Chauhans** and **Gahadavalas**.
xa: Cholas as non-participant: **UPPSC 2015**.
The **Chauhans** and **Chandelas** rose after the struggle exhausted all three.
The struggle lasted nearly **two centuries**.

68.s: The tripartite struggle for Kannauj began when which of the following rulers clashed with Dharmapala and Dhruva?
68.x: The struggle began when Gurjara-Pratihara ruler Vatsaraja, around 780–800 CE, clashed with Dharmapala and Rashtrakuta ruler Dhruva.
68.tq: Link the opening phase to the ruler who initiated the clash.
xs: **Vatsaraja** (c. **780-800 CE**) began the struggle by clashing with **Dharmapala** and **Dhruva** — option **(3)** is correct (UPSC).
**Nagabhata II** and **Mihira Bhoja** belong to later phases; **Indra III** sacked Kannauj c. **916 CE**.
xa: Phase I: Vatsaraja takes Kannauj, defeats Dharmapala; **Dhruva** defeats both and withdraws.
Dhruva ruled **780-793 CE**.
⚠ Dhruva's opponent was **Vatsaraja**, not Nagabhata II.

68.s:
Arrange the following events of the struggle for Kannauj in the correct chronological order:
A. Dharmapala installs Chakrayudha at Kannauj
B. Vatsaraja takes Kannauj
C. Nagabhata II ousts Chakrayudha
D. Mihira Bhoja and Mahendrapala I hold Kannauj for decades
68.x: The sequence was Vatsaraja's occupation, Dharmapala's installation of Chakrayudha, Nagabhata II's ousting of Chakrayudha, and the later Pratihara control under Mihira Bhoja and Mahendrapala I.
68.tq: Fix the first event in the late eighth century and then follow the succession of installed and removed rulers.
xs: Order: **Vatsaraja → Chakrayudha installed → Nagabhata II ousts him → Bhoja and Mahendrapala I** — option **(1) B, A, C, D**.
Phase I (late **8th c.**): **Vatsaraja** takes Kannauj.
Phase II (early **9th c.**): **Dharmapala** installs **Chakrayudha**; Phase III: **Nagabhata II** ousts him.
Phase IV (late **9th c.**): **Mihira Bhoja** and **Mahendrapala I** hold Kannauj for decades.
xa: Under Bhoja the empire ran from the **Himalayas to the Narmada**.
**Govinda III** defeated both Nagabhata II and Dharmapala, then retreated.
Dharmapala held a **grand durbar** at Kannauj.

68.s: During the second phase of the struggle for Kannauj, Dharmapala removed which ruler and installed Chakrayudha in his place?
68.x: Dharmapala removed the Pratihara nominee Indrayudha and installed Chakrayudha as his puppet ruler at Kannauj.
68.tq: Test the installed–removed ruler pair directly.
xs: Dharmapala removed **Indrayudha**, the Pratihara nominee — option **(2)** is correct.
He installed his puppet **Chakrayudha** and held a **grand durbar** at Kannauj.
xa: ⚠ **Indrayudha** = removed; **Chakrayudha** = installed.
The **Khalimpur plates** say Chakrayudha was installed with the **approval of northern kings**.
**Nagabhata II** later ousted Chakrayudha.

68.s:
With reference to the northern campaigns of the Rashtrakutas, consider the following statements:
1. Dhruva defeated both Vatsaraja and Dharmapala.
2. Dhruva retained the northern territories permanently after his victories.
3. Dhruva returned to the south after taking booty.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
68.x: Dhruva defeated Vatsaraja and Dharmapala, took booty and returned south. His campaign did not result in permanent retention of northern territory.
68.tq: Separate military success and booty from the false claim of permanent territorial control.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1: **Dhruva** defeated **Vatsaraja and Dharmapala** — correct.
Statement 2: he **withdrew** — the raids gave **loot and prestige, not lasting territory** — wrong.
Statement 3: he took **booty** and **returned south** — correct.
xa: APPSC GS 2023: Dhruva "**jumped into the fight**".
Dhruva ruled **780-793 CE**.
⚠ The **Sanjan plates** describe **Govinda III**, not Dhruva.

68.s: Indra III's campaign against Kannauj around 916 CE was directed against which Pratihara ruler?
68.x: Rashtrakuta ruler Indra III sacked Kannauj around 916 CE after defeating Pratihara ruler Mahipala I.
68.tq: Pair the date of the campaign with the ruler who was defeated.
xs: **Indra III** sacked Kannauj c. **916 CE** after defeating Pratihara **Mahipala I** — option **(3)** is correct.
**Nagabhata II** was beaten by **Govinda III**; **Mihira Bhoja** and **Mahendrapala I** held Kannauj earlier.
xa: After Indra III's raid the **Pratiharas declined**.
New Rajput states followed: **Chandelas**, **Chauhans**.
Rashtrakuta capital: **Manyakheta (Malkhed)**.

68.s: Which one of the following pairs of a Rashtrakuta ruler and the Pratihara ruler he defeated in the north is correctly matched?
68.x: Govinda III defeated Nagabhata II. Dhruva's Pratihara opponent was Vatsaraja, not Nagabhata II or Nagabhata I (a common trap). Indra III defeated Mahipala I c. 916 CE, not Vatsaraja.
68.tq: Dhruva vs Vatsaraja; Govinda III vs Nagabhata II; Indra III vs Mahipala I.
xs: **Govinda III — Nagabhata II** is correct — option **(2)**.
⚠ **Dhruva**'s opponent was **Vatsaraja**, not Nagabhata II or Nagabhata I — a UPSC-notes trap.
**Indra III** defeated **Mahipala I**, not Vatsaraja.
xa: Govinda III also defeated **Dharmapala**, then retreated after a **Himalayan** campaign.
The **Sanjan plates** describe Govinda III's campaign.
Indra III sacked Kannauj c. **916 CE**.

68.s: The Sanjan plates, dated to 871 CE and associated with Amoghavarsha I, provide information about which event?
o: Dharmapala's installation of Chakrayudha at Kannauj
68.x: The Sanjan plates, issued during the reign of Rashtrakuta ruler Amoghavarsha I in 871 CE, describe Govinda III's Himalayan campaign.
68.tq: Combine the source, date and dynasty clues before identifying the event.
xs: The Sanjan plates describe **Govinda III's Himalayan campaign** — option **(2)** is correct.
They are **Rashtrakuta** plates of **Amoghavarsha I** (**871 CE**).
**Chakrayudha's installation** is in the **Khalimpur plates**; **Indra III's sack** came c. **916 CE**.
xa: Quote: his horses "drank the icy waters of **Himalayan** streams, his elephants tasted the **Ganga**".
⚠ **Sanjan** = Rashtrakuta; **Gwalior** = Pratihara; **Khalimpur** = Pala.

68.s: Which source records the victories of Nagabhata II over Chakrayudha and Dharmapala?
68.x: The Gwalior prashasti of Mihira Bhoja records Nagabhata II's victories over Chakrayudha and Dharmapala.
68.tq: Use the source–ruler–victory association rather than the dynasty name alone.
xs: The **Gwalior prashasti** records **Nagabhata II**'s victories over **Chakrayudha** and **Dharmapala** — option **(4)** is correct.
It is a **Pratihara** record of **Mihira Bhoja**.
**Sanjan plates** = Govinda III's campaign; **Khalimpur plates** = Chakrayudha's installation.
xa: ⚠ **Sanjan** = Rashtrakuta; **Gwalior** = Pratihara; **Khalimpur** = Pala.
Nagabhata II was in turn defeated by **Govinda III**.

68.s: Which statement best expresses the long-term outcome of the tripartite struggle for Kannauj?
o: The Palas retained Kannauj continuously from the eighth to the tenth century.
The Cholas converted Kannauj into their northern capital.
The Pratiharas finally held Kannauj, but no power retained it permanently for a long period.
The Rashtrakutas permanently ruled Kannauj for nearly two centuries.
68.x: Kannauj was finally held by the Pratiharas under Bhoja and Mahendrapala I, but no single power permanently retained it for a long period.
68.tq: Distinguish final dominance from permanent and uninterrupted control.
xs: The **Pratiharas** finally held Kannauj, but **no power held it permanently** for long — option **(3)** is correct.
Final holders: **Bhoja** and **Mahendrapala I**.
The **Cholas** were not part of the struggle; the **Rashtrakutas** only raided.
xa: Duration: nearly **two centuries**, **8th-10th c.**
Pratihara decline after **Indra III**'s raid → **Chandelas**, **Chauhans**.
All three powers were **exhausted**.

68.s: What was one important consequence of the exhaustion of all three powers involved in the struggle for Kannauj?
o: The permanent Rashtrakuta annexation of Bengal
The abolition of regional kingdoms in northern India
The immediate restoration of Harsha's empire
The emergence of new Rajput states such as the Chandelas and Chauhans
68.x: The exhaustion of the Palas, Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas, along with Pratihara decline after Indra III's raid, opened the way for new Rajput states such as the Chandelas and Chauhans.
68.tq: Trace the political consequence of weakening major powers to the rise of regional states.
xs: Exhaustion of all three led to new Rajput states — **Chandelas** and **Chauhans** — option **(4)** is correct.
The **Pratiharas** declined after **Indra III**'s raid.
xa: The overall significance: a shift of power to **regional kingdoms**.
Indra III defeated Pratihara **Mahipala I** c. **916 CE**.
**Chauhans** were not a party to the struggle itself.

68.s: The struggle for Kannauj is historically significant because it illustrates which broader development in early medieval India?
o: The disappearance of dynastic competition in northern India
The complete centralisation of power under one pan-Indian emperor
The shift of political power towards regional kingdoms
The replacement of agriculture by maritime trade as the main economic base
68.x: The struggle demonstrates the shift of power to regional kingdoms during early medieval India.
68.tq: Identify the broad historical interpretation supported by the political pattern.
xs: The struggle shows the **shift of power to regional kingdoms** — option **(3)** is correct.
No power held Kannauj permanently, and all three ended **exhausted**.
xa: New Rajput states followed: **Chandelas**, **Chauhans**.
Kannauj stood for the title of **Samrat** of North India.
AP angle: Rashtrakuta pressure on the **Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi** ran in parallel.

68.s: Which Rashtrakuta ruler's pressure on the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi ran parallel to the northern campaigns, according to the political context of the period?
68.x: Rashtrakuta ruler Dhruva defeated Vishnuvardhana IV of the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi, showing the parallel Deccan dimension of Rashtrakuta expansion.
68.tq: Link the ruler with the correctly identified parallel campaign and opponent.
xs: **Dhruva** defeated **Vishnuvardhana IV** of the **Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi** — option **(2)** is correct.
That Deccan pressure ran **in parallel** with the northern campaigns.
xa: Dhruva (**780-793 CE**) also defeated **Vatsaraja** and **Dharmapala** in the north.
**Govinda III** led the Himalayan campaign; **Indra III** sacked Kannauj.
**Amoghavarsha I** issued the **Sanjan plates** (**871 CE**).

68.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I
(a) Khalimpur Inscription
(b) Matsya Nyaya
(c) Dharmapala
(d) Param Saugat
List-II
(i) Selection of Gopala to end Matsya Nyaya
(ii) Law of the Jungle
(iii) Title meaning a devout Buddhist
(iv) Founder of the Vikramashila Mahavihara
68.x: The Khalimpur inscription records Gopala's selection, Matsya Nyaya means the law of the jungle, Dharmapala founded the Vikramashila Mahavihara, and Param Saugat, his title, marks a devout Buddhist, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iv, d-iii.
68.tq: Match the clear pairs, then compare the last two.
n: The Khalimpur Inscription is associated with Dharmapala. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-17]
The Khalimpur Inscription mentions the selection or election of Gopala. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-17]
Matsya Nyaya means the Law of the Jungle. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-17]
Dharmapala held the title Param Saugat. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-17]
The title Param Saugat indicates Buddhist affiliation. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-17]
The Khalimpur Inscription links Dharmapala with Gopala and Matsya Nyaya. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-17]
xs: The correct match is **a-i, b-ii, c-iv, d-iii** — option **(2)**.
**Khalimpur Inscription** → **selection of Gopala** to end **Matsya Nyaya**; **Matsya Nyaya** → **Law of the Jungle**.
**Dharmapala** → founder of **Vikramashila**; **Param Saugat** → his title showing **Buddhist affiliation**.
xa: The Khalimpur plates also say **Chakrayudha** was installed at **Kannauj** with the approval of northern kings.
⚠ **Sanjan** = Rashtrakuta; **Gwalior** = Pratihara; **Khalimpur** = Pala.
Dharmapala removed Pratihara nominee **Indrayudha** and installed puppet **Chakrayudha**.
**Dhruva** defeated both **Vatsaraja and Dharmapala**.

68.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I
(a) Govinda III
(b) Sanjan and Radhanpur plates
(c) Nagabhata II
(d) Khalimpur Inscription
List-II
(i) Rashtrakuta king
(ii) Record Govinda III's northern victories
(iii) Gurjara-Pratihara king defeated by Govinda III
(iv) Records the election of Gopala
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
68.x: Govinda III was a Rashtrakuta king, his Sanjan and Radhanpur plates record his northern victories, Nagabhata II was the Gurjara-Pratihara king he defeated, and the Khalimpur inscription of Dharmapala records Gopala's election, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
68.tq: Recall the dynasty and records of Govinda III.
n: The Sanjan Copper Plates are associated with Govinda III. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-17]
The Radhanpur Copper Plates are associated with Govinda III. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-17]
Govinda III belonged to the Rashtrakuta dynasty. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-17]
Govinda III defeated the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-17]
xs: The correct match is **a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv** — option **(3)**.
**Govinda III** → **Rashtrakuta** king; **Sanjan and Radhanpur plates** → his victory over **Nagabhata II**.
**Nagabhata II** → **Gurjara-Pratihara** king defeated by Govinda III; **Khalimpur Inscription** → election of **Gopala**.
xa: Sanjan plates: Govinda III's horses "drank the icy waters of Himalayan streams".
⚠ Dhruva's opponent was **Vatsaraja**; Govinda III's was **Nagabhata II**.
**Indra III** sacked **Kannauj** c. **916 CE**.
The **Gwalior prashasti** records Nagabhata II's victories over **Chakrayudha** and **Dharmapala**.

68.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: After Harsha, Kannauj became a centre of attraction for competing powers.
The Tripartite Struggle aimed at controlling Ujjain.
The Tripartite Struggle involved the Palas, Gurjara-Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas.
Kannauj was also known as Mahodaya and Mahodayashri.
68.x: Option B is incorrect: the Tripartite Struggle was fought for control of Kannauj, not Ujjain. Kannauj became the prize after Harsha, was called Mahodaya or Mahodayashri, and the Palas, Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas fought over it.
68.tq: Recall the object of the Tripartite Struggle.
n: After Harsha, Kannauj became a centre of attraction for competing powers. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #144 · pp 250-252]
Kannauj was also known as Mahodaya. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #144 · pp 250-252]
Kannauj was also known as Mahodayashri. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #144 · pp 250-252]
The objective of the Tripartite Struggle was control of Kannauj. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #144 · pp 250-252]
The Pala dynasty participated in the Tripartite Struggle. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #144 · pp 250-252]
The Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty participated in the Tripartite Struggle. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #144 · pp 250-252]
The Rashtrakuta dynasty participated in the Tripartite Struggle. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #144 · pp 250-252]
xs: The incorrect statement is that the struggle aimed at **controlling Ujjain** — option **(2)**.
The Tripartite Struggle was for **control of Kannauj** in the **8th–9th century CE**.

The others are correct: Kannauj became a **centre of attraction** after **Harsha**; the **Pala, Gurjara-Pratihara and Rashtrakuta** dynasties fought; Kannauj was called **Mahodaya** and **Mahodayashri**.
xa: Kannauj was a symbol of imperial sovereignty — title of **Samrat** of North India.
It gave **Gangetic-Doab** wealth and access to Arabian Sea trade via **Gujarat**.
Not part of it: **Cholas** (UPPSC 2015), Pallavas, Chauhans.
Winner: the **Pratiharas** (**Bhoja**, **Mahendrapala I**).

69.s: Gopala's accession to power is best described as follows:
o: He was elected by notables to end a period of anarchy known as matsyanyaya.
He inherited Bengal from his father, the last Gupta ruler of Magadha.
He seized power after defeating the Sena ruler of Bengal.
He was appointed by Dharmapala after the conquest of Kannauj.
69.x: Gopala was elected by regional notables to bring an end to matsyanyaya, a period of anarchy, around the middle of the eighth century.
69.tq: Identify the accession mechanism rather than the dynasty or military achievement.
xs: **Gopala** was **elected by notables** to end **matsyanyaya** (anarchy) — option **(1)** is correct (UPSC).
This was c. mid-**8th c.**; the **Khalimpur plate** of **Dharmapala** records it.
Gopala **displaced** the later Guptas of Magadha — he did not inherit from them; the **Senas** came **after** the Palas.
xa: UPPSC 2021: kings chosen by the people = **Gopala** and **Nandivarman II Pallavamalla**.
Gopala built **Odantapuri** (APPSC GS 2018).
He also displaced the **Khadgas** of east Bengal.

69.s:
Which of the following developments is associated with Gopala?
1. Displacement of the later Guptas of Magadha.
2. Displacement of the Khadgas of eastern Bengal.
3. Construction of Odantapuri.
Select the correct answer.
69.x: Gopala displaced the later Guptas in Magadha and the Khadgas in eastern Bengal, and he is associated with the construction of Odantapuri.
69.tq: Check whether the ruler's political and cultural achievements are all included.
xs: All three are Gopala's — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
He displaced the **later Guptas of Magadha** and the **Khadgas** of east Bengal.
He built **Odantapuri** (APPSC GS 2018).
xa: Odantapuri is at **Bihar Sharif**, Nalanda district; about **12,000** monks.
Odantapuri was a **model for Tibetan monasteries**.
Gopala was **elected** c. mid-**8th c.**

69.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Dharmapala installed Chakrayudha at Kannauj.
2. Dharmapala was defeated by Dhruva and by Nagabhata II near Monghyr.
3. Dharmapala founded Vikramashila.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
69.x: All three are correct: Dharmapala (c. 770-810) installed the puppet Chakrayudha at Kannauj, was defeated by Dhruva and by Nagabhata II near Monghyr, and founded Vikramashila. Hence D.
69.tq: Combine military reverses, political intervention and institutional patronage in one ruler profile.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: **Dharmapala** installed **Chakrayudha** at Kannauj — correct.
Statement 2: he was beaten by **Dhruva** and by **Nagabhata II** near **Monghyr** — correct.
Statement 3: he founded **Vikramashila** (BPSC 2022) — correct.
xa: Dharmapala ruled c. **770-810**.
**Somapura** (Paharpur, Bangladesh) is also credited to Dharmapala.
Buddhist texts were compiled at **Nalanda** under Dharmapala; his **seal** was found there.

69.s: Which Pala ruler is associated with the revival of Pala power and was defeated by Rajendra Chola?
69.x: Mahipala I, whose reign is placed around c. 977–1027, revived Pala power and was defeated by Rajendra Chola.
69.tq: Use the paired achievement to distinguish one ruler from the other Palas.
xs: **Mahipala I** (c. **977-1027**) revived Pala power and was defeated by **Rajendra Chola** — option **(4)** is correct.
**Gopala** was the elected founder; **Devapala** made the Nalanda grant; **Ramapala** was the last strong ruler.
xa: **Ramapala** (c. **1072-1126**): Kaivarta revolt, **Jagaddala**.
**Dharmapala** (c. **770-810**) founded **Vikramashila**.
The **Senas** succeeded the Palas in Bengal.

69.s:
Which of the following correctly describes Ramapala?
1. He was the last strong Pala ruler.
2. His reign witnessed the Kaivarta revolt.
3. He extended influence over Kamarupa and Kalinga.
4. He is associated with Jagaddala.
Select the correct answer.
69.x: Ramapala, c. 1072–1126, is described as the last strong Pala ruler. His reign is associated with the Kaivarta revolt, campaigns involving Kamarupa and Kalinga, and Jagaddala.
69.tq: Test the complete achievement profile of a ruler through a coded combination.
xs: All four statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
**Ramapala** (c. **1072-1126**) was the **last strong** Pala ruler, facing the **Kaivarta revolt**.
He extended influence over **Kamarupa** and **Kalinga** and founded **Jagaddala**.
xa: **Ramacharita** by **Sandhyakar Nandi** is about Ramapala and the Kaivarta revolt.
**Vikramashila** reached its **zenith under Ramapala**.
Jagaddala (Varendra, Bangladesh) **translated books into Tibetan**.

69.s: Which one of the following statements about Lakshmanasena is correct?
o: He founded Vikramashila and was defeated by Dhruva.
He revived Pala power and was defeated by Rajendra Chola.
He was the last Sena ruler, whose court poet was Jayadeva, and he was ousted by Bakhtiyar Khilji.
He founded Somapura and granted five villages to Balaputradeva.
69.x: Lakshmanasena was the last Sena ruler; Jayadeva was associated with his court, and Lakshmanasena was ousted by Bakhtiyar Khilji.
69.tq: Use the ruler–court poet–political fate combination to identify the correct option.
xs: **Lakshmanasena** was the **last Sena** ruler, patron of **Jayadeva**, ousted by **Bakhtiyar Khilji** — option **(3)** is correct.
**Vikramashila** / defeat by Dhruva = **Dharmapala**; defeat by Rajendra Chola = **Mahipala I**.
The **five villages** grant was by **Devapala**.
xa: Sena founders: **Samantasena** / **Vijayasena**, then **Ballalasena**.
Bakhtiyar Khilji also destroyed Pala-era centres c. **1193-1200**.

69.s: Which of the following pairs of rulers are noted for having been chosen by the people (or notables) rather than by inheritance?
69.x: Gopala was elected by notables to end matsyanyaya, and Nandivarman II Pallavamalla was also chosen (UPPSC 2021). Dharmapala and Devapala succeeded by inheritance, and Narasimhavarman I and Mahendravarman I were hereditary Pallava kings.
69.tq: Elected kings: Gopala (Pala) and Nandivarman II (Pallava).
xs: **Gopala** and **Nandivarman II Pallavamalla** were chosen by the people — option **(1)** is correct (UPPSC 2021).
Gopala was **elected by notables** to end **matsyanyaya**.
**Dharmapala** and **Devapala** were later Pala kings in succession, not elected.
xa: Gopala's election is recorded in the **Khalimpur plate** of Dharmapala.
Gopala built **Odantapuri**.

69.s: Balaputradeva, who established a monastery at Nalanda, was the ruler of:
69.x: Balaputradeva was a Shailendra ruler of Suvarnadvipa or Suvarnabhumi. His envoy requested Devapala to grant five villages for maintaining the monastery at Nalanda.
69.tq: Match the foreign ruler with his geographical and dynastic identity.
xs: **Balaputradeva** was the **Shailendra** ruler of **Suvarnadvipa/Suvarnabhumi** — option **(2)** is correct.
He built a **monastery at Nalanda**.
xa: At his envoy's request **Devapala granted five villages** (BPSC 2018; **Nalanda copper plate**).
**Pala-style bronzes** in Southeast Asia show maritime cultural exchange (UPSC).
**Kamarupa** and **Kalinga** came under Pala influence under **Ramapala**.

69.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Acharya)        List-II (Association)
a. Shilabhadra          i. Jagaddala
b. Shantarakshita       ii. Nalanda, head in Harsha's time
c. Atisha Dipankara     iii. Nalanda; founded Samye monastery
   Shrijnana
d. Sakya Sri Bhadra     iv. Vikramashila; revived Buddhism in Tibet

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
69.x: Shilabhadra was associated with Nalanda in Harsha's time; Shantarakshita went to Tibet and founded Samye; Atisha was linked with Vikramashila; and Sakya Sri Bhadra was associated with Jagaddala.
69.tq: Start with the distinctive acharya–institution pair and complete the matching code.
xs: Correct code: **a–ii, b–iii, c–iv, d–i** — option **(1)**.
**Shilabhadra** — Nalanda head in Harsha's time; **Shantarakshita** — Nalanda, founded **Samye**.
**Atisha Dipankara Shrijnana** — **Vikramashila**, revived Buddhism in Tibet; **Sakya Sri Bhadra** — **Jagaddala**.
xa: Sakya Sri Bhadra took **Tantric Buddhism** to Tibet.
⚠ Trap (BPSC 2025): **Kautilya** was not a Nalanda acharya.
Vikramashila trained monks for **Tibet**.

69.s: Which one of the following was NOT an acharya associated with the Pala-era Buddhist mahaviharas?
69.x: Kautilya was not a Nalanda acharya (BPSC 2025 trap). Shilabhadra headed Nalanda in Harsha's time, Shantarakshita of Nalanda founded Samye monastery in Tibet, and Atisha of Vikramashila revived Buddhism in Tibet.
69.tq: Kautilya is the odd one out among Nalanda acharyas.
xs: **Kautilya** was not a Nalanda acharya — option **(2)** is the answer (BPSC 2025 trap).
**Shilabhadra** and **Shantarakshita** were Nalanda acharyas; **Atisha** was of **Vikramashila**.
xa: **Sakya Sri Bhadra** belonged to **Jagaddala**.
Andhra's **Dharmakirti** taught at Nalanda.
Nalanda was founded by **Kumaragupta I** (Gupta).

69.s: At the request of the envoy of the Shailendra ruler Balaputradeva, which Pala king granted five villages for the monastery at Nalanda?
69.x: Devapala granted five villages, as recorded in the Nalanda copper plate (BPSC 2018). Gopala was the elected founder, Dharmapala founded Vikramashila, and Mahipala I revived Pala power later.
69.tq: Balaputradeva + five villages = Devapala (Nalanda copper plate).
xs: **Devapala** granted **five villages** at Balaputradeva's envoy's request — option **(3)** is correct (BPSC 2018).
The grant is recorded in the **Nalanda copper plate**.
**Gopala** = elected founder; **Dharmapala** = Vikramashila; **Mahipala I** = later revival.
xa: **Balaputradeva** was a **Shailendra** ruler of **Suvarnadvipa/Suvarnabhumi**.
**Pala-style bronzes** in SE Asia show maritime exchange.

69.s:
Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?

Mahavihara — Present location
69.x: Somapura Mahavihara is located at Paharpur in Naogaon district of present-day Bangladesh. Vikramashila was at Antichak in Bhagalpur, Jagaddala was in Varendra, and Odantapuri was at Bihar Sharif.
69.tq: Start from the sure location and eliminate the swapped-place pairs.
xs: **Somapura — Paharpur, Naogaon** is correct — option **(2)**.
**Vikramashila** is at **Antichak, Bhagalpur**; **Jagaddala** is in **Varendra**, Naogaon.
**Odantapuri** is at **Bihar Sharif**, Nalanda district.
xa: Somapura (Dharmapala) is in **Bangladesh**; famed for grand-scale **terracotta** ornamentation.
Jagaddala was founded by **Ramapala**.
The five = the **Panchamahavihara** of Tibetan sources.

69.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the major Mahaviharas of the Pala period:
1. The five Mahaviharas are collectively called the Panchamahavihara in Tibetan sources.
2. Vikramashila was founded by Gopala.
3. Both Vikramashila and Somapura were founded by Dharmapala.
4. Nalanda was founded by the Gupta ruler Kumaragupta I.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
69.x: Statement 1 is correct: Tibetan sources call the five the Panchamahavihara. Statement 2 is wrong: Vikramashila was founded by Dharmapala, not Gopala (Gopala built Odantapuri). Statement 3 is correct: Dharmapala founded both Vikramashila and Somapura. Statement 4 is correct: Nalanda was founded by Kumaragupta I; the other four were Pala foundations. Hence options A, C and D, which include statement 2 or omit 1/4, are wrong.
69.tq: Gopala-Odantapuri, Dharmapala-Vikramashila and Somapura, Ramapala-Jagaddala, Kumaragupta I-Nalanda.
xs: Statements 1, 3 and 4 are correct — option **(2) 1, 3 and 4 only**.
Statement 1: Tibetan sources call the five the **Panchamahavihara** — correct.
Statement 2: **Vikramashila** was founded by **Dharmapala**, not Gopala (**Odantapuri**) — wrong.
Statements 3 and 4: **Dharmapala** founded **Vikramashila** and **Somapura**; **Kumaragupta I** founded **Nalanda** — correct.
xa: ⚠ Trap (BPSC 2023): Vikramashila is in **Bhagalpur (not Banka)**.
**Jagaddala** was founded by **Ramapala**.

69.s:
Consider the following statements about Vikramashila Mahavihara:
1. It had 208 cells and a cruciform central stupa.
2. It was a centre of Tantric (Vajrayana) Buddhism and logic and trained monks for Tibet.
3. It reached its zenith under Dharmapala.
4. It is located in Banka district of Bihar.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
69.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: Dharmapala founded it, but it reached its zenith under Ramapala. Statement 4 is wrong: it is at Antichak in Bhagalpur district, not Banka (BPSC 2023 trap). So only A fits; B, C and D include a wrong statement.
69.tq: Founder vs zenith and Bhagalpur vs Banka are the classic traps for Vikramashila.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: **208 cells**, **cruciform central stupa** — correct; Statement 2: **Tantric/Vajrayana** and logic, trained monks for Tibet — correct.
Statement 3: founded by Dharmapala but at its **zenith under Ramapala** — wrong.
Statement 4: it is at **Antichak, Bhagalpur**, **not Banka** (BPSC 2023 trap) — wrong.
xa: It stood on the **Ganga**; its walls had **terracotta panels**.
**Atisha Dipankara Shrijnana** of Vikramashila revived Buddhism in Tibet.

69.s: The destruction of major Pala-period centres of learning by Bakhtiyar Khilji is generally placed approximately in which period?
69.x: The destruction is generally placed around 1193–1200. A separate chronological tradition gives 1194 specifically for the destruction of Nalanda, while Jagaddala was sacked in the early thirteenth century.
69.tq: Use the approximate range rather than confusing it with a later event.
xs: **Bakhtiyar Khilji** destroyed the centres c. **1193-1200** — option **(4)** is correct.
Some notes give **1194** for Nalanda.
xa: **Jagaddala** was sacked in the early **13th c.**
Bakhtiyar Khilji also ousted the last Sena, **Lakshmanasena**.
The Palas were the **last great royal patrons of Buddhism** in India.

69.s: Which one of the following is the odd one out in the context of early-medieval Pala centres of learning?
69.x: Taxila was an ancient centre in Gandhara and does not belong to the early-medieval Pala group. Nalanda, Vikramashila and Somapura were important centres under Pala patronage.
69.tq: Separate the chronologically different institution from the Pala-period group.
xs: **Taxila** is the odd one out — option **(4)** is the answer.
Taxila was an ancient **Gandhara** centre, not Pala-era.
**Vikramashila**, **Somapura** (Dharmapala) and **Nalanda** (Pala patronage) are Pala-era centres.
xa: **Valabhi** was the **Hinayana** centre of Harsha's time.
Panchamahavihara: **Odantapuri, Vikramashila, Somapura, Jagaddala, Nalanda**.

69.s: Which statement correctly distinguishes Valabhi from the Pala-period centres of learning?
o: Valabhi was the principal Vajrayana centre founded by Dharmapala.
Valabhi was a Hinayana centre associated with the time of Harsha.
Valabhi was the monastery built by Balaputradeva at Nalanda.
Valabhi was located in Varendra and founded by Ramapala.
69.x: Valabhi was known as a Hinayana centre during the time of Harsha. It was distinct from the major Pala-period Mahaviharas.
69.tq: Discriminate between similar Buddhist learning-centre classifications.
xs: **Valabhi** was a **Hinayana** centre of **Harsha**'s time — option **(2)** is correct.
The Vajrayana centre founded by Dharmapala is **Vikramashila**; Varendra / Ramapala = **Jagaddala**.
xa: **Taxila** = ancient **Gandhara** centre — also not Pala-era.
Nalanda was the **Mahayana** counterpart.
**Balaputradeva** built a monastery at **Nalanda**, not Valabhi.

69.s: Which one of the following statements regarding Pala sculpture and manuscripts is correct?
