n: William Jones founded the Asiatic Society in 1784. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 86-89]
Cunningham became Archaeological Surveyor in 1861. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 86-89]
Curzon appointed Marshall as Director-General in 1901. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 86-89]
The Ancient Monuments Preservation Act was enacted during the viceroyalty of Lord Curzon. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 86-89]
xs: The correct match is **a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**William Jones** founded the **Asiatic Society** in **1784**; **Cunningham** became **Archaeological Surveyor** in **1861**.
**Curzon** appointed **John Marshall** as **Director-General** in **1901**; Marshall took charge in **1902**.
The **Ancient Monuments Preservation Act** (**1904**) was enacted during the **viceroyalty** of **Lord Curzon**.
xa: The **Department of Archaeological Survey** was established in **1871**.
ASI motto: **"Pratnakirti Apavarini"**.
⚠ **1861** = ASI set up under **Canning** (founder **Alexander Cunningham**); **1904** = Monuments Act under **Curzon**.
If Canning is not among the options for "who created the ASI", **Curzon** (who revived and reorganised it) is the intended answer.

172.s:
Arrange the following developments in chronological order:
A. Ancient Monuments Preservation Act
B. Asiatic Society
C. Department of Archaeological Survey
D. Marshall takes charge
172.x: The Asiatic Society came in 1784, the Archaeological Survey department in 1871, Marshall took charge in 1902 and the Ancient Monuments Preservation Act followed in 1904, giving B, C, D, A.
172.tq: Arrange the developments by year.
n: William Jones founded the Asiatic Society in 1784. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 86-89]
The Department of Archaeological Survey was established in 1871. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 86-89]
Marshall took charge as Director-General in 1902. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 86-89]
The Ancient Monuments Preservation Act was enacted in 1904. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 86-89]
xs: The correct order is **B, C, D, A** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Asiatic Society** founded by **William Jones** in **1784** → **Department of Archaeological Survey** established in **1871**.
**Marshall** took charge as Director-General in **1902** → **Ancient Monuments Preservation Act** in **1904** under **Curzon**.
xa: **Cunningham** became **Archaeological Surveyor** in **1861**.
**Curzon** appointed **Marshall** as **Director-General** in **1901**.
The **AMASR Act 1958** protects monuments over **100 years** old.

172.s:
Consider the following statements about Lord Canning:
I. His tenure mentioned in this context was 1856–1862.
II. He was the last Governor-General under the Company.
III. He was the first Viceroy under the Crown.
IV. He was associated with the Allahabad High Court established in 1866.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
172.x: I, II and III are correct: Canning served from 1856 to 1862, as the last Governor-General under the Company and the first Viceroy under the Crown. IV is false because his term ended before the Allahabad High Court came in 1866.
172.tq: Compare Canning's tenure with the 1866 date.
n: Lord Canning was the Viceroy associated with the establishment of the High Courts. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #134 · pp 237-238]
The Allahabad High Court was established in 1866. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #134 · pp 237-238]
Lord Canning served from 1856 to 1862. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #134 · pp 237-238]
Lord Canning was the last Governor-General under the Company. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #134 · pp 237-238]
Lord Canning was the first Viceroy under the Crown. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #134 · pp 237-238]
xs: Statements **I, II and III** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
I is correct: **Lord Canning** served from **1856** to **1862**.
II and III are correct: he was the **last Governor-General** under the **Company** and the **first Viceroy** under the **Crown**.
IV is not supported: the notes link Canning with the **establishment of the High Courts** within his **1856-62** tenure, not a court of **1866**.
xa: Canning became Viceroy under the **GoI Act 1858**; he announced the **Queen's Proclamation** of **1858**.
His tenure saw the **Revolt of 1857**, the **Indian Councils Act 1861**, the **portfolio system** and **income tax**.
Universities at **Calcutta, Bombay, Madras** came in **1857** under Canning.
The **Madras High Court** came under the **Indian High Courts Act 1861** (est. **1862**).

172.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I
(a) Vernacular Press Act
(b) Repeal of the Vernacular Press Act
(c) First census attempt, 1872
(d) Queen's Proclamation, 1858
List-II
(i) Lord Ripon
(ii) Lord Lytton
(iii) Lord Mayo
(iv) Lord Canning
172.x: Lytton passed the Vernacular Press Act (1878), Ripon repealed it (1882), the first census attempt of 1872 came under Mayo, and Canning announced the Queen's Proclamation of 1858, giving a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv.
172.tq: Link each measure with the Viceroy in office at the time.
n: Lord Lytton introduced the Vernacular Press Act. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #106 · pp 197-199]
Lord Lytton was associated with the Delhi Durbar of 1877. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #106 · pp 197-199]
Lord Ripon repealed the Vernacular Press Act. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #106 · pp 197-199]
Lord Ripon was associated with the Factory Act. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #106 · pp 197-199]
xs: The correct match is **a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Lord Lytton** passed the **Vernacular Press Act** (**1878**); **Lord Ripon** repealed it in **1882**.
The **first census** was attempted under **Lord Mayo** in **1872**; **Lord Canning** is linked with the **Queen's Proclamation** of **1858**.
xa: The **first synchronous census** came in **1881** under **Ripon**.
Lytton also passed the **Arms Act (1878)** and the **Royal Titles Act**; held the **Delhi Durbar** of **1877**.
Ripon's **Local Self-Government Resolution 1882** earned him the title "**Father of Local Self-Government**".
⚠ Lytton owns three Acts (Royal Titles, VPA, Arms); **Ripon** only **repealed** the VPA.

172.s: Which Governor-General is associated with the Third Anglo-Burmese War and the last major territorial expansion?
172.x: Lord Dufferin (1884 to 1888) fought the Third Anglo-Burmese War of 1885, which annexed Upper Burma as the last major territorial expansion.
172.tq: Recall the war of each Viceroy.
n: Lord Dufferin was associated with the Third Anglo-Burmese War. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #106 · pp 197-199]
Lord Dufferin's tenure saw the last major territorial expansion. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #106 · pp 197-199]
Lord Dufferin served as Governor-General from 1884 to 1888. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #106 · pp 197-199]
xs: **Lord Dufferin** (**1884** to **1888**) is linked with the **Third Anglo-Burmese War** — so option **(4)** is correct.
His tenure saw the **last major territorial expansion**; the Third Burma War was fought in **1885**.
**Curzon** is linked with the **Partition of Bengal**, **Minto II** with the **Morley-Minto Reforms**, **Hardinge II** with the shift of the capital to **Delhi**.
xa: The **Indian National Congress** was founded in **1885** during Dufferin's viceroyalty.
Dufferin was followed by **Lord Lansdowne** (**1888-94**) — **Indian Councils Act 1892**, **Durand Commission (1893)**.
Before him came **Lord Ripon** (**1880-84**) — **Ilbert Bill (1883)**.

172.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Lord Linlithgow served during 1936–1944.
II. Lord Linlithgow is associated with the Second World War and the August Offer.
III. Lord Linlithgow is associated with the Cripps context and Quit India.
IV. Lord Wavell is associated with the First Afghan War.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
172.x: I, II and III are correct: Linlithgow ruled from 1936 to 1944 and saw the Second World War, the August Offer, the Cripps Mission and Quit India. IV is false because the First Afghan War belongs to Lord Auckland.
172.tq: Check each statement separately.
n: Lord Auckland was associated with the First Afghan War. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #106 · pp 197-199]
Lord Linlithgow served as Governor-General from 1936 to 1944. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #106 · pp 197-199]
Lord Linlithgow was associated with the Second World War. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #106 · pp 197-199]
Lord Linlithgow was associated with the August Offer. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #106 · pp 197-199]
Lord Linlithgow was associated with the Cripps context. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #106 · pp 197-199]
Lord Linlithgow was associated with the Quit India Movement. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #106 · pp 197-199]
Lord Wavell was associated with the Simla Conference. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #106 · pp 197-199]
Lord Wavell was associated with the Interim Government. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #106 · pp 197-199]
xs: Statements **I, II and III** are correct — so option **(4)** is correct.

173.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the parliamentary inquiries into the affairs of the East India Company:
1. A Select Committee was appointed by Parliament in 1772.
2. The Select Committee was headed by Burgoyne.
3. A Secret Committee was also appointed to inquire into Company affairs.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
173.x: In 1772, Parliament appointed a Select Committee headed by Burgoyne and a Secret Committee to investigate the Company's affairs.
173.tq: Combine the year, committee names and chairmanship before selecting the coded option.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1 correct: Parliament appointed a **Select Committee** in **1772**.
Statement 2 correct: the Select Committee was headed by **Burgoyne**.
Statement 3 correct: a **Secret Committee** was also appointed to inquire into Company affairs.
xa: The two committees' reports led to the **Regulating Act, 1773**.
Background: after **Buxar (1764)**, **Shah Alam** granted the **Diwani** of Bengal, Bihar, Orissa in **1765**.
The Regulating Act **recognised the political and administrative functions** of the Company.

173.s: Which one of the following best describes the constitutional significance of the Regulating Act of 1773?
o: It ended the Company's commercial monopoly in India.
It marked the first step by the British Parliament to control the East India Company and recognised its political and administrative functions.
It constituted the Ministry of Law and Justice as the oldest organ of the Government of India.
It ended the dual system of control over the Company's territories.
173.x: The Regulating Act was the first parliamentary measure to control the Company and formally recognised its political and administrative functions.
173.tq: Choose the option stating the precise constitutional significance rather than a later reform.
xs: The Regulating Act was the **first step by the British Parliament to control the East India Company** and **recognised its political and administrative functions** — option **(2)**.
Ending **"Double Government"** (the dual system) was the work of the **GoI Act, 1858**, not 1773.
The **Ministry of Law and Justice** traces to the **Charter Act 1833**, not to 1773.
xa: **1784** (Pitt's India Act) set the **dual system** that lasted until **1858**.
The Act followed the **1772** Select Committee (**Burgoyne**) and Secret Committee reports.
APPSC-GS **2019** trap: the Act did **not** abolish the **Court of Directors**.

173.s: Which of the following correctly describes the Supreme Court established at Calcutta under the Regulating Act?
o: One Chief Justice and four judges with jurisdiction limited to Bombay
One Chief Justice and three judges with civil and criminal jurisdiction
Three Chief Justices and one judge with only military jurisdiction
One Chief Justice and two judges with only revenue jurisdiction
173.x: The Supreme Court at Calcutta, established in 1774, consisted of one Chief Justice and three judges and exercised civil and criminal jurisdiction.
173.tq: Separate the composition of the court from the later jurisdictional amendments.
xs: The **Supreme Court at Calcutta (1774)** had **1 Chief Justice + 3 judges** with **civil and criminal jurisdiction** — option **(2)**.
It sat at **Calcutta**, not Bombay, and its jurisdiction was not limited to military or revenue matters.
xa: The **1781** Act of Settlement later excluded **revenue** matters from the Court's jurisdiction.
The **1781** Act also exempted the **GG, Council and Company servants** for **acts in their official capacity**.
Undefined jurisdiction over the Council and Indians caused **Council-Court clashes** — a defect of 1773.
AP angle: a **Madras Supreme Court (1801)** was set up for British subjects.

173.s: Which one of the following was NOT a defect of the arrangement created by the Regulating Act?
o: The Governor-General possessed an unrestricted veto over his Council.
The jurisdiction of the Supreme Court over the Council was undefined.
The undefined jurisdiction of the Supreme Court caused clashes between the Council and the Court.
The Governor-General could be outvoted by his Council.
173.x: The Governor-General did not possess a veto and could be outvoted by his Council. The undefined jurisdiction of the Supreme Court led to Council-Court clashes.
173.tq: Find the statement that reverses the known defect rather than merely changing a name or date.
xs: The GG possessing an **unrestricted veto** was NOT a defect — he had **no veto** at all — so option **(1)** is the answer.
A real defect: the GG **could be outvoted by his council**, as **Hastings** repeatedly was.
Another real defect: the Supreme Court's jurisdiction over the Council and over Indians was **undefined**, causing **Council-Court clashes**.
xa: Remedy for the outvoting: the **Act of 1786** gave the GG **override power**.
Remedy for the clashes: the **1781 Act of Settlement** exempted **official acts** and **revenue** matters.
The **Charter Act of 1793** extended the overriding power to the **governors of the presidencies**.

173.s: Which one of the following statements about the Regulating Act of 1773 is NOT correct?
o: It provided for a Supreme Court at Calcutta.
It abolished the Court of Directors of the Company.
It required the Court of Directors to report on revenue, civil and military affairs to the British Government.
It was the first step by the British Parliament to control the Company.
173.x: The Act did not abolish the Court of Directors (APPSC-GS 2019 'incorrect statement'). Instead it made the Directors report to the British Government on revenue, civil and military affairs. It also provided for a Supreme Court at Calcutta, set up in 1774, and it was Parliament's first step to control the Company.
173.tq: 1773 kept the Directors and made them report.
xs: The Regulating Act did **not abolish the Court of Directors** — so option **(2)** is the incorrect statement.
It did set up a **Supreme Court at Calcutta (1774)** and required the Directors to **report** on revenue, civil and military affairs.
It was the **first step by the British Parliament to control the Company**.
xa: This exact "incorrect statement" was asked in **APPSC-GS 2019**.
Supreme Court: **1 Chief Justice + 3 judges**, civil + criminal jurisdiction.
Its defects were remedied by the **1781** Act of Settlement and the **Act of 1786**.

173.s:
Arrange the following developments in chronological order:
A. Amending Act, also called the Act of Settlement
B. Regulating Act
C. Act of 1786
D. Pitt's India Act

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
173.x: The correct sequence is Regulating Act of 1773, Amending Act of 1781, Pitt's India Act of 1784 and Act of 1786.
173.tq: Fix the earliest and latest Acts first, then place the 1781 and 1784 measures between them.
xs: Correct order: **Regulating Act (1773)** → **Amending Act / Act of Settlement (1781)** → **Pitt's India Act (1784)** → **Act of 1786** — option **(1) B, A, D, C**.
**1781** curbed the Supreme Court; **1784** set the dual system; **1786** gave the GG override power.
xa: ⚠ **1781** = Act of Settlement (curbs Supreme Court); **1786** = override power (**Cornwallis**).
The **Charter Act of 1793** extended the override power to the presidency governors.
The **1784** dual system lasted until the **GoI Act 1858** ended **"Double Government"**.

173.s:
Consider the following statements about the Amending Act of 1781 (Act of Settlement):
1. It exempted the Governor-General, his Council and Company servants from the Supreme Court's jurisdiction for acts done in their official capacity.
2. It brought revenue matters within the Supreme Court's jurisdiction.
3. It directed the Court to respect the personal laws of Hindus and Muslims.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
173.x: Statement 1 is correct: official acts of the GG, Council and Company servants were exempted. Statement 2 is wrong: revenue matters were excluded from, not brought into, the Court's jurisdiction. Statement 3 is correct: the Court had to respect Hindu and Muslim personal laws. Hence 1 and 3 only.
173.tq: 1781 cut the Court down (exemptions, no revenue) - it never widened it.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 correct: the **GG, Council and Company servants** were exempted for **acts in their official capacity**.
Statement 2 wrong: **revenue** matters were **excluded from**, not brought into, the Court's jurisdiction.
Statement 3 correct: the Court had to respect the **personal laws** of Hindus and Muslims.
xa: The **1781** Act is also called the **Act of Settlement**.
It remedied the **1773** defect of undefined jurisdiction that caused **Council-Court clashes**.
The Supreme Court at Calcutta had been set up in **1774** with **1 Chief Justice + 3 judges**.

173.s:
Consider the following statements about the Act of 1786:
1. It allowed the Governor-General to override his Council in special cases and also to act as Commander-in-Chief.
2. It was passed to meet Lord Cornwallis's condition for accepting the office of Governor-General.
3. It extended the overriding power to the governors of Bombay and Madras.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
173.x: Statement 2 is correct: the Act met Cornwallis's condition for taking office. Statement 1 is correct: the GG could override his Council in special cases and also be Commander-in-Chief. Statement 3 is wrong: the overriding power was extended to the presidency governors by the Charter Act of 1793, not by the Act of 1786. So '2 only' misses statement 1, and options with statement 3 are wrong.
173.tq: 1786 = override for the GG (Cornwallis); 1793 = override for governors too.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
1 is correct: the **Act of 1786** let the GG **override his council** in special cases and be **Commander-in-Chief**.
2 is correct: it was passed to meet **Lord Cornwallis**'s condition for accepting office.
3 is wrong: the **Charter Act of 1793** extended the overriding power to the governors of the presidencies.
xa: ⚠ **1781** = **Act of Settlement** (curbs the Supreme Court); **1786** = override power (Cornwallis).
The **1786** Act corrected the **1773** defect under which **Hastings** was repeatedly outvoted.
The **Regulating Act 1773** set up the **Supreme Court at Calcutta (1774)**: **1 Chief Justice + 3 judges**.

173.s: The overriding power given to the Governor-General under the Act of 1786 was intended to correct which defect of the Regulating Act?
o: The commercial monopoly of the Company
The absence of a Board of Control
The repeated outvoting of the Governor-General by his Council
The absence of a Supreme Court at Calcutta
173.x: The Act of 1786 addressed the defect under which the Governor-General, including Hastings, could be repeatedly outvoted by his Council.
173.tq: Link a constitutional power to the administrative problem it was designed to solve.
xs: The override power corrected **the repeated outvoting of the Governor-General by his Council** — option **(3)**.
Under the **1773** Act the GG had **no veto**; **Hastings** was repeatedly outvoted.
A **Supreme Court at Calcutta** already existed (set up **1774**), so its absence was not the defect.
xa: The other 1773 defect — **Council-Court clashes** — was remedied by the **1781** Act of Settlement.
The **1786** Act was passed for **Lord Cornwallis**, who also became **Commander-in-Chief**.
The **Charter Act of 1793** extended the override power to presidency governors.

173.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the significance of the constitutional measures from 1773 to 1858?
o: The Regulating Act began parliamentary control, while Pitt's India Act introduced a dual system that continued until the Government of India Act, 1858 ended Double Government.
Pitt's India Act began parliamentary control, while the Regulating Act ended Double Government in 1773.
The Act of 1786 began parliamentary control, while the Charter Act of 1833 ended Double Government in 1786.
The Amending Act of 1781 began parliamentary control, while the Regulating Act ended Double Government in 1784.
173.x: The Regulating Act of 1773 began parliamentary control. Pitt's India Act of 1784 established the dual system, which lasted until the Government of India Act of 1858 ended Double Government.
173.tq: Track the beginning, continuation and termination of the constitutional arrangement.
xs: **1773** (Regulating Act) began parliamentary control; **1784** (Pitt's India Act) set the dual system that lasted until the **GoI Act 1858** ended **Double Government** — option **(1)**.
The other options swap the Acts: the **1781** and **1786** Acts only remedied defects of 1773.
xa: The **1781** Act of Settlement curbed the Supreme Court; the **1786** Act gave the GG override power.
The **Ministry of Law and Justice** traces to the **Charter Act 1833**, not to 1773.
AP angle: **Madras Supreme Court (1801)** and **Madras Regulations 1816** (Munsiff and Panchayat courts).

173.s: Which one of the following correctly identifies the Act from which the Ministry of Law and Justice, described as the oldest organ of the Government of India, traces its origin?
173.x: The Ministry of Law and Justice traces its origin to the Charter Act of 1833, which introduced the Law Member and the first Law Commission.
173.tq: Connect the modern institutional legacy with the historical Act that created its legal foundation.
xs: The **Ministry of Law and Justice**, the oldest organ of GoI, traces to the **Charter Act of 1833** — option **(4)**.
It does not trace to the **Regulating Act 1773**, which began parliamentary control.
The **Charter Act of 1793** is known for extending the GG's override power to the presidency governors.
xa: **1784** (Pitt's India Act) set the dual system that lasted until **1858**.
**1786**: GG could override his council and be Commander-in-Chief (**Cornwallis**).

174.s: The Charter Act of 1813 ended the Company's trade monopoly in India but retained its exclusive right to trade in:
174.x: The Act ended the general trade monopoly in India but retained the Company's exclusive trade in tea and with China.
174.tq: Test the exception to a broad statement instead of accepting that the entire monopoly ended.
xs: The **Charter Act 1813** ended the general India trade monopoly but kept the Company's exclusive right to trade in **tea and with China** — option **(4)**.
Those two monopolies ended only with the **Charter Act 1833**.
xa: CGPSC **2022** trap: "the 1813 Act abolished the Company's trade monopoly" is marked **not true** because tea and China trade were kept.
The **1813** Act extended the charter by **20 years** and asserted the **sovereignty of the British Crown**.
It also gave **Rs 1,00,000 (1 lakh) a year** for education and let **missionaries** enter India.

174.s: The Company's exclusive right to trade in tea and with China was abolished by the:
174.x: The Charter Act of 1833 removed the Company's remaining monopoly over tea trade and trade with China.
174.tq: Separate the general Indian trade monopoly from the later tea-and-China exception.
xs: The tea and China trade monopoly was abolished by the **Charter Act of 1833** — option **(3)**.
The **1813** Act had ended only the general India trade monopoly, keeping **tea** and **China**.
**1833** ended **all commercial functions**; the Company became **purely administrative**.
xa: 1833 also removed curbs on **European immigration and property purchase** in India.
1833 made the **Governor-General of Bengal** the **Governor-General of India** (first: **Bentinck**).
1833 is called the **"final step towards centralisation"**.

174.s:
Consider the following statements about the education grant under the Charter Act of 1813:
1. It provided Rs 10,00,000 a year.
2. It was meant for the revival of literature, the encouragement of learned natives and the promotion of science.
3. It was the first step towards State responsibility for education.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
174.x: Statement 1 is wrong: the grant was Rs 1,00,000 (1 lakh) a year; Rs 10 lakh is a known misprint. Statement 2 is correct: those were its three purposes. Statement 3 is correct: it was the first step towards State responsibility for education. Hence 2 and 3 only; every option with 1 is wrong.
174.tq: 1813 grant = 1 lakh, not 10 lakh.
xs: Statements 2 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 2 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 wrong: the grant was **Rs 1,00,000 (1 lakh) a year**; **Rs 10,00,000** is a known misprint.
Statement 2 correct: it was for **revival of literature**, **encouragement of learned natives** and **promotion of science**.
Statement 3 correct: it was the **first step towards State responsibility for education**.
xa: The **1813** Act also let **missionaries** enter India and propagate religion.
It made training of **civil servants** compulsory.
**Andhra:** it mandated public education as part of Company governance.

174.s: Which one of the following correctly explains the significance of the Charter Act of 1813 in relation to Christian missionaries?
o: It officially sanctioned the entry of missionaries and propagation of Christianity in India.
It prohibited missionaries from entering India.
It transferred missionary activities exclusively to provincial governments.
It permitted only commercial agents to enter India.
174.x: Under Evangelical pressure and the influence of figures such as William Wilberforce and Charles Grant, the Act allowed missionaries to enter India and propagate Christianity.
174.tq: Distinguish official permission for missionary activity from commercial or administrative provisions.
xs: The **1813** Act let **missionaries** enter India and "officially sanctioned the **propagation of Christianity**" — option **(1)**.
This came from pressure of **Evangelicals** — **William Wilberforce** and **Charles Grant** — together with Utilitarians.
xa: The same Act gave **Rs 1 lakh a year** for education — the **first step towards State responsibility for education**.
**1813** is remembered for opening India to **free trade** and missionaries.
⚠ Do not confuse Wilberforce/Grant (1813) with **Trevelyan** and **Robert Lowe**, who backed open competition (1853).

174.s:
Which of the following statements about the Charter Act of 1813 are correct?
1. It asserted the sovereignty of the British Crown over the Company's Indian possessions.
2. It made civil-servant training compulsory.
3. It extended the Charter for 20 years.
4. It mandated public education as part of Company governance in Andhra.

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
174.x: All four statements describe provisions or significance associated with the Charter Act of 1813, including its application to public education as part of Company governance in Andhra.
174.tq: Check the general constitutional, administrative and regional implications together rather than isolating the education grant.
xs: All four statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
Statement 1: it **asserted the sovereignty of the British Crown** over the Company's Indian possessions.
Statement 2: **civil-servant training** was made compulsory.
Statement 3: the charter was extended for **20 years**; statement 4: in **Andhra** it mandated public education.
xa: UPSC **2019** key on 1813 sovereignty: statements **1** and **2** correct.
The **1813** Act ended the general trade monopoly but kept **tea** and **China** trade.
⚠ The **1853** Act renewed authority with **no fixed 20-year term** ("until Parliament should otherwise provide").

174.s:
Consider the following statements about the Charter Act of 1833:
1. It gave the Governor-General-in-Council exclusive legislative power for all British India.
2. The presidencies of Bombay and Madras kept concurrent law-making powers.
3. Laws made under it were called 'Acts' instead of 'Regulations'.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
174.x: Statement 1 is correct: legislative power for all British India was given exclusively to the GG-in-Council. Statement 2 is wrong: the presidencies lost their law-making powers (restored only by the Indian Councils Act 1861). Statement 3 is correct: laws were now called Acts, earlier Regulations. Hence 1 and 3 only.
174.tq: 1833 = peak of centralisation; presidencies lost law-making till 1861.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 correct: the **GG-in-Council** got **exclusive legislative power** for all British India.
Statement 2 wrong: the **presidencies lost law-making powers**.
Statement 3 correct: laws were now called **"Acts"** (earlier **"Regulations"**).
xa: The presidencies' power was restored by the **Indian Councils Act 1861** to **Bombay** and **Madras**.
1833 added a **Law Member** as the **4th** member of the GG's council.
1833 is the **peak of centralisation**.

174.s: The Law Member added to the Governor-General's Council under the Charter Act of 1833 was the:
o: Third member, and the first was Lord Hastings
Fourth member, and the first was T. B. Macaulay
Sixth member, and the first was Robert Lowe
Fifth member, and the first was Charles Trevelyan
174.x: The Law Member was the fourth member of the Governor-General's Council, and T. B. Macaulay was the first to hold the position.
174.tq: Combine the numerical position with the first office-holder to avoid a swapped-person option.
xs: The Law Member was the **fourth member** of the GG's council, and the first was **T.B. Macaulay** — option **(2)**.
Macaulay became Law Member in **1834**.
**Robert Lowe** and **Charles Trevelyan** are linked to open competition (1853), not the Law Membership.
xa: The **first Law Commission (1834)** under Macaulay drafted the **Indian Penal Code**.
Macaulay also wrote the **Minute on Education (1835)**.
The **Ministry of Law and Justice** is traced to this **1833** Act.

174.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the first Law Commission in India:
1. It was established in 1834.
2. It was under the chairmanship of T. B. Macaulay.
3. It drafted the Indian Penal Code.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
174.x: The first Law Commission was established in 1834 under Macaulay and drafted the Indian Penal Code.
174.tq: Verify the year, chairmanship and principal legal work as three linked facts.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
The **first Law Commission** was set up in **1834**, under **Macaulay**.
It drafted the **Indian Penal Code** — the **IPC** came from his draft.
xa: Macaulay was the **first Law Member (1834)**, the **4th** member of the GG's council under the **1833** Act.
His Commons speech on the **1833** Bill: "The Company is an **anomaly**..." (UPPSC **2017**).

174.s: Section 87 of the Charter Act of 1833 provided that no Indian should be barred from office on the grounds of:
o: Province, gender, tribe or political opinion
Religion, place of birth, descent or colour
174.x: Section 87 declared that religion, place of birth, descent or colour should not bar an Indian from holding office.
174.tq: Retain the exact four grounds instead of substituting broader modern equality categories.
xs: **Section 87** of the 1833 Act: no Indian barred from office on grounds of **religion, place of birth, descent or colour** — option **(3)**.
Caste, gender, language or property are not the grounds named in Section 87.
xa: **Raja Ram Mohan Roy** first demanded Indians in the services in **1832**.
Open competitive exams came only with the **1853** Act, which abolished the Directors' **patronage**.
APPSC-GS **2018** key: appointments were made exclusively by the Directors **till 1853**.

174.s: The part of the Bengal Presidency separated and placed under the Agra Presidency by the Charter Act of 1833 was later renamed the:
174.x: The separated territory was placed under the Agra Presidency in 1834 and was renamed the North-Western Provinces in 1836.
174.tq: Link the administrative reorganisation with its later official name, not with a neighbouring province.
xs: The separated part (present **UP**) was renamed the **North-Western Provinces** in **1836** — option **(4)**.
The **1833** Act provided for splitting the **Bengal Presidency**; UP went under the **Agra Presidency** in **1834**.
xa: UPPSC **2021** key: the area placed under Agra Presidency in **1834** was present-day UP.
**Agra** later sent one of the **4** provincial members to the **1853** Central Legislative Council.

174.s: Which one of the following statements is correct regarding the Charter Act of 1833?
o: It represented the final step towards centralisation and made the Company purely administrative.
It abolished the office of the Governor-General of Bengal without creating a successor.
It was the first Charter Act to renew the Company's authority for a fixed 20-year term.
It restored the law-making powers of the presidencies.
174.x: The Charter Act of 1833 is regarded as the final step towards centralisation and converted the Company into a purely administrative body.
174.tq: Combine the distinctive significance and institutional consequence of the Act.
xs: The **1833** Act was the **final step towards centralisation** and made the Company **purely administrative** — option **(1)**.
It did not abolish the GG's office without a successor: the **GG of Bengal** became the **GG of India**.
It did not restore presidency law-making — presidencies **lost** it; restoration came in **1861**.
The **no-fixed-20-year-term** renewal belongs to **1853**; **1813** had extended the charter **20 years**.
xa: 1833 ended the **tea** and **China** trade monopoly.
1833 removed curbs on **European immigration and property purchase**.
1833 added a **Law Member** (**Macaulay**) as **4th** member.

174.s: The statement, “The Company is an anomaly but it is part of a system where everything is an anomaly,” was made by Macaulay in the context of the:
174.x: Macaulay made this observation in his speech in the House of Commons on the Bill that became the Charter Act of 1833.
174.tq: Identify the Act from the context of the quoted political remark.
xs: Macaulay said "The Company is an **anomaly**..." in his Commons speech on the Bill that became the **Charter Act of 1833** — option **(3)**.
This was asked in UPPSC **2017**.
xa: The 1833 Act ended all **commercial functions** — the Company became purely administrative.
Macaulay became the **first Law Member** in **1834**.
His **Minute on Education** dates to **1835**.

174.s: Macaulay's Minute on Education is associated with the year:
174.x: Macaulay's Minute on Education was issued in 1835.
174.tq: Distinguish the year of the education minute from the nearby years of civil-service reform.
xs: Macaulay's **Minute on Education** dates to **1835** — option **(3)**.
**1800** is **Fort William College**; **1832** is **Ram Mohan Roy**'s demand; **1854** is the **Macaulay Committee** on the ICS.
xa: Macaulay was the **first Law Member (1834)**.
The **1813** Act had earlier given **Rs 1 lakh a year** — the first step towards State responsibility for education.

174.s: Which one of the following was a major change introduced by the Charter Act of 1853 in the recruitment to the civil services?
o: Civil-service appointments were transferred to the provincial governments.
All civil-service appointments were made by the Board of Control without examination.
Appointments were reserved exclusively for university graduates nominated by the Directors.
The Directors' patronage was abolished and open competitive examination was introduced.
174.x: The Act abolished the patronage of the Court of Directors and introduced open competition for civil-service recruitment.
174.tq: Identify the authority whose patronage was removed and the method that replaced it.
xs: The **1853** Act abolished the Directors' **patronage** and introduced **open competitive examination** — option **(4)**.
APPSC-GS **2018** key: appointments were made exclusively by the Directors **till 1853**.
xa: **Charles Trevelyan** and **Robert Lowe** supported open competition.
The **Macaulay Committee (1854)** replaced nomination with competitive exams, preferring **university graduates**.
⚠ Some notes give the Macaulay report as **1855**.

174.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Macaulay Committee on the Indian Civil Service:
1. It was constituted in 1854.
2. It favoured the replacement of nomination by competitive examinations.
3. It gave preference to university graduates.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
174.x: The Macaulay Committee was constituted in 1854, recommended competitive examinations in place of nomination, and favoured university graduates.
174.tq: Check each recruitment reform separately before selecting the coded combination.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
The **Macaulay Committee** on the ICS came in **1854**, after the **1853** Act.
It replaced **nomination** with **competitive exams** and preferred **university graduates**.
xa: ⚠ Some notes give the report year as **1855**.
The **1853** Act abolished the Directors' **patronage**; **Trevelyan** and **Robert Lowe** backed open exams.
**Fort William College (1800, Wellesley)** was replaced by **Haileybury (1806)**.

174.s:
Consider the following statements about the legislative arrangement under the Charter Act of 1853:
1. Six new legislative members were added, forming a separate Central Legislative Council.
2. Four of them were appointed by the provincial governments of Madras, Bombay, Bengal and Agra, marking the first local representation.
3. The remaining two were the Commander-in-Chief and the Law Member.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
174.x: Statement 1 is correct: six legislative members were added, making a separate Central Legislative Council (the 'mini-Parliament'). Statement 2 is correct: four came from Madras, Bombay, Bengal and Agra, the first local representation. Statement 3 is wrong: the other two were the Chief Justice and one judge of the Calcutta Supreme Court. Hence 1 and 2 only.
174.tq: 6 = 4 provinces + 2 judges of the Calcutta Supreme Court.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 correct: **6 new legislative members** formed a separate **Central Legislative Council**.
Statement 2 correct: **4** came from **Madras, Bombay, Bengal and Agra** — the first local representation.
Statement 3 wrong: the other two were the **Chief Justice** and one judge of the **Calcutta Supreme Court**.
xa: The Council is called the **"mini-Parliament"**.
The **1853** Act separated the **legislative and executive functions** of the GG's Council.
**1853** is the **last Charter Act** (**Government of India Act 1853**).

174.s: The expression that the Indian territories of the East India Company were held “in trust” is associated with the:
174.x: The Charter Act of 1853 continued the Company's authority over its Indian territories in trust for the British Crown, its heirs and successors.
174.tq: Discriminate between the Charter Acts by attaching the exact phrase to the correct year.
xs: The **Charter Act of 1853** held the Indian territories "**in trust** for Her Majesty, her heirs and successors" — option **(2)**.
The trust lasted "**until Parliament should otherwise provide**" (APPSC-GS **2018**).
xa: Fill-in-the-blank bait: answer **Charter Act**, not Regulating Act.
Unlike **1813**, the **1853** Act gave **no fixed 20-year term**.
The **1813** Act asserted the **sovereignty of the British Crown** over Indian possessions.

174.s:
Consider the following statements about the growth of central control:
1. The Act of 1773 made the Governor of Bengal the Governor-General of Bengal and subordinated Bombay and Madras.
2. The Act of 1786 allowed the Governor-General to override his council.
3. The Charter Act of 1853 restored legislative power to Bombay and Madras.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
174.x: Statement 1 is correct: 1773 created the GG of Bengal and subordinated Bombay and Madras. Statement 2 is correct: 1786 gave the GG power to override his council. Statement 3 is wrong: the 1853 Act set up a Central Legislative Council with provincial members; legislative power went back to Bombay and Madras only under the Indian Councils Act 1861. Hence 1 and 2 only.
174.tq: Centralisation rises to 1833; reversal (decentralisation) = 1861.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 correct: **1773** made the Governor of Bengal **GG of Bengal** and subordinated Bombay and Madras.
Statement 2 correct: **1786** let the GG **override his council**.
Statement 3 wrong: **1853** set up a **Central Legislative Council**; power returned to Bombay and Madras only under the **Indian Councils Act 1861**.
xa: **1784**: **Board of Control**; stricter supervision of the presidencies.
**1793**: greater control over Bombay and Madras; override extended to governors.
**1833**: **GG of India** with **exclusive legislative power** — peak of centralisation.

174.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched regarding civil-service education and recruitment?
o: Raja Ram Mohan Roy — first demanded Indian participation in services in 1853
Haileybury — replaced Fort William College in 1806
Charter Act of 1813 — introduced open competitive examinations for the ICS
Fort William College — established in 1806 by Wellesley
174.x: Fort William College was established in 1800 under Wellesley, and Haileybury replaced it in 1806. Raja Ram Mohan Roy's demand came in 1832, while open examinations were associated with the Charter Act of 1853.
174.tq: Find the single correctly matched pair among closely related dates and reforms.
xs: **Haileybury** replaced **Fort William College** in **1806** — option **(2)**.
**Raja Ram Mohan Roy** made his demand in **1832**, not 1853.
Open competitive exams came from the **1853** Act, not 1813.
**Fort William College** was set up in **1800** by **Wellesley**, not 1806.
xa: The **1813** Act made **civil-servant training** compulsory.
The **Macaulay Committee (1854)** preferred **university graduates**.
**Section 87** (1833): no Indian barred from office on religion, birth, descent or colour.

174.s:
With reference to the Madras Presidency, consider the following statements:
1. The Madras High Court was linked as a court of record to the Charter Act of 1853.
2. The High Court itself came under the Indian High Courts Act of 1861.
3. The Madras High Court was established in 1853 itself.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
174.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The High Court itself came under the Indian High Courts Act of 1861 and was established in 1862, not in 1853.
174.tq: Separate the earlier constitutional association from the later establishment date.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 correct: the Madras High Court "**court of record**" is linked to the **1853** Act.
Statement 2 correct: the High Court came under the **Indian High Courts Act 1861**.
Statement 3 wrong: it was established in **1862**, not 1853.
xa: The same **1861** year saw the **Indian Councils Act** restore law-making to **Bombay** and **Madras**.
**1853** was the **last Charter Act**.

174.s: Which of the following correctly identifies the last Charter Act and the subsequent constitutional endpoint of the Company's rule?
o: Charter Act of 1833; Government of India Act of 1858
Charter Act of 1853; Government of India Act of 1858
Charter Act of 1853; Indian Councils Act of 1861
Charter Act of 1861; Government of India Act of 1858
174.x: The Charter Act of 1853 was the last Charter Act, and the Government of India Act of 1858 ended the East India Company's rule by transferring authority to the Crown.
174.tq: Use the last Act and the later endpoint of Company rule as a two-part chronological pair.
xs: The last Charter Act was **1853**, and the endpoint was the **Government of India Act 1858** — option **(2)**.
**1833** was not the last; the **Indian Councils Act 1861** came after Company rule ended.
xa: The **1853** Act is also called the **Government of India Act 1853**.
1853 opened the path to a **legislature** and a **merit-based ICS**.
1853 held territories "in trust" **until Parliament should otherwise provide**.

174.s:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
A. Battle of Plassey
B. Battle of Buxar
C. Grant of Diwani rights
D. Regulating Act
174.x: Plassey was fought in 1757, Buxar in 1764, Diwani rights came in 1765 and the Regulating Act in 1773, giving A, B, C, D.
174.tq: Arrange the events by year.
n: The Battle of Plassey was fought in 1757. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #131 · pp 234-235]
The Battle of Buxar was fought in 1764. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #131 · pp 234-235]
The East India Company received Diwani rights in 1765. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #131 · pp 234-235]
The Regulating Act was enacted in 1773. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #131 · pp 234-235]
xs: The correct order is **A, B, C, D** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Battle of Plassey** **1757** → **Battle of Buxar** **1764** → **Diwani rights** **1765** → **Regulating Act** **1773**.
xa: After Buxar, **Shah Alam** granted the **Diwani** of Bengal, Bihar, Orissa to the Company.
**Pitt's India Act** followed in **1784**.
The **Charter Act 1813** ended the Company's monopoly in Indian trade; **1833** ended its commercial functions.

174.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I
(a) Regulating Act
(b) Pitt's India Act
(c) Charter Act
(d) Government of India Act

List-II
(i) 1858
(ii) 1773
(iii) 1813
(iv) 1784
174.x: The Regulating Act was 1773, Pitt's India Act 1784, the Charter Act 1813 and the Government of India Act 1858, giving a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i.
174.tq: Recall the year of each Act.
n: The Regulating Act was enacted in 1773. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #131 · pp 234-235]
Pitt's India Act was enacted in 1784. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #131 · pp 234-235]
The Charter Act of 1813 ended the East India Company's monopoly in Indian trade. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #131 · pp 234-235]
The Government of India Act of 1858 ended the rule of the East India Company. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #131 · pp 234-235]
xs: The correct match is **a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Regulating Act** **1773**; **Pitt's India Act** **1784**; **Charter Act** **1813**; **Government of India Act** **1858**.
xa: The **1858** Act ended the **rule** of the **East India Company**.
**Charter Act 1813** ended the trade monopoly in India but kept **tea** and **China** trade, ended in **1833**.
The **Charter Act 1853** was the **last Charter Act**.
**1833**: **Lord William Bentinck** became the first **GG of India**.

175.s:
Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?

System — Person associated with its introduction
o: Ryotwari System — Alexander Read and Thomas Munro
175.x: The Ryotwari System was associated with Alexander Read and Thomas Munro. John Shore helped plan the Permanent Settlement, while Holt Mackenzie proposed the Mahalwari System.
175.tq: Match the system with its actual originator and eliminate swapped-person traps.
xs: The **Ryotwari System** is correctly matched with **Alexander Read and Thomas Munro** — option **(2)**.
The **Permanent Settlement** was introduced by **Lord Cornwallis**, planned with **John Shore** — not Shore alone.
**Mahalwari** was proposed by **Holt Mackenzie (1822)**, not Cornwallis; Mackenzie had nothing to do with the Permanent Settlement.
xa: Ryotwari began experimentally in **Baramahal (1792)**; general Madras adoption came in **1820**.
**Mountstuart Elphinstone** extended Ryotwari to **Bombay**.
⚠ Mahalwari: **Mackenzie 1822** = proposal; **Bird / Bentinck 1833** = revision.

175.s:
With reference to the Permanent Settlement, consider the following statements:
1. It was introduced in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa in 1795.
2. It was planned by Lord Cornwallis with the assistance of John Shore.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
175.x: Statement 1 is incorrect: the Permanent Settlement was introduced in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa in 1793, not 1795 (APPSC-G2 2025 trap). Statement 2 is correct: Cornwallis planned it with John Shore. Hence '2 only'; 'Both', '1 only' and 'Neither' are wrong.
175.tq: Permanent Settlement = Cornwallis + John Shore, 1793 (not 1795).
xs: Only statement 2 is correct — option **(2) 2 only**.
Statement 1 wrong: the Permanent Settlement came in **1793**, not **1795** (APPSC-G2 **2025** trap).
Statement 2 correct: **Cornwallis** planned it with **John Shore**.
xa: It began as a **decennial (10-year)** settlement, made permanent in **1793**.
In Andhra it was applied in **1802**.
APPSC-GS **2024**: Permanent Settlement = **Cornwallis**.

175.s:
Which of the following statements regarding the Permanent Settlement is correct?

1. It initially began as a decennial settlement.
2. It was subsequently made permanent.
3. Zamindari rights were alienable, rentable and heritable.

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
175.x: The Permanent Settlement began as a ten-year or decennial settlement and was later made permanent. Zamindari rights were alienable, rentable and heritable.
175.tq: Combine the settlement-period detail with the legal nature of zamindari rights.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
It began as a **decennial (10-year)** settlement and was **made permanent in 1793**.
Zamindari rights were **alienable, rentable and heritable**.
xa: Zamindars were recognised as **proprietors**.
Reasons for fixity: **assured income**, low collection cost, a **loyal landlord class**, hope of land improvement.
Demand fixed very high → **no share of later growth** to the state.

175.s: Which one of the following correctly contrasts the distribution of agricultural gains under the zamindari arrangement?
o: The gains primarily went to the Company and not to the zamindars.
The gains from agriculture went to the zamindars rather than to the Company.
The gains were retained entirely by the cultivators.
The gains were divided equally between the ryots and the village community.
175.x: Under the zamindari system, the gains from agriculture went to the zamindars, not to the Company.
175.tq: Watch the reversed comparison between zamindars and the Company.
xs: Under zamindari, **gains from agriculture went to the zamindars**, not the Company — option **(2)**.
Cultivation and prices rose after **1800**, but the **fixed demand** gave the Company nothing extra (APPSC-GS **2022**).
Cultivators did not keep the gains — they were reduced to **tenants-at-will**.
xa: Effects: **absentee landlordism**, **sub-infeudation**, **rack-renting**.
Zamindars moved to cities like **Calcutta** and left collection to agents.

175.s: Under the Sunset Law associated with the Permanent Settlement, an estate could be auctioned when:
o: the annual revenue was not paid by sunset on the due date
the tenant refused to accept a patta
the zamindar failed to improve the land within ten years
175.x: If the required revenue was not paid by sunset of the due date, the estate could be auctioned.
175.tq: Focus on the precise trigger for an estate sale and reject broader consequences.
xs: Under the **Sunset Law**, an estate was auctioned if revenue was **not paid by sunset of the due date** — option **(1)**.
It did not deal with pattas, land improvement or prices.
xa: Permanent vs Ryotwari default: estate **forfeited (Sunset Law)** vs **land auctioned**.
Many old zamindars lost estates to **urban merchants and moneylenders** at auction.
**Haftam (1799)** and **Panjam (1812)** let zamindars seize tenants' property.

175.s: The sale of many old zamindari estates under the Permanent Settlement contributed to the emergence of:
o: a new body of village karanams
a class of hereditary ryot proprietors in Madras
a new landed class of urban merchants and moneylenders
a class of Palegar intermediaries in Rayalaseema
175.x: Many old zamindars lost their estates for arrears, which were purchased by urban merchants and moneylenders, creating a new landed class.
175.tq: Trace the ownership change caused by arrears and auction sales.
xs: Estate sales created **a new landed class of urban merchants and moneylenders** — option **(3)**.
Many old zamindars lost estates for **arrears** under the Sunset Law.
xa: Zamindari areas → **merchant-landlords**; ryotwari and mahalwari areas → **moneylender-landlords**.
**Karanams** were village officers under the Collector in Ryotwari — not a new class.
**Palegars** were suppressed by **Munro**, not created.

175.s: Which regulations empowered zamindars to seize the property of tenants under the Permanent Settlement?
175.x: The regulations of 1799, known as Haftam, and 1812, known as Panjam, enabled zamindars to seize tenants' property.
175.tq: Pair the two regulations with their coercive effect rather than with settlement dates.
xs: The **Haftam (1799)** and **Panjam (1812)** regulations let zamindars seize tenants' property — option **(3)**.
**1822** and **1833** are Mahalwari regulations; **1793** made the settlement permanent.
xa: The result was **endless litigation** between zamindars and tenants.
Peasants were reduced to **tenants-at-will**.

175.s:
Which of the following developments was associated with the Permanent Settlement?
1. Absentee landlordism
2. Sub-infeudation
3. Rack-renting
4. Reduction of peasants to tenants-at-will
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
175.x: All four were effects of the Permanent Settlement. The system strengthened landlordism, encouraged layers of subordinate interests and exposed peasants to insecure tenancy and high rents.
175.tq: Recognise a complete cluster of social and agrarian consequences.
xs: All four were effects of the Permanent Settlement — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
**Absentee landlordism**: zamindars moved to **Calcutta**, leaving agents to collect.
**Sub-infeudation** and **rack-renting** spread; peasants became **tenants-at-will**.
xa: Andhra effects: absentee landlordism, sub-infeudation, **no investment in land**, loss of estates for arrears.
Land became a **saleable commodity** concentrated in few hands.

175.s: According to the commonly cited distribution of rent under the Permanent Settlement, what share was retained by the zamindar?
175.x: The commonly cited distribution gave the state 10/11 of the rent collected and the zamindar 1/11. Some accounts mention a 9/10 and 1/10 division, but the cited assessment here uses 1/11.
175.tq: Distinguish the zamindar's retained share from the much larger state share.
xs: The zamindar kept **1/11** of the rent — option **(2)**; the state took **10/11**.
Some notes give **9/10** to government and **1/10** to the zamindar in Andhra — the commonly cited split is 10/11 : 1/11.
xa: The demand was fixed at a **very high level** — no share of later growth for the state.
Ryotwari revenue was also high, often **50%+** of produce.

175.s: Which of the following was NOT a rationale advanced for making the Permanent Settlement revenue demand fixed?
o: Ensuring that the Company would receive every future increase in agricultural prices
Reducing the cost of revenue collection
Securing an assured income for the Company
175.x: The rationale included assured income, lower collection costs, a loyal landlord class and the hope that zamindars would improve the land. A fixed demand actually prevented the Company from receiving additional revenue from later price increases.
175.tq: Find the option that contradicts the economic consequence of revenue fixity.
xs: Getting **every future increase in agricultural prices** was NOT a rationale — option **(2)**; a **fixed** demand gave the Company nothing extra.
Real rationales: **fixed, assured income**, **low collection cost** and a **loyal landlord class**.
xa: Another rationale: the hope that **zamindars would improve land**.
APPSC-GS **2022**: gains from agriculture went to the **zamindars**, not the Company.

175.s: The first experimental introduction of the Ryotwari system in the Madras Presidency took place in which area?
175.x: The first experiment was conducted in Baramahal, comprising areas such as Salem, Krishnagiri, Dharmapuri and Tiruvannamalai.
175.tq: Distinguish the first experimental area from the later area of wider implementation.
xs: Ryotwari was first introduced experimentally in **Baramahal** — option **(1)** (APHQ **2008** key).
It was done by **Captain Alexander Read**, assisted by **Thomas Munro**, in **1792**.
The **Ceded Districts** came later (**1802**) — that is the first in **Andhra**.
xa: Exam angle: "first in Andhra" = **Rayalaseema**; "in the Madras Presidency" = **Baramahal**.
Munro was **Collector of South Canara** in **1799**.

175.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the geographical distribution of revenue systems in the Madras Presidency is correct?
o: Haveli lands were permanently settled with zamindars before British control.
The Northern Circars were entirely under Ryotwari from the beginning.
The Northern Circars were mainly under zamindari settlement, while Haveli lands later came under Ryotwari.
The Ceded Districts were mainly governed through the Mahalwari system.
175.x: The Northern Circars were mainly zamindari areas, whereas Haveli lands under direct British control later came under Ryotwari.
175.tq: Compare neighbouring regional arrangements and identify the qualified statement.
xs: The **Northern Circars** were mainly **zamindari**, while **Haveli** lands later came under **Ryotwari** — option **(3)**.
Haveli lands were under **direct Company control**, not settled with zamindars.
The **Ceded Districts** were the Ryotwari heartland, not Mahalwari.
xa: Haveli lands were grouped into **mootahs** and auctioned to **mootahdars**; many fell into arrears.
The Northern Circars were obtained in **1765-66** (Mughal farman + Nizam treaty).

175.s: Under the Ryotwari system, which of the following rights was available to the ryot so long as the assessment was paid?
o: Only the right to cultivate, without transfer rights
The right to sell, mortgage, gift or lease the land
The right to remit all land revenue permanently
The right to collect revenue from other cultivators
175.x: The ryot held proprietary rights and could sell, mortgage, gift or lease the land as long as the assessment was paid.
175.tq: Identify the legal incidents of ryot ownership rather than confusing them with revenue-collection powers.
xs: The ryot could **sell, mortgage, gift or lease the land** as long as the assessment was paid — option **(2)**.
These were **proprietary rights**; he was not evicted while revenue was paid.
xa: Assessment was fixed on **land, not crop**.
On default the **land was auctioned**.
Problems: **over-assessment**, no proper records, corrupt subordinates → peasants to **moneylenders**.

175.s:
Consider the following statements about the Ryotwari settlement:
1. Settlement was made ryot by ryot.
2. Revenue was fixed on the land rather than directly on the crop produced.
3. The assessment was ordinarily revised about every thirty years.
4. Karanams and village officers worked under the Collector.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
175.x: All four statements describe features of the Ryotwari arrangement: individual settlement, land-based assessment, periodic revision and supervision through village officers under the Collector.
175.tq: Test a cluster of features while checking whether the option preserves the full set.
xs: All four statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
Settlement was **ryot by ryot**; assessment fixed on **land, not crop**.
Revised about **every 30 years**; **karanams** and village officers worked under the **Collector**.
xa: APPSC-GS **2018** asked these Ryotwari features.
Ryots had **proprietary rights** — sell, mortgage, gift, lease.
**Alice Thorner**: ryotwari **destroyed the village system** and isolated farmers.

175.s:
Consider the following statements about the Ryotwari system:
1. In the Andhra region it was first introduced in the Ceded Districts (Rayalaseema) by Thomas Munro in 1802.
2. It was adopted generally across the Madras Presidency in 1820, when Munro was Governor.
3. It was first introduced in the Andhra region in the Northern Circars.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
175.x: Statement 1 is correct: Munro brought Ryotwari to Rayalaseema in 1802. Statement 2 is correct: general adoption in the Madras Presidency came in 1820 under Munro as Governor. Statement 3 is wrong: the Northern Circars were mainly zamindari, only Haveli lands came under Ryotwari later. So options with statement 3 are wrong.
175.tq: First in Andhra = Rayalaseema 1802; first in Madras Presidency = Baramahal 1792; general = 1820.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 correct: Ryotwari first came to Andhra in **Rayalaseema** by **Munro** in **1802**.
Statement 2 correct: general Madras adoption in **1820** under Munro as **Governor**.
Statement 3 wrong: the **Northern Circars** were mainly **zamindari**.
xa: A **2018** PYQ stem gave the date as **1808**; the answer is still **Munro**.
From **1808** village-lease settlements replaced ryotwari in the Ceded Districts until restored around **1820**.

175.s: Thomas Munro's headquarters as the first Collector of the Ceded Districts was located at:
175.x: Munro's headquarters as the first Collector of the Ceded Districts was at Anantapur.
175.tq: Separate an official headquarters from the place of death and the wider regional headquarters.
xs: Munro's HQ as first **Collector of the Ceded Districts (1800)** was **Anantapur** — option **(2)**.
**Pattikonda** (Kurnool) is where he died of cholera in **1827**.
xa: He was **Principal Collector of the Ceded Districts** from **1800-07** (some notes say 1802 for the start).
He was buried at **Gooty**.
PYQ **2025**: Munro = **first Principal Collector of Rayalaseema**.

175.s:
Arrange the following stages of Thomas Munro's career in chronological order:
A. Governor of Madras
B. Assistant to Alexander Read in the Baramahal
C. Principal Collector of the Ceded Districts
D. President of the Judicial Commission
175.x: Munro served as Assistant to Read in the Baramahal, Principal Collector of the Ceded Districts, President of the Judicial Commission, and finally Governor of Madras.
175.tq: Fix the earliest and latest posts first, then place the middle appointments.
xs: Order: Assistant to Read (**1792-99**) → Principal Collector, Ceded Districts (**1800-07**) → Judicial Commission (**1814-18**) → Governor of Madras (**1820-27**) — option **(1) B, C, D, A**.
In between he was **Collector of South Canara** (**1799**).
xa: He died at **Pattikonda** on **6 July 1827**, buried at **Gooty**.
As Governor he saw general Ryotwari adoption in Madras (**1820**).

175.s: Which of the following best represents Thomas Munro's administrative philosophy?
o: Exclusive reliance on village headmen and moneylenders
Direct contact with cultivators, no intermediaries and communication in fluent Telugu
Permanent fixation of revenue irrespective of local conditions
Indirect rule through zamindars and complete absence of official contact with cultivators
175.x: Munro favoured direct contact with cultivators, avoided intermediaries and was fluent in Telugu. He was also particularly fond of Rayalaseema.
175.tq: Choose the option that combines the distinctive elements of a stated administrative philosophy.
xs: Munro stood for **direct contact with cultivators, no intermediaries**, and spoke **fluent Telugu** — option **(2)**.
He **distrusted Palegars** and big intermediaries, so indirect rule through zamindars is the opposite.
xa: He worked **without interpreters**.
Rayalaseema was chosen because it had **no strong zamindars**.
PYQ **2025**: Munro = **first Principal Collector of Rayalaseema**.

175.s:
Consider the following statements about Sir Thomas Munro:
1. He served as Governor of Madras from 1820 to 1827.
2. He died of cholera at Pattikonda in Kurnool district in 1827.
3. He was buried at Anantapur, his headquarters as Collector.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
175.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: Munro was Governor of Madras 1820-27 and died of cholera at Pattikonda (Kurnool) on 6 July 1827. Statement 3 is wrong: Anantapur was his headquarters as Collector of the Ceded Districts, but he was buried at Gooty. So every option containing 3 is wrong.
175.tq: Munro: HQ Anantapur, died Pattikonda, buried Gooty.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 correct: **Governor of Madras 1820-27**.
Statement 2 correct: died of cholera at **Pattikonda** (Kurnool), **6 July 1827**.
Statement 3 wrong: he was buried at **Gooty**; **Anantapur** was his Collector HQ.
xa: UPSC notes give his governorship as **1819-26**.
He was born **27 May 1761** in **Glasgow**.

175.s:
With reference to the Mahalwari System, consider the following statements:

1. Holt Mackenzie proposed the system in 1822.
2. It was revised under Lord William Bentinck in 1833.
3. R. M. Bird was associated with the revision.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
175.x: Holt Mackenzie proposed the Mahalwari System in 1822. It was revised under Bentinck in 1833, with R. M. Bird associated with that revision.
175.tq: Keep the original proposal distinct from the later revision and its associated official.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
**Holt Mackenzie** proposed Mahalwari in **1822**.
It was revised under **Bentinck** in **1833**, by **R.M. Bird**.
xa: Mackenzie's law: **Regulation VII of 1822**; Bird's revision: **Regulation IX of 1833**.
**James Thomason** carried on Bird's settlement in the NWP.
⚠ Some notes credit **Bentinck (1833)** as originator — that is only the revision.

175.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below the Lists:

List-I (Official)
a. Holt Mackenzie
b. R.M. Bird
c. James Thomason

List-II (Role)
i. Carried on Bird's settlement in the NWP
ii. Devised the Mahalwari system
iii. Revised the system through a survey-based settlement

The correct matching is:
175.x: Holt Mackenzie devised the system, R.M. Bird revised it through survey-based settlement, and James Thomason carried on Bird's settlement in the NWP.
175.tq: Start from the sure official–role pair and eliminate codes that repeat the wrong function.
xs: **Mackenzie** devised it, **Bird** revised it, **Thomason** carried it on — option **(1) a–ii, b–iii, c–i**.
**Holt Mackenzie**: **Regulation VII of 1822**.
**R.M. Bird**: **Regulation IX of 1833**, survey-based settlement.
xa: Bird is called the **"father of land settlement in north India"**.
**Thomason** was Lt.-Governor of the NWP.

175.s:
Arrange the following developments associated with land revenue administration in chronological order:
A. Baramahal came under Company control after the Third Mysore War
B. Regulation VII of 1822 associated with Holt Mackenzie
C. Regulation IX of 1833 associated with R.M. Bird
D. Permanent Settlement made permanent
175.x: Baramahal came under Company control in 1792, the Permanent Settlement became permanent in 1793, Regulation VII was issued in 1822 and Regulation IX in 1833.
175.tq: Fix the earliest and latest events first, then place the two nineteenth-century regulations.
xs: Order: Baramahal (**1792**) → Permanent Settlement made permanent (**1793**) → **Regulation VII of 1822** → **Regulation IX of 1833** — option **(1) A, D, B, C**.
Baramahal came after the **Third Mysore War**; 1822 is **Mackenzie**, 1833 is **Bird**.
xa: Ryotwari: Rayalaseema **1802**, general Madras **1820**.
**Haftam 1799**, **Panjam 1812**.

175.s: Which statement correctly describes the unit and method of assessment under the Mahalwari system?
o: The individual ryot was the sole unit; revenue was collected only by zamindars
The province was the unit; revenue was permanently fixed by the Company
The mahal was the unit; revenue was fixed for the village or estate and collected through the headman or village community
The profession was the unit; revenue was collected through urban merchants
175.x: Under Mahalwari, the mahal meant a village or estate. Revenue was fixed for it and collected by the headman or village community, with each cultivator liable for his share.
175.tq: Split the question into unit, assessment and collection authority.
xs: Under Mahalwari the **mahal** (village or estate) was the unit; revenue was fixed for it and collected by the **headman or village community** — option **(3)**.
Each cultivator was liable for his share; it was **periodically revised**.
xa: Individual ryots = **Ryotwari**; zamindars = **Permanent Settlement**.
Mahalwari broke village solidarity through **collective liability**.
On default the **village was collectively liable**.

175.s: The common ownership arrangements associated with the Mahalwari system were known as:
175.x: Common ownership arrangements under the Mahalwari framework were called Bhai Chara or Mahali.
175.tq: Discriminate between closely related revenue terms from different systems.
xs: Mahalwari joint-ownership forms were called **"Bhai Chara" or "Mahali"** — option **(2)**.
**Zabt** and **taccavi** were Mughal; **Peshkash** and **Haveli** are Andhra revenue terms.
xa: **Moturpha** was a tax on professions, trades and looms in Madras.
Mahalwari: **joint village ownership**, unit = **mahal**.

175.s: In Andhra Pradesh, the Mahalwari-type arrangement is specifically associated with which area or areas?
175.x: The Mahalwari-type arrangement is placed in Nellore and Chittoor in the relevant regional account; in some accounts, Nellore alone is specifically mentioned.
175.tq: Use regional identification while avoiding confusion with named Zamindari estates.
xs: In Andhra, the Mahalwari-type arrangement is linked to **Nellore and Chittoor** — option **(2)**.
Some notes give **Nellore** only; there **village headmen** collected and remitted the tax.
**Vizianagaram, Bobbili, Pithapuram, Nuzvid** were zamindaris under the Permanent Settlement.
xa: All three systems ran in Andhra: zamindari in the **Circars**, ryotwari in the **Ceded Districts**, mahalwari in **Nellore**.
Farmers depended on **village elders**.

175.s: The Mahalwari system of land revenue was introduced mainly in which of the following regions?
o: North-Western Provinces and parts of Punjab
175.x: Mahalwari covered the North-Western Provinces (Agra-Oudh) and parts of Punjab, plus Central India (APPSC 2018). Bengal, Bihar, Odisha and the Northern Circars were Permanent Settlement areas; Madras and Bombay were Ryotwari areas.
175.tq: Mahalwari = NWP + Punjab; Ryotwari = Madras + Bombay; Zamindari = Bengal.
xs: Mahalwari was mainly in the **North-Western Provinces and parts of Punjab** — option **(2)** (APPSC-GS **2018**).
**Bengal, Bihar**, **Odisha** and the **Northern Circars** were Permanent Settlement areas; **Madras and Bombay** were Ryotwari.
xa: Mahalwari also covered the Gangetic valley and **Central India** — about **30%** of British India.
Proposed by **Holt Mackenzie (1822)**.

175.s: Who assisted Thomas Munro in suppressing the Palegars in the Ceded Districts before the introduction of Ryotwari settlement?
175.x: Munro suppressed the Palegars with the assistance of officer Campbell before bringing the Ceded Districts under Ryotwari settlement.
175.tq: Discriminate between persons associated with administration, resistance and nomenclature.
xs: Munro suppressed the Palegars with military officer **Campbell** — option **(2)**.
**Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy** was a Kurnool Polygar who revolted in the **1840s**.
**Vijayarama Gajapati Raju** was the Vizianagaram zamindar defeated at **Padmanabham (1794)**.
**Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao** proposed the name **Rayalaseema**.
xa: About **80** palegars resisted; suppression took **18** months.
Uyyalawada looted the treasury at **Kovela Kuntla**.

175.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the land arrangements in Coastal Andhra:
1. Coastal lands were divided into Haveli and Zamindari areas.
2. Haveli areas were under direct Company control.
3. Zamindars in Zamindari areas paid peshkash.
4. The auction system was never used in Haveli areas.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
175.x: Haveli areas were directly controlled by the Company, while Zamindars paid peshkash. The auction system was initially used in Coastal Andhra, including Haveli lands, so statement 4 is false.
175.tq: Find the exception created by the absolute word 'never'.
xs: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct — option **(1) 1, 2 and 3 only**.
Coastal lands were **Haveli** (direct Company control) and **Zamindari**; zamindars paid **peshkash**.
Statement 4 wrong: **Haveli** lands were **auctioned** — grouped into **mootahs** and sold to **mootahdars**.
xa: Old estates of **Vizianagaram, Bobbili and Pithapuram** came under peshkash.
Mootahs were held like proprietary estates after **1802**; many fell into arrears.
The **Madras Inam Commission (1858)** confirmed valid **inam** titles on a **quit-rent**.

175.s: The Permanent Settlement introduced by Cornwallis in 1793 was implemented in Andhra in 1802 with which immediate effect?
o: The auction system was abolished and the tax was fixed
The zamindars were replaced by village headmen
Land revenue was remitted during every crop failure
All Zamindari estates were immediately abolished
175.x: In Andhra, Cornwallis's 1793 Act was implemented in 1802; it abolished the auction system and fixed the tax. Zamindari abolition occurred much later in 1948.
175.tq: Apply the general settlement policy to its Andhra implementation.
xs: When Cornwallis's **1793** settlement was implemented in Andhra in **1802**, **the auction system was abolished and the tax was fixed** — option **(1)**.
Zamindars were not replaced or abolished; abolition came only in **1948**.
There was **no famine remission** under British revenue systems.
xa: Agreements ran for **10** years; farmers were reduced to **tenants**.
Andhra effects: absentee landlordism, **sub-infeudation**, no investment in land.
Some notes give the Andhra split as **9/10** to government, **1/10** to the zamindar.

175.s: Which legislation provided for the full conversion of Zamindari estates into Ryotwari holdings in the Madras Presidency?
o: Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948
175.x: The Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948 provided for the abolition of estates and their conversion into Ryotwari holdings.
175.tq: Match the exact statute with its administrative purpose.
xs: Full conversion came with the **Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948** — option **(3)**.
**1793** made the zamindari settlement permanent — it created, not abolished, zamindaris.
xa: Some notes date zamindari abolition to **1952** (First Plan).
APHQ **2025** order ends with zamindari abolition (**1948**) after **Guntur (1788)**, **Padmanabham (1794)**, **Ryotwari (1802)**.
The **Madras Inam Commission (1858)** dealt with **inam** (rent-free) titles.

175.s:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
A. Guntur was acquired by the Company
B. Battle of Padmanabham
C. Ceded Districts were obtained from the Nizam
D. Permanent Settlement was applied in the Circars and Ryotwari was introduced in Rayalaseema
175.x: The correct sequence is Guntur acquired in 1788, Battle of Padmanabham in 1794, Ceded Districts obtained in 1800, and the 1802 settlements.
175.tq: Fix the earliest and latest dates first, then place the middle events.
xs: Order: **Guntur (1788)** → **Padmanabham (1794)** → Ceded Districts from the Nizam (**1800**) → Permanent Settlement in Circars + Ryotwari in Rayalaseema (**1802**) — option **(1) A, B, C, D**.
This follows the APHQ **2025** order.
xa: The **Northern Circars** came earlier, in **1765-66**.
**Uyyalawada**'s revolt came in the **1840s**; zamindari abolition in **1948**.

175.s: Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy's revolt in the 1840s is associated with which incident?
o: Defeating the Vizianagaram zamindar at Padmanabham
Introducing the Mahalwari system in Nellore
Obtaining the Northern Circars through a Mughal farman
Looting the treasury at Kovela Kuntla
175.x: During the Kurnool Polygar revolt in the 1840s, Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy looted the treasury at Kovela Kuntla.
175.tq: Link the rebel with the specific action and place.
xs: **Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy**'s **1840s** revolt is linked to **looting the treasury at Kovela Kuntla** — option **(4)**.
He was a **Kurnool Polygar**; Padmanabham (**1794**) was the Vizianagaram zamindar's defeat.
xa: Palegar resistance (**Uyyalawada**) followed **Munro**'s ryotwari in Rayalaseema.
Munro had suppressed about **80** palegars with **Campbell**.

175.s: Haveli lands were grouped into mootahs and auctioned to mootahdars after 1802. The mootahdars generally held them as—
175.x: After 1802, mootahs were auctioned to mootahdars, who held them in the manner of proprietary estates. Many mootahdars later failed and fell into arrears.
175.tq: Identify the legal-economic character of the holding created by a settlement arrangement.
xs: **Mootahdars** held the auctioned mootahs as **proprietary estates** after **1802** — option **(2)**.
Many failed and **fell into arrears**.
xa: **Haveli** lands were under direct Company control (vs **Zamindari**).
Haveli lands used auction, village or ryotwari methods.

175.s: Which statement about village-lease settlements in the Ceded Districts is correct?
o: They replaced ryotwari after Munro left in 1808 and continued until ryotwari was restored around 1820.
They preceded the 1792 Baramahal experiment and ended in 1799.
They were introduced only in the Northern Circars and never in the Ceded Districts.
They permanently replaced all forms of direct settlement in Rayalaseema.
175.x: Village-lease settlements, in which village headmen acted as lessees, replaced ryotwari in the Ceded Districts after Munro's departure from 1808 onward and lasted until about 1820.
175.tq: Track the temporary replacement and subsequent restoration of a revenue system.
xs: **Village-lease settlements** replaced ryotwari after Munro left (**1808** onward) until ryotwari was **restored around 1820** — option **(1)**.
Village **headmen** acted as lessees.
They were in the **Ceded Districts**, not the Circars, and were not permanent.
xa: A **2018** PYQ stem gave the Andhra ryotwari date as **1808**; the answer is still **Munro**.
