General Madras adoption came in **1820** under Munro as Governor.

175.s: The Madras Inam Commission was established in which year to investigate which matter?
175.x: The Madras Inam Commission was constituted in 1858 to investigate rent-free inam titles.
175.tq: Pair the commission with both its year and its specific purpose.
xs: The **Madras Inam Commission** came in **1858** to investigate **inam (rent-free) titles** — option **(3)**.
**1793**, **1802** and **1822** belong to the Permanent Settlement, mootahs and Mahalwari.
xa: Valid titles were confirmed on payment of a **quit-rent**.
Full ryotwari conversion of estates came in **1948**.

175.s: Why did rigid land revenue demands frequently push ryots towards moneylenders?
o: The government accepted revenue only in manufactured goods
Moneylenders alone were authorised to cultivate government land
Revenue had to be paid in cash even when crops failed
Ryots were prohibited from selling agricultural produce
175.x: The inflexible cash demand continued even during crop failures, forcing ryots to borrow from Mahajans and often mortgage or lose their land.
175.tq: Trace the cause-effect chain from revenue rigidity to indebtedness.
xs: Revenue had to be **paid in cash even when crops failed** — option **(3)**.
This rigid cash demand drove ryots to **moneylenders (Mahajans)**, then mortgage and eviction.
xa: There was **no famine remission**, unlike the Mughal **zabt**.
Cash revenue forced **cash crops** (indigo, cotton, opium, jute).
Result: rural indebtedness and **land alienation**.

175.s: Which feature distinguished the rigid British revenue demand from the Mughal zabt system mentioned in the context of agrarian administration?
o: The Mughal system imposed no assessment on agricultural land
The Mughal system provided a one-third share arrangement and taccavi loans
The British system provided taccavi loans to every ryot
The British system routinely remitted revenue during famine
175.x: The Mughal zabt is described as involving a one-third share and taccavi loans, whereas the British demand was rigid and offered no famine remission.
175.tq: Contrast the two systems through their treatment of risk and relief.
xs: The Mughal **zabt** had a **one-third share** and **taccavi loans** — option **(2)**.
The British demand gave **no famine remission**.
xa: Mahalwari broke village solidarity through **collective liability**.
All three systems took revenue in **cash** regardless of harvest.

175.s: Which of the following correctly explains the economic effect of cash-based land revenue assessment?
o: It encouraged the cultivation of commercial crops such as indigo, cotton, opium and jute
It transferred all agricultural profits directly to cultivators
It eliminated dependence on markets by encouraging subsistence crops alone
It prevented the sale and mortgage of agricultural land
175.x: The need to meet cash revenue demands encouraged cultivation of commercial crops such as indigo, cotton, opium and jute.
175.tq: Infer the cropping response from the pressure to obtain cash.
xs: Cash revenue forced **commercial crops — indigo, cotton, opium, jute** — option **(1)**.
Profits did not go to cultivators; land became **saleable** and indebtedness grew.
xa: Ryotwari areas: the **American Civil War** cotton slump → defaults → land to moneylenders.
Low investment in agriculture; **overcrowding** as ruined artisans fell back on land.

175.s: Which pairing of newly strengthened rural classes with the areas in which they emerged is correct?
o: Merchant-landlords — Zamindari areas; moneylender-landlords — Ryotwari and Mahalwari areas
Moneylender-landlords — Zamindari areas; merchant-landlords — Ryotwari areas only
Artisan-landlords — all areas; merchants — no rural areas
Village headmen — Zamindari areas; zamindars — Ryotwari areas only
175.x: Merchant-landlords became prominent in Zamindari areas, while moneylender-landlords emerged particularly in Ryotwari and Mahalwari areas.
175.tq: Match each rural class with the revenue system that enabled its rise.
xs: **Merchant-landlords** rose in **zamindari** areas; **moneylender-landlords** in **ryotwari and mahalwari** areas — option **(1)**.
Old zamindars lost estates to **urban merchants and moneylenders** at auction.
xa: The common result: **rural indebtedness + land alienation**.
Land became a **saleable commodity**, concentrated in few hands.

175.s: Which of the following was NOT identified as a major problem of the Ryotwari system?
o: Permanent fixing of revenue at a low and unchangeable rate
175.x: Ryotwari suffered from over-assessment, inadequate records and unclear boundaries. Its revenue was periodically revised and often heavy, not permanently fixed at a low rate.
175.tq: Find the option that contradicts the characteristic weaknesses of the system.
xs: **Permanent fixing at a low, unchangeable rate** was NOT a Ryotwari problem — option **(4)**; Ryotwari was **periodically revised** and high.
Real problems: **over-assessment**, **no proper land records**, **unclear boundaries**, corrupt subordinate officials.
xa: Ryotwari revenue was often **50%+** of produce.
Revision came about **every 30 years**.
The **Permanent Settlement** was the one **fixed forever**.

175.s: Which one of the following correctly describes revenue fixation under the three principal land revenue systems?
o: Permanent Settlement—periodically revised; Ryotwari—fixed forever; Mahalwari—fixed forever
Permanent Settlement—fixed forever; Ryotwari—fixed forever; Mahalwari—no revenue assessment
Permanent Settlement—fixed forever; Ryotwari—periodically revised; Mahalwari—periodically revised
Permanent Settlement—annually revised; Ryotwari—fixed forever; Mahalwari—annually revised
175.x: Revenue was fixed permanently under the Permanent Settlement, whereas assessments under the Ryotwari and Mahalwari systems were periodically revised.
175.tq: Compare the rate-setting column across all three systems and watch for reversed descriptions.
xs: Permanent Settlement **fixed forever**; Ryotwari and Mahalwari **periodically revised** — option **(3)**.
None of the systems was revised annually.
xa: Settlement with: **zamindars** / **individual ryots** / **village community (mahal)**.
Ownership: zamindar as proprietor / cultivator as owner / village jointly.

175.s:
Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?

a. Permanent Settlement — Zamindar
b. Ryotwari System — Individual farmer
c. Mahalwari System — Lambardar

d. Mahalwari System — Individual ryot
175.x: The zamindar was the collector under the Permanent Settlement, the individual farmer under the Ryotwari System, and the village headman or lambardar under the Mahalwari System. The individual ryot was not the collector under Mahalwari.
175.tq: Separate the person with whom settlement was made from the person responsible for collection.
xs: Pairs a, b and c are correct — option **(2) a, b and c only**.
Collection: **Zamindar** (Permanent), **individual farmer** (Ryotwari), village headman **lambardar** (Mahalwari).
Pair d wrong: Mahalwari settled with the **village community**, not the individual ryot.
xa: Intermediaries: present / absent / limited.
Mahalwari joint ownership: **Bhai Chara** or **Mahali**.

175.s: Which one of the following correctly states the consequence of default under the Ryotwari and Mahalwari systems respectively?
o: Revenue permanently remitted; village ownership abolished
175.x: Under the Ryotwari System, the cultivator's land could be seized on default. Under the Mahalwari System, the village was collectively liable for the revenue.
175.tq: Compare default consequences in sequence and avoid transferring the zamindari penalty to other systems.
xs: On default: Ryotwari — **land seized**; Mahalwari — **village collectively liable** — option **(3)**.
Zamindari confiscation or auction belongs to the **Permanent Settlement**.
xa: Zamindari defaults fell under the **Sunset Law**.
Mahalwari's **collective liability** broke village solidarity.

175.s:
Consider the following statements about the three major land-revenue settlements:
1. They made land a transferable commodity.
2. They contributed to the formation of a loyal landlord class.
3. They were associated with rural indebtedness and peasant revolts.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
175.x: The three settlements made land transferable, helped create a loyal landlord class and contributed to rural indebtedness, which in turn fed peasant revolts.
175.tq: Test the common long-term significance of several systems through cumulative statements.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
The settlements made **land a transferable commodity** and produced a **loyal landlord class**.
They led to **rural indebtedness** and **peasant revolts**.
xa: They shaped agrarian class structure that land reforms after **1947** tried to undo.
All three were **extractive**, with revenue in **cash** regardless of harvest.

175.s: Alice Thorner criticised the Ryotwari system on the ground that it—
o: abolished all direct contact between the state and zamindars
created a permanent landlord class in the Northern Circars
made the village community the sole unit of settlement
destroyed the village system and isolated farmers from the government
175.x: Alice Thorner argued that Ryotwari destroyed the village system and isolated individual farmers from the government.
175.tq: Associate a named critic with the precise argument attributed to her.
xs: **Alice Thorner** said ryotwari **destroyed the village system and isolated farmers from the government** — option **(4)**.
Making the village the unit is **Mahalwari**; a landlord class in the Circars is **zamindari**.
xa: Another criticism: the state became the **"ultimate landlord"**.
Ryotwari revenue was **as heavy as Zamindari rent**.

175.s: The statement that the state became the “ultimate landlord” was particularly connected with which criticism?
o: Permanent Settlement transferred all ownership to individual cultivators.
Inam grants were confirmed without any quit-rent.
Mahalwari abolished the role of village communities.
Ryotwari revenue was as heavy as Zamindari rent despite direct settlement with ryots.
175.x: The criticism held that the state became the ultimate landlord and that Ryotwari revenue could be as burdensome as Zamindari rent.
175.tq: Separate the formal ownership arrangement from the practical burden of revenue demand.
xs: The state as **"ultimate landlord"** goes with the criticism that **Ryotwari revenue was as heavy as Zamindari rent** — option **(4)**.
This held despite **direct settlement with ryots**.
xa: Ryotwari revenue was often **50%+** of produce.
**Alice Thorner**: ryotwari **isolated farmers** from the government.

175.s: Which of the following correctly expresses the principal Andhra contrast in land-revenue systems?
o: All three systems operated only in Rayalaseema
Mahalwari in the Circars, Zamindari in Rayalaseema and Ryotwari in Nellore
Ryotwari in the Circars, Mahalwari in Rayalaseema and Zamindari in Nellore
Zamindari in the Circars, Ryotwari in the Ceded Districts and Mahalwari in Nellore
175.x: The Andhra pattern was Zamindari in the Circars, Ryotwari in the Ceded Districts and a Mahalwari-type arrangement in Nellore.
175.tq: Use a three-region comparison to distinguish closely related settlement systems.
xs: **Zamindari in the Circars, Ryotwari in the Ceded Districts, Mahalwari in Nellore** — option **(4)**.
This contrast — **Munro**'s Rayalaseema ryotwari vs zamindari **Circars** — is a core APPSC point.
xa: Circar zamindaris: **Vizianagaram, Bobbili, Peddapuram, Pithapuram, Nuzvid**.
Ryotwari came to Rayalaseema in **1802**.
Some notes add **Chittoor** to Nellore for Mahalwari.

175.s: Why is Thomas Munro particularly remembered in relation to Rayalaseema?
o: He replaced all ryotwari settlements with village leases permanently.
He was the first Principal Collector of Rayalaseema and established the direct ryot–state relationship there.
He introduced permanent Zamindari in the Northern Circars.
He served as the first head of the Madras Inam Commission.
175.x: Munro is remembered as the first Principal Collector of Rayalaseema and for establishing its direct relationship between the ryot and the state through ryotwari administration.
175.tq: Connect an official designation with its lasting regional legacy.
xs: Munro was the **first Principal Collector of Rayalaseema** and set up the **direct ryot-state relationship** there — option **(2)** (PYQ **2025**).
He did not bring zamindari to the Circars; village leases replaced his ryotwari only after he left (**1808**).
xa: HQ: **Anantapur**; died at **Pattikonda**, buried at **Gooty** (**1827**).
He spoke **Telugu** fluently and worked without interpreters.

175.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: The Permanent Settlement covered Bengal, Bihar, Odisha and Varanasi.
The Permanent Settlement was associated with Lord Cornwallis.
The Permanent Settlement was introduced in Madras and Coorg.
Zamindars were recognised as proprietors or landowners in the permanently settled areas.
175.x: Option C is incorrect: the Permanent Settlement covered Bengal, Bihar, Odisha and Varanasi, while Madras and Coorg came under Ryotwari. Its link with Cornwallis and zamindars as owners is correct.
175.tq: Check the area in each statement.
n: The Permanent Settlement was associated with Lord Cornwallis. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #110 · pp 202-205]
The Permanent Settlement mainly covered Bengal, Bihar, Odisha and Varanasi. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #110 · pp 202-205]
The Permanent Settlement recognised zamindars as proprietors or landowners. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #110 · pp 202-205]
xs: The incorrect statement is "**The Permanent Settlement was introduced in Madras and Coorg**" — so option **(3)** is the answer.
**Madras** and **Coorg** came under the **Ryotwari Settlement**.
The **Permanent Settlement** covered **Bengal**, **Bihar**, **Odisha**, **Varanasi** and was linked with **Lord Cornwallis**.
Zamindars were recognised as **proprietors** or **landowners** — statement (4) is correct.
xa: The Permanent Settlement was introduced in **1793** (not **1795**), planned with **John Shore**.
In Andhra it was implemented in **1802** in the **Northern Circars**.
It covered about **19%** of the British-occupied area; Ryotwari **51%**; Mahalwari **30%**.

175.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Permanent Settlement established a Government–Zamindar revenue relationship.
II. Ryotwari established a Government–Ryot revenue relationship.
III. Mahalwari established a Government–Village/Mahal revenue relationship.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
175.x: All three are correct: the Permanent Settlement dealt with the zamindar, Ryotwari with the ryot, and Mahalwari with the village or mahal.
175.tq: Recall who paid revenue under each system.
n: The Permanent Settlement established a government–zamindar revenue relationship. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #110 · pp 202-205]
The Ryotwari Settlement established a government–ryot revenue relationship. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #110 · pp 202-205]
The Mahalwari Settlement established a government–village or mahal revenue relationship. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #110 · pp 202-205]
xs: All three statements are correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
I: **Permanent Settlement** — **Government–zamindar** relationship.
II: **Ryotwari** — **Government–ryot** relationship (individual ryots).
III: **Mahalwari** — **Government–village** or **mahal** relationship.
xa: Collection: **zamindar** (Permanent), **individual farmer** (Ryotwari), **village headman (lambardar)** (Mahalwari).
Intermediaries: present (Permanent), absent (Ryotwari), limited (Mahalwari).
Revenue: **permanently fixed** vs **periodically assessed** vs **periodically revised**.

175.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I
 a. Permanent Settlement
 b. Ryotwari Settlement
 c. Mahalwari Settlement
 d. Bengal Tenancy Act

List-II
 i. Mahal or village community
 ii. Lord Cornwallis
 iii. Thomas Munro and Alexander Read
 iv. Rights of landlords and tenants
175.x: The Permanent Settlement is linked to Lord Cornwallis, Ryotwari to Thomas Munro and Alexander Read, Mahalwari to the mahal or village community, and the Bengal Tenancy Act to rights of landlords and tenants, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv.
175.tq: Recall the person or feature of each settlement.
n: The Permanent Settlement was associated with Lord Cornwallis. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #110 · pp 202-205]
The Ryotwari Settlement was associated with Thomas Munro and Alexander Read. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #110 · pp 202-205]
The Mahalwari Settlement was associated with the mahal or village community. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #110 · pp 202-205]
The Bengal Tenancy Act dealt with the rights of landlords and tenants. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #110 · pp 202-205]
The village community or collective was the landholder under the Mahalwari Settlement. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #110 · pp 202-205]
xs: The correct match is **a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Permanent Settlement** — **Lord Cornwallis**; **Ryotwari** — **Thomas Munro and Alexander Read**.
**Mahalwari** — the **mahal** or **village community**; **Bengal Tenancy Act** — **rights of landlords and tenants**.
xa: The **Bengal Tenancy Act** was enacted in **1885** for **Bengal** and **Bihar**.
**Mahalwari** was devised by **Holt Mackenzie** (**1822**), revised by **R.M. Bird** (**1833**).
**Munro** is called the **Father of Ryotwari**.

175.s: The Bengal Tenancy Act of 1885 dealt with which subject?
o: Auction of Zamindaris under the Sunset Clause
175.x: The Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 dealt with the rights of landlords and tenants in Bengal and Bihar. Auction under the Sunset Clause belongs to the Permanent Settlement.
175.tq: Recall the subject of the 1885 Act.
n: The Sunset Clause required revenue payment by a prescribed sunset deadline. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #110 · pp 202-205]
Failure to pay revenue by the prescribed sunset deadline led to the auction of the zamindari. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #110 · pp 202-205]
The Bengal Tenancy Act dealt with the rights of landlords and tenants. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #110 · pp 202-205]
Thomas Munro extended the Ryotwari Settlement to almost all parts of Madras except permanently settled areas. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #110 · pp 202-205]
The Mahalwari revenue assessment was based on the village or community. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #110 · pp 202-205]
xs: The **Bengal Tenancy Act** of **1885** dealt with the **rights of landlords and tenants** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It applied to **Bengal** and **Bihar**.
Auction of zamindaris under the **Sunset Clause** belongs to the **Permanent Settlement**; village-community assessment is **Mahalwari**.
xa: **Sunset Law**: revenue due by **sunset** of the due date or the estate was **auctioned**.
Zamindari rights were **hereditary**, **transferable** or **saleable**.
The Permanent Settlement **strengthened landlords** and **increased pressure** on **peasants**.

175.s:
Match the Ryotwari-related item in List-I with the correct detail in List-II:
List-I
 a. First Ryotwari association
 b. Main area
 c. Other areas
 d. Ryotwari landholder

List-II
 i. Ryot or peasant
 ii. Madras
 iii. Baramahal, Tamil Nadu, from 1792 onward
 iv. Parts of Bombay, Assam, Coorg and Eastern Bengal
175.x: Ryotwari first began in Baramahal, Tamil Nadu, from 1792; its main area was Madras; it also covered parts of Bombay, Assam, Coorg and Eastern Bengal; and the landholder was the ryot, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.
175.tq: Recall the start, area and landholder of Ryotwari.
n: The Ryotwari Settlement mainly covered Madras, parts of Bombay, Assam and Coorg. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #110 · pp 202-205]
The first Ryotwari association began in 1792 onward in Baramahal, Tamil Nadu. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #110 · pp 202-205]
The Ryotwari Settlement also covered Eastern Bengal. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #110 · pp 202-205]
The ryot or peasant was recognised as the proprietor under the Ryotwari Settlement. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #110 · pp 202-205]
The peasant or ryot was the landholder under the Ryotwari Settlement. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #110 · pp 202-205]
xs: The correct match is **a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i** — so option **(1)** is correct.
First association: **Baramahal**, **Tamil Nadu**, from **1792**; main area: **Madras**.
Other areas: **parts of Bombay**, **Assam**, **Coorg**, **Eastern Bengal**; landholder: the **ryot** or **peasant**.
xa: **Alexander Read**, assisted by **Thomas Munro**, began it in Baramahal.
**Munro** introduced Ryotwari in **Rayalaseema (Ceded Districts)** in **1802**.
General Madras Presidency adoption came in **1820**; **Elphinstone** extended it to **Bombay**.

175.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect about the first Ryotwari association?
o: Alexander Read was assisted by Munro.
The initial demand was 30% of the estimated produce.
It was associated with Baramahal in Tamil Nadu.
175.x: Option B is incorrect: the first Ryotwari demand was 50% of the estimated produce, not 30%. Baramahal, 1792 and Read assisted by Munro are correct.
175.tq: Check the figure in each statement.
n: The first Ryotwari association began in 1792 onward in Baramahal, Tamil Nadu. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #110 · pp 202-205]
Alexander Read was assisted by Thomas Munro in the first Ryotwari association. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #110 · pp 202-205]
The initial Ryotwari revenue demand was 50% of the estimated produce. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #110 · pp 202-205]
xs: The incorrect statement is "**The initial demand was 30% of the estimated produce**" — so option **(2)** is the answer.
The initial Ryotwari demand was **50%** of the **estimated produce**.
It began in **Baramahal**, **Tamil Nadu**, from **1792**, by **Alexander Read** assisted by **Munro** — all correct.
xa: **Baramahal** = **Salem, Krishnagiri, Dharmapuri, Tiruvannamalai**; came to the Company after the **Third Mysore War (1792)**.
Ryotwari assessment was revised about **every 30 years**.
⚠ **30%** is the Mahalwari share of the British-occupied area, not the Ryotwari demand.

175.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: Under Ryotwari, a bad harvest resulted in an automatic general exemption from revenue.
Statement B: Under Ryotwari, occasional remission or reduction of revenue was possible.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
175.x: A is false: Ryotwari gave no automatic general exemption after a bad harvest. B is true because occasional remission or reduction was possible.
175.tq: Check each statement separately.
n: Ryotwari provided no automatic general exemption after a bad harvest. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #110 · pp 202-205]
Occasional remission or reduction of revenue was possible under Ryotwari after a bad harvest. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #110 · pp 202-205]
xs: Statement A is false and B is true — so option **(4)** is correct.
Under Ryotwari there was **no automatic general exemption** after a **bad harvest**.
**Occasional remission** or **reduction** of revenue was possible.
xa: Ryotwari lacked famine remission, unlike the Mughal **zabt** (**one-third** share, **taccavi** loans).
Rigid cash demand drove ryots to **moneylenders (Mahajans)**.
Ryots were not evicted while revenue was paid; they could **sell, mortgage, gift** land.

175.s:
Match the settlement with its approximate share of the British-occupied area:
List-I
 a. Permanent Settlement
 b. Ryotwari
 c. Mahalwari
 d. Ryotwari and Mahalwari together

List-II
 i. About 19%
 ii. About 51%
 iii. About 30%
 iv. About 81%
175.x: The Permanent Settlement covered about 19%, Ryotwari about 51% and Mahalwari about 30% of British-held land, so Ryotwari and Mahalwari together covered about 81%, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
175.tq: Recall each share and add the last two.
n: The Permanent Settlement covered approximately 19% of the British-occupied area. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #110 · pp 202-205]
The Ryotwari Settlement covered approximately 51% of the British-occupied area. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #110 · pp 202-205]
The Mahalwari Settlement covered approximately 30% of the British-occupied area. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #110 · pp 202-205]
xs: The correct match is **a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Permanent Settlement** about **19%**, **Ryotwari** about **51%**, **Mahalwari** about **30%** of the British-occupied area.
Ryotwari and Mahalwari together thus cover about **81%**.
xa: Mahalwari areas: **NWP (Agra-Oudh region), Punjab, Central India**.
Permanent Settlement areas: **Bengal, Bihar, Odisha**, **Varanasi**.
Ryotwari areas: **Madras**, parts of **Bombay**, **Assam**, **Coorg**.

175.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding the Taluqdari System?
o: The Taluqdari System was associated with Bombay.
The Taluqdari System was not associated with Bombay.
The Taluqdari System was associated with the Awadh region.
The Taluqdari System was associated with Awadh or Oudh.
175.x: Option A is incorrect: the Taluqdari System was linked with Awadh (Oudh), not Bombay. The other options all say this correctly.
175.tq: Recall the region of the Taluqdari System.
n: The Taluqdari System was associated with Awadh or Oudh. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #110 · pp 202-205]
The Taluqdari System was not associated with Bombay. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #110 · pp 202-205]
xs: The incorrect statement is "**The Taluqdari System was associated with Bombay**" — so option **(1)** is the answer.
The **Taluqdari System** was associated with **Awadh** or **Oudh**, **not** with **Bombay**.
Options (2), (3) and (4) all state this correctly.
xa: **Mahalwari:** revenue assessment based on the **village** or **community**; unit = **mahal**.
Mahalwari joint ownership arrangements were called **"Bhai Chara"** or **"Mahali"**.
**Bombay** came under **Ryotwari**, extended there by **Mountstuart Elphinstone**.

176.s:
Consider the following statements about the stages of colonialism in India:
1. The finance-capital stage, with British capital in railways, plantations and banks, began in 1813.
2. In the free-trade stage (1813-1858), India became a market for British goods and a source of raw materials.
3. The mercantilist stage (1757-1813) was marked by Company trade monopoly, direct plunder and Bengal revenue used to buy export goods.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
176.x: Statements 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 1 is wrong: the finance-capital stage began in 1858; 1813 (Charter Act) opened the free-trade stage. So 2 and 3 only.
176.tq: 1757 - 1813 - 1858: mercantile, free trade, finance capital.
xs: Statements **2 and 3** are correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
1 is wrong: the **finance-capital** stage began in **1858**, not **1813**.
2 is correct: **free trade** stage (**1813-1858**) — India a market for British goods and source of raw materials.
3 is correct: **mercantilist** stage (**1757-1813**) — Company trade monopoly, direct plunder, Bengal revenue buying exports.
xa: The three stages were proposed by **R.P. Dutt** (**India Today**), drawing on **Karl Marx**.
The **Charter Act 1813** ended the Company's monopoly → **one-way free trade**.
Railways gave a **guaranteed 5% interest** to British investors.

176.s: The interpretation of colonialism in terms of mercantile, industrial-capital and finance-capital stages was proposed by:
o: Dadabhai Naoroji in Poverty and Un-British Rule in India
Richard Strachey in the Famine Code
Arthur Cotton in an irrigation report
176.x: R.P. Dutt proposed the three-stage interpretation in India Today, drawing on Karl Marx.
176.tq: Match the analytical framework with its author and work, not with other economic critics.
xs: The three-stage interpretation was proposed by **R.P. Dutt** in **India Today** — option **(1)**, drawing on **Karl Marx**.
**Naoroji**'s **Poverty and Un-British Rule** is the drain-theory text; **Strachey** is linked to the Famine Code; **Arthur Cotton** to the Godavari anicut.
xa: R.P. Dutt was a **later Marxist writer**, not an original drain theorist.
⚠ Do not confuse **R.P. Dutt** (India Today) with **R.C. Dutt** (**Economic History of India**).

176.s: Who popularised the Drain of Wealth Theory in colonial India?
176.x: Dadabhai Naoroji popularised the Drain of Wealth Theory and was known as the Grand Old Man and the father of Indian Nationalism.
176.tq: Direct identification of the proponent associated with a theory.
xs: The Drain of Wealth theory was popularised by **Dadabhai Naoroji** — option **(4)** (APPSC-GS **2025**).
**R.C. Dutt**, **Ranade** and **Digby** developed or expanded it but did not popularise it.
xa: Naoroji's book: **"Poverty and Un-British Rule in India"** (**1901**).
He first stated it in **"England's Debt to India" (1867)** and coined **"moral drain"**.
He is called the **"Grand Old Man"** and **"father of Indian Nationalism"**.

176.s:
Consider the following statements about Dadabhai Naoroji:
1. He coined the term 'moral drain'.
2. He wrote 'Economic History of India'.
3. He first stated the drain argument in 'England's Debt to India' (1867).
Which of the statements given above are correct?
176.x: Statement 3 is correct. Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is wrong: 'Economic History of India' (2 vols, 1901-03) is R.C. Dutt's; Naoroji's main book is 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India' (1901). So 1 and 3 only.
176.tq: Naoroji = Poverty and Un-British Rule; R.C. Dutt = Economic History.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
1 is correct: **Dadabhai Naoroji** coined **"moral drain"**.
2 is wrong: **"Economic History of India"** is by **R.C. Dutt**; Naoroji wrote **"Poverty and Un-British Rule in India"** (**1901**).
3 is correct: he first stated the drain in **"England's Debt to India" (1867)**.
xa: **William Digby** wrote **"'Prosperous' British India"** (**1901**).
**M.G. Ranade** wrote **"Essays on Indian Economics"**.
The drain theory was **popularised by Naoroji** (APPSC-GS **2025**).
Naoroji was called the "**Grand Old Man**".

176.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: R.C. Dutt — Economic History of India
William Digby — Essays on Indian Economics
G. Subramania Iyer — Economic History of India
176.x: R.C. Dutt wrote Economic History of India in two volumes. Prosperous British India was written by William Digby, while Essays on Indian Economics was associated with M.G. Ranade.
176.tq: Use the author–work pair and reject swapped authors.
xs: **R.C. Dutt — Economic History of India** is correctly matched — option **(1)**.
**'Prosperous' British India** was by **William Digby**, not Ranade.
**Essays on Indian Economics** was by **M.G. Ranade**, not Digby.
xa: R.C. Dutt's work ran to **2 vols, 1901-03**; he critiqued the drain with Naoroji and **Dinshaw Wacha**.
⚠ **Naoroji** = Poverty and Un-British Rule; **R.C. Dutt** = Economic History; **Digby** = 'Prosperous' British India.

176.s: Which of the following best describes the Drain of Wealth from India?
o: Transfer of Indian wealth to England without an adequate economic or material return
Movement of Indian capital from agriculture to indigenous industries
Exchange of Indian primary goods for British capital goods on equal terms
Import of British gold and silver into Indian markets
176.x: The Drain represented the transfer of India's wealth to England without a corresponding economic or material return.
176.tq: Apply the definition rather than selecting an associated but incorrect trade feature.
xs: The drain was **Indian wealth sent to England with no economic or material return** — option **(1)**.
India's **export surplus** brought **no gold or silver**; it paid British office and war expenses.
xa: The drain began with the **Diwani of Bengal (1765)**.
Components: **Home Charges**, interest, salaries and pensions, railway returns, military spending, profits.
**Unequal trade** was also a component.

176.s: The Drain of Wealth from India is considered to have begun with the:
176.x: The drain is traced to the grant of the Diwani of Bengal in 1765, after which Indian resources were transferred to England without economic return.
176.tq: Chronological discrimination among closely related colonial milestones.
xs: The drain began with the **Diwani of Bengal (1765)** — option **(1)**.
**1757** opens the mercantilist stage; **1793** is the Permanent Settlement; the **Suez Canal (1869)** tightened British control later.
xa: In the mercantilist stage, **Bengal revenue** bought export goods.
Naoroji's first statement of the drain: **1867**.

176.s:
Consider the following statements about the drain of wealth:
1. In response, the Moderates demanded an expansion of military expenditure.
2. The drain stifled capital formation and industrialisation in India.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
176.x: Statement 1 is wrong: the Moderates demanded cuts in military spending, along with lower land revenue, abolition of the salt tax and protective tariffs. Statement 2 is correct. So 2 only.
176.tq: Moderates wanted less military spending.
xs: Only statement **2** is correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
1 is wrong: the **Moderates** demanded **cuts in military spending**, lower land revenue, abolition of **salt tax** and **protective tariffs**.
2 is correct: the drain **stifled capital formation and industrialisation**.
xa: The drain also **shattered the myth of British benevolence**.
Drain meaning: wealth sent to England **with no economic or material return**; began with the **Diwani of Bengal (1765)**.
Naoroji's drain reason (APPSC-GS **2024**): **profits of British capitalists** — ⚠ NOT an excess of imports.

176.s:
Consider the following statements about the components of the drain:
1. Salaries and pensions of British civil and military officials were remitted to Britain.
2. Home Charges covered the costs of the Secretary of State's India Office in London, paid from Indian revenue.
3. The interest component was interest on loans raised from Indian peasants.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
176.x: Statement 2 is correct. Statement 3 is wrong: the interest was on public debt raised in Britain. Statement 1 is correct. So 1 and 2 only.
176.tq: Home Charges + interest on British debt + salaries/pensions + profits.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — so option **(3)** is correct.
1 is correct: **salaries and pensions** of British civil and military officials were remitted home.
2 is correct: **Home Charges** covered the **Secretary of State's India Office** costs in London from Indian revenue.
3 is wrong: the **interest** was on the **public debt raised in Britain**.
xa: **Guaranteed railway returns**: assured interest (**5%**) to British investors.
**Military expenditure** was the largest single budget head.
**Profits** of British capitalists, merchants and banks and **unequal trade** were also components.

176.s:
Consider the following statements about the drain:
1. Military expenditure was the smallest of the drain components.
2. British railway investors were guaranteed a 5% return whether or not the lines earned.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
176.x: Statement 2 is correct. Statement 1 is wrong: India paid for the British Indian Army and imperial wars (Afghanistan, Burma); military spending was the largest single budget head. So 2 only.
176.tq: Military = largest head.
xs: Only statement **2** is correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
1 is wrong: **military expenditure** (British Indian Army, imperial wars in **Afghanistan**, **Burma**) was the **largest** single budget head.
2 is correct: British railway investors got a guaranteed **5%** return whether or not the lines earned.
xa: **Home Charges**: India Office costs in London.
**Interest** on the public debt raised in Britain.
India's **export surplus** brought no gold or silver — it paid for British office and war expenses.

176.s: Which of the following was identified as a reason for the Drain of Wealth in the context of British colonial rule?
o: Excess imports of gold into India
Rapid growth of Indian-owned heavy industries
Profits taken by British capitalists from India
High domestic savings by Indian peasants
176.x: Profits taken by British capitalists from India were a recognised reason for the drain. An excess of imports was not the stated explanation.
176.tq: Choose the precise drain cause instead of the reversed trade claim.
xs: Per Naoroji, the drain came from **profits taken by British capitalists from India** — option **(3)** (APPSC-GS **2024**).
⚠ Trap: the drain was NOT an **excess of imports**; India's export surplus brought **no gold or silver**.
xa: Naoroji popularised the theory (APPSC-GS **2025**).
Drain effects: stifled **capital formation** and **industrialisation**.

176.s:
Consider the following statements about India's export surplus under colonial rule:
1. It did not generally result in corresponding imports of gold or silver.
2. It helped meet British office and war expenses.
3. It represented a complete economic return to India for its exports.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
176.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The export surplus financed British expenses and invisible imports rather than providing India with a complete economic return.
176.tq: Separate the true components of export surplus from the reversed conclusion.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 correct: the **export surplus** brought **no gold or silver**.
Statement 2 correct: it paid British **office and war expenses** and invisible imports.
Statement 3 wrong: the drain is exactly wealth sent **with no economic or material return**.
xa: APPSC **2023** key: India had a **strong industrial base** before British rule.
Colonial legacy: **deindustrialisation** + drain of wealth.

176.s:
Consider the following statements about deindustrialisation:
1. The Charter Act of 1813 ended the Company's monopoly and opened India to British machine-made goods.
2. By 1850, India imported about one-half of all British cotton exports.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
176.x: Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is wrong: by 1850 India imported about one-fourth of British cotton exports. So 1 only.
176.tq: 1813 Charter Act; one-fourth by 1850.
xs: Only statement **1** is correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
1 is correct: the **Charter Act 1813** ended the Company's monopoly → **one-way free trade**, British machine goods almost duty-free.
2 is wrong: by **1850** India imported **one-fourth** of all British cotton exports.
xa: Lancashire cloth was first offered in Bengal in **1786**; by **1793** Indian calicoes and muslins were displaced.
**Heavy duties** blocked Indian manufactures in Britain.
Causes per **B.D. Basu**: loss of patronage, free trade, raw-material export, internal **transit and customs duties**, railways.

176.s: The term “one-way free trade” in the context of Indian deindustrialisation refers to
o: Free export of Indian manufactures and prohibition of British imports
Low-duty entry of British goods into India while Indian goods faced heavy duties in Britain
Exclusive trade between Indian princely states
Equal tariff treatment for Indian and British manufactures
176.x: British goods entered India almost duty-free, whereas Indian manufactures faced heavy duties in Britain.
176.tq: Discriminate between equal free trade and an unequal tariff arrangement.
xs: **One-way free trade**: British goods entered India at **low duty** while Indian goods faced **heavy duties in Britain** — option **(2)**.
It followed the **Charter Act 1813**.
xa: By **1793** Indian calicoes and muslins were displaced.
Comparative note: IMF-World Bank **Structural Adjustment Programmes** caused deindustrialisation by the same logic.

176.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the causes of deindustrialisation:
1. Railways carried British goods into the interior.
2. Artisans were forced to reveal trade secrets.
3. Internal transit duties and customs duties affected indigenous trade.
4. British traders were denied special privileges.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
176.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. British traders received special privileges, so statement 4 is false.
176.tq: Test a cluster of causes while reversing one key relationship.
xs: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct — option **(1) 1, 2 and 3 only**.
**Railways** carried British goods inland; artisans were forced to **divulge trade secrets**; **transit and customs duties** hurt trade.
Statement 4 wrong: British traders got **special privileges**.
xa: Causes are from **B.D. Basu**'s list.
Weavers were coerced by Company agents (**Bolt, 1772**).

176.s:
Consider the following statements about the results of deindustrialisation:
1. Ruined artisans moved to the land, causing overcrowding of agriculture and disguised unemployment.
2. Karl Marx said the British had 'inundated the very mother country of cotton with cottons'.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
176.x: Statement 2 is correct: Marx's phrase. Statement 1 is correct: the collapse of town handicrafts pushed artisans onto the land. So both.
176.tq: Collapse of handicrafts -> pressure on land.
xs: Both statements are correct — so option **(3)** is correct.
1 is correct: artisans pushed onto the land caused **overcrowding of agriculture** and **disguised unemployment**.
2 is correct: **Karl Marx** said the British "**inundated the very mother country of cotton with cottons**".
xa: Town handicrafts suffered a "**sudden and complete collapse**".
Famines also pushed weavers into agriculture or wage labour.
Artisans were even forced to divulge **trade secrets**.

176.s: The cotton excise duty imposed during 1894–96 on Indian mill cloth was intended to
o: promote the export of Indian handlooms to China
abolish all duties on Indian textiles
offset the import duty on British goods
176.x: The cotton excise duty of 1894–96 on Indian mill cloth was imposed to offset the import duty and is a classic example of tariff policy.
176.tq: Connect the date range with the purpose of the tariff measure.
xs: The **cotton excise duty (1894-96)** on Indian mill cloth was meant to **offset the import duty** on British goods — option **(3)**.
It is the classic example of colonial **tariff policy**.
xa: The Moderates demanded **protective tariffs** for Indian industry.
**Cotton mills** in Maharashtra and Gujarat were **Indian-owned**; jute mills were foreign-owned.

176.s: During the British period in Andhra, which sector provided the second-largest employment after agriculture?
176.x: Textiles provided the second-largest employment in Andhra after agriculture during the British period.
176.tq: Directly identify the sector associated with the stated employment rank.
xs: **Textiles** were Andhra's **second-largest employment after agriculture** in the British period — option **(4)** (APPSC-GS **2025**).
**Machilipatnam** was the most famous handloom and textile port of the **16th-17th centuries**.
xa: Andhra products: **Srikakulam** muslin, **Uppada** jamdani silk, **Ponduru** khadi.
**Nellore** was the world leader in **manganese** (**1892-1929**).

176.s:
Consider the following statements about Machilipatnam:
1. Its fame as a handloom and textile port came only in the 19th century.
2. It was known for chintz, dyed fabrics and muslins.
3. The Dutch set up their first Andhra factory there.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
176.x: Statement 1 is wrong: Machilipatnam was the most famous handloom and textile port of the 16th-17th centuries. Statement 2 is correct. Statement 3 is correct (APHQ 2017). So 2 and 3 only.
176.tq: Machilipatnam = 16th-17th c. chintz port, first Dutch factory.
xs: Statements **2 and 3** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
1 is wrong: **Machilipatnam** was the most famous textile port of the **16th-17th centuries**.
2 is correct: known for **chintz** (painted cloth), **dyed fabrics** and **muslins**.
3 is correct: the **Dutch** set up their first Andhra factory there (APHQ **2017**).
xa: ⚠ **Srikakulam** = muslin; **Eluru** = carpets; **Kurnool** = blankets; **Nellore** = towels.
**Uppada** = Jamdani silk; **Ponduru** = fine hand-spun **khadi**.
**Textiles** were the **second-largest employment after agriculture** in Andhra (APPSC-GS **2025**).

176.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Place)
 a. Srikakulam
 b. Machilipatnam
 c. Nellore
 d. Eluru

List-II (Product)
 i. Towels
 ii. Carpets
 iii. Muslin
 iv. Dyed clothes

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
176.x: Srikakulam is associated with muslin, Machilipatnam with dyed clothes, Nellore with towels and Eluru with carpets.
176.tq: Start from the sure place–product pairs and eliminate codes.
xs: **Srikakulam–Muslin, Machilipatnam–Dyed clothes, Nellore–Towels, Eluru–Carpets** — option **(1) a–iii, b–iv, c–i, d–ii**.
Machilipatnam's broader range was **chintz**, dyed fabrics and muslins, but in the place table it is **dyed clothes**; muslin goes to **Srikakulam**.
xa: **Kurnool** = blankets; **Tuni** = long cloths.
**Uppada** = jamdani silk; **Ponduru** = fine hand-spun khadi.
Silk clothes: **Peddapuram, Dharmavaram, Adoni, Bellary**.

176.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Uppada was associated with jamdani silk.
2. Ponduru was known for fine hand-spun khadi.
3. Ponduru is associated with Srikakulam.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
176.x: Uppada was known for jamdani silk, while Ponduru was known for fine hand-spun khadi and is associated with Srikakulam.
176.tq: Check each component of the named weaving-centre associations.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
**Uppada** = **jamdani silk**; **Ponduru** = fine hand-spun **khadi**, in **Srikakulam**.
xa: **Srikakulam** itself was famous for **muslin**.
Andhra's examinable textile set: **Machilipatnam, Srikakulam, Uppada, Ponduru**.

176.s:
Consider the following statements about indigo:
1. Under the Tinkathiya system, indigo had to be grown on 3/20 of each holding.
2. The Indigo Revolt of 1859-60 broke out in Gujarat.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
176.x: Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is wrong: the Indigo Revolt of 1859-60 was in Bengal. So 1 only.
176.tq: Indigo = Bengal-Bihar.
xs: Only statement **1** is correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
1 is correct: under **Tinkathiya**, indigo was grown on **3/20** of each holding.
2 is wrong: the **Indigo Revolt (1859-60)** broke out in **Bengal**.
xa: Indigo regions: **Bengal**, **Bihar**; jute: **Bengal**; tea: **Assam**.
Peasants grew cash crops to pay the **cash revenue**, not by choice → **famines** frequent.
**Triangular trade:** Indian **opium to China** → Chinese **tea** to Britain → British **manufactures to India**.

176.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Crop)
 a. Cotton
 b. Jute
 c. Opium
 d. Tea

List-II (Main region)
 i. Assam
 ii. Bengal
 iii. Deccan, Gujarat and Berar
 iv. Bengal-Bihar and Malwa

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
176.x: Cotton was associated with the Deccan, Gujarat and Berar; jute with Bengal; opium with Bengal-Bihar and Malwa; and tea with Assam.
176.tq: Start with the distinctive Assam–tea pair and complete the regional matches.
xs: **Cotton–Deccan, Gujarat, Berar; Jute–Bengal; Opium–Bengal-Bihar, Malwa; Tea–Assam** — option **(1) a–iii, b–ii, c–iv, d–i**.
**Indigo** (not in the list) belonged to **Bengal, Bihar**.
xa: First tea company: **Assam Company, 1839**.
First jute mill: **Rishra (Bengal), 1855**.
Indian **opium** fed the triangular trade with **China**.

176.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the triangular trade involving India, China and Britain?
o: Indian tea to China, Chinese manufactures to Britain, British opium to India
Indian opium to China, Chinese tea and silver to Britain, British manufactures to India
Indian silver to Britain, British tea to China, Chinese manufactures to India
British cotton to China, Chinese opium to India, Indian tea to Britain
176.x: The triangular trade consisted of Indian opium going to China, Chinese tea and silver going to Britain, and British manufactures going to India.
176.tq: Follow the direction of each commodity in the triangular exchange.
xs: **Indian opium to China → Chinese tea and silver to Britain → British manufactures to India** — option **(2)**.
India supplied the raw commodity, not tea or silver.
xa: Opium regions: **Bengal-Bihar, Malwa**.
The **Suez Canal (1869)** tightened British control of trade.

176.s:
Assertion (A): Famines became frequent in areas affected by the commercialisation of agriculture.
Reason (R): Cash crops increasingly replaced food crops, reducing food security.

Select the correct answer.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
176.x: Both statements are true, and the replacement of food crops by cash crops directly explains the decline in food security and the increased frequency of famines.
176.tq: Test whether the reason directly explains the asserted consequence.
xs: **Both A and R are true** and R is the **correct explanation** of A — option **(1)**.
Cash crops replaced food crops, so **food security fell** and **famines** became frequent.
xa: **1854-1901**: **24** famines, about **29 million** deaths.
**Gajula Lakshmi Narasu Setti** reported famines from commercialisation in **"The Crescent"**.

176.s: Which newspaper and organisation are associated with Gajula Lakshmi Narasu Setti in the context of famine-related criticism in Andhra?
o: The Crescent and Chennapatnam Swadeshi Sangam
The Hindu and Madras Mahajana Sabha
Amrita Bazar Patrika and Indian Association
176.x: Gajula Lakshmi Narasu Setti reported Andhra famines in his paper The Crescent and founded the Chennapatnam Swadeshi Sangam.
176.tq: Match the individual with the publication and organisation associated with him.
xs: **Gajula Lakshmi Narasu Setti**: newspaper **"The Crescent"** and the **Chennapatnam Swadeshi Sangam (1852)** — option **(1)**.
He reported famines caused by **commercialisation of agriculture**.
xa: Andhra famines: **Guntur 1832-33** (**Dokkala / Nandana Karuvu**), **Kurnool 1866**.
Late **19th** century: **11** famines in Andhra; **1865-66** the most severe.

176.s:
Consider the following statements about peasant protection laws:
1. The Punjab Land Alienation Act, 1900, sought to stop the transfer of land from agriculturists to non-agriculturist moneylenders.
2. The Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act, 1879, protected peasants against moneylenders.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
176.x: Statement 2 is correct: it followed the Deccan riots of 1875. Statement 1 is correct. So both.
176.tq: Both laws target moneylenders.
xs: Both statements are correct — so option **(3)** is correct.
1 is correct: the **Punjab Land Alienation Act, 1900** stopped land transfer to **non-agriculturist moneylenders**.
2 is correct: the **Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act, 1879** protected peasants against **moneylenders**, after the Deccan riots of **1875**.
xa: The **cotton excise duty (1894-96)** on Indian mill cloth is the classic "tariff policy" example.
The **Famine Code** of **1883** was based on the **Strachey** report.
Rigid cash demand drove ryots to **moneylenders (Mahajans)**.

176.s:
Consider the following statements about the Guntur famine of 1832-33:
1. It is known as Dokkala or Nandana Karuvu.
2. It killed about two lakh people and was the worst famine in the south.
3. It led to the Krishna anicut built under MacDonnell.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
176.x: Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is correct: about half the population died (APHQ 2019). Statement 3 is wrong: the famine pushed irrigation, notably Arthur Cotton's Godavari anicut (1847-52); MacDonnell headed the 1901 famine commission. So only two.
176.tq: Guntur famine -> Arthur Cotton's Godavari anicut.
xs: **Only two** statements (1 and 2) are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
1 is correct: the **Guntur famine (1832-33)** is called **Dokkala / Nandana Karuvu**.
2 is correct: about **2 lakh** died, half the population — the worst in the south.
3 is wrong: it led to **Arthur Cotton's** **Godavari anicut** (**1847-52**); **MacDonnell** headed the **1901** famine commission.
xa: Missionary **John Clough**'s canal relief project = best-known relief effort.
⚠ Guntur famine = **1832-33**; **Kurnool** famine = **1866**.
**1876-78 Great Famine** devastated **Rayalaseema** and parts of coastal Andhra.

176.s:
Consider the following statements about the Kurnool famine of 1866:
1. Budda Vengalareddy of Uyyalawada fed the people and later received a gold medal from Queen Victoria.
2. About 40% of the district's people died.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
176.x: Statement 2 is correct. Statement 1 is correct: he received the medal on 1 January 1877. So both.
176.tq: Kurnool 1866 = Budda Vengalareddy.
xs: Both statements are correct — so option **(3)** is correct.
1 is correct: **Budda Vengalareddy** of **Uyyalawada** fed the people; got a gold medal from **Victoria** (**1 Jan 1877**).
2 is correct: **40%** of the district died in the **1866 Kurnool** famine.
xa: In the late 19th century Andhra had **11** famines; **1865-66** was the most severe.
**Ganjam**: ryots switched from paddy to **cotton** in the **American Civil War (1861-65)**; prices collapsed after it.
**Northern Coastal Famine (1945)**: **K.S. Gupta** formed a Famine Relief Committee.

176.s:
Consider the following statements about famines:
1. Between 1854 and 1901 India had 24 famines that killed about 9 million people.
2. Andhra suffered eleven famines in the late 19th century, 1865-66 being the most severe.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
176.x: Statement 2 is correct. Statement 1 is wrong: the 24 famines of 1854-1901 killed about 29 million. So 2 only.
176.tq: 24 famines, 29 million deaths.
xs: Only statement **2** is correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
1 is wrong: the **24 famines** of **1854-1901** killed about **29 million**, not 9 million.
2 is correct: Andhra had **11** famines in the late 19th century; **1865-66** the most severe.
xa: The **Bengal famine 1943** killed about **3 million**.
The **1832-33 Guntur** famine (**Dokkala Karuvu**) killed about **2 lakh**.
**1876-78 Great Famine**: relief was **laissez-faire**.

176.s:
Match List-I (Famine Commission) with List-II (Context):
List-I
a. Campbell
b. Richard Strachey
c. Lyall
d. MacDonnell
List-II
i. 1901, under Curzon
ii. 1866 Orissa famine
iii. 1880, after the Great Famine of 1876-78
iv. 1897-98, after the 1896-97 famine
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
176.x: Campbell = 1866 Orissa famine; Strachey = 1880, after 1876-78 (its report led to the 1883 Famine Code); Lyall = 1897-98; MacDonnell = 1901 (Curzon). Option A swaps Campbell and Strachey, B swaps Strachey and Lyall, D swaps Campbell and MacDonnell.
176.tq: Campbell 1866, Strachey 1880, Lyall 1898, MacDonnell 1901.
xs: The correct match is **a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Campbell**: **1866 Orissa famine**; **Richard Strachey**: **1880**, after the Great Famine of **1876-78** (Lytton).
**Lyall**: **1897-98**, after the **1896-97** famine (Elgin II); **MacDonnell**: **1901** under **Curzon**.
xa: The **Famine Code** (**1883**) was based on the **Strachey** report.
Famine Commission chain: **Strachey** (Lytton) → **Lyall** (Elgin II) → **MacDonnell** (Curzon).
The **Hilton Young Commission (1926)** dealt with **currency**, not famine.

176.s: What was the principal economic cause associated with the Ganjam famine of 1865–66?
o: The Company stopped collecting revenue in the Northern Circars.
Irrigation expansion caused rice prices to fall after the war.
Ryots shifted from cotton to paddy during the American Civil War.
Ryots shifted from paddy to cotton during the American Civil War, followed by a collapse in cotton prices.
176.x: During the American Civil War, ryots shifted from paddy to cotton. After the war, cotton prices collapsed and rice became scarce, contributing to the Ganjam famine.
176.tq: Trace the cause-effect chain instead of selecting an isolated crop or price statement.
xs: During the **American Civil War (1861-65)** Ganjam ryots switched **from paddy to cotton**, then **cotton prices collapsed** — option **(4)**.
Option 3 reverses the switch.
xa: After the war, rice was scarce — food shortage when demand ended (**1865**).
People migrated to **South Africa, Sri Lanka, Mauritius**.
In Ryotwari areas the cotton slump caused **defaults** and land loss to moneylenders.

176.s: Which of the following statements correctly describes the Great Madras Famine of 1876–78?
o: The famine was confined to Bengal and relief was organised exclusively through grain imports.
Laissez-faire relief aggravated the famine, while John Clough’s canal project was a notable relief effort.
It affected only Hyderabad and was relieved through the Temple wage alone.
It began after the Northern Coastal cyclones of 1945.
176.x: The Great Madras Famine affected Rayalaseema and coastal Andhra. Laissez-faire relief worsened the crisis, while missionary John Clough’s canal relief project was a notable response.
176.tq: Apply the relationship between policy failure, affected region and relief initiative.
xs: In the **Great Famine (1876-78)**, **laissez-faire relief** made things worse; **John Clough**'s canal relief project was the best-known relief effort — option **(2)**.
It devastated **Rayalaseema** and parts of coastal Andhra, not just Bengal.
The **1945** Northern Coastal Famine came after cyclones — a different event.
xa: The **Strachey** Commission (**1880**) followed this famine.
The Great Famine came under **Lytton**; its report led to the **Famine Code (1883)**.

176.s: The Famine Code, based on the report of the Richard Strachey Famine Commission, was issued in:
176.x: The Famine Code was issued in 1883 on the basis of the Strachey Commission report (APPSC-G1 2022). 1866 is the Campbell Commission (Orissa famine), 1880 is when the Strachey Commission was appointed, and 1901 is the MacDonnell Commission.
176.tq: Strachey Commission 1880 -> Famine Code 1883.
xs: The **Famine Code** was issued in **1883**, based on the **Strachey** report — option **(3)** (APPSC-G1 **2022**).
**1880** is the Strachey Commission itself; **1866** is Campbell; **1901** is MacDonnell.
xa: The Strachey Commission followed the Great Famine of **1876-78** (**Lytton**).

176.s: The Bombay Spinning and Weaving Company, established in 1854, is associated with which person?
176.x: The Bombay Spinning and Weaving Company was established in 1854 by Cowasji Nanabhai Davar.
176.tq: Use the founder–enterprise association and reject names linked with other economic issues.
xs: The **Bombay Spinning and Weaving Co. (1854)** is linked to **Cowasji Nanabhai Davar** (C.N. Davar) — option **(3)**.
**Purshottamdas Thakurdas** argued for a **1s 4d** rupee; **Arthur Cotton** built anicuts.
xa: ⚠ First cotton mill = **Bombay 1854**; first jute mill = **Rishra 1855**.
Cotton mills were **Indian-owned** in **Maharashtra** and **Gujarat**.

176.s:
Consider the following statements about early modern industry in India:
1. TISCO was incorporated in 1907 at Jamshedpur.
2. The first jute mill was set up at Rishra in Bengal in 1855.
3. The Assam Company, the first tea company, was set up in 1854.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
176.x: Statement 2 is correct: Rishra, 1855. Statement 3 is wrong: the Assam Company dates from 1839; 1854 is the Bombay Spinning and Weaving Co. (first cotton mill). Statement 1 is correct. So 1 and 2 only.
176.tq: Tea 1839, cotton 1854, jute 1855, TISCO 1907.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — so option **(3)** is correct.
1 is correct: **TISCO** was incorporated in **1907** at **Jamshedpur**.
2 is correct: first jute mill at **Rishra (Bengal)**, **1855**.
3 is wrong: the **Assam Company** dates from **1839**; **1854** is the **Bombay Spinning and Weaving Co.** (first cotton mill).
xa: The first cotton mill was founded by **C.N. Davar** (**Cowasji Nanabhai Davar**).
**Nellore** district was the world leader in **manganese** (**1892-1929**); **mica** also from Nellore.
Andhra jute mills: **Chittivalasa and Nellimarla**; first Andhra railway **Puttur-Renigunta (1862)**.

176.s: The first railway in the Andhra region mentioned in the context of colonial industrial development was opened between:
176.x: The first railway was the Puttur-Renigunta line, opened in 1862.
176.tq: Use the exact terminal-pair distinction to avoid confusing railways with industrial centres.
xs: Andhra's first railway ran between **Puttur and Renigunta (1862)** — option **(3)**.
**Chittivalasa and Nellimarla** were jute mills, not a rail line.
xa: Railways guaranteed **5%** interest to British investors.
Railways carried raw materials out and British goods inland.

176.s: Which one of the following statements about early industrialisation in Andhra Pradesh is NOT correctly matched?
176.x: Ponduru was associated with Andhra textiles, not an iron and steel plant. Chittivalasa and Nellimarla had jute mills, while Rajahmundry had a paper mill.
176.tq: Find the industry–location mismatch among otherwise familiar Andhra associations.
xs: **Ponduru — iron and steel plant** is wrongly matched — option **(1)**; Ponduru is known for fine hand-spun **khadi**.
**Rajahmundry** = paper mill; **Chittivalasa** and **Nellimarla** = jute mills (**1920s**).
xa: Cotton ginning was at **Anantapur, Guntur, East Godavari, Kurnool**.
The first iron and steel unit was **TISCO (1907)** at **Jamshedpur**.

176.s: During 1892-1929, which district of the Andhra region was a world leader in the production of manganese?
176.x: Nellore district was the world leader in manganese during 1892-1929 (APHQ 2019 key; some sources credit Vizag). Kurnool, Anantapur and Guntur are associated with cotton ginning, not world-leading manganese output.
176.tq: Nellore = manganese (APHQ 2019) and mica.
xs: **Nellore** district was the world leader in **manganese** in **1892-1929** — option **(3)** (APHQ **2019** key).
Some notes say **Vizag** district (world No.1 till **1929**).
xa: Nellore was also known for **mica**.
Nellore manganese + Andhra textiles = Andhra's examinable pair.

176.s:
Consider the following statements about the Hilton Young Commission (1926):
1. Its recommendation of a central bank led to the Reserve Bank of India in 1935.
2. It fixed the rupee at 1 shilling 4 pence.
3. It was the Royal Commission on Indian Currency and Finance.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
176.x: Statement 3 is correct. Statement 2 is wrong: it fixed the rupee at 1s 6d; Indian business (Purshottamdas Thakurdas) wanted 1s 4d. Statement 1 is correct. So 1 and 3 only.
176.tq: Hilton Young = 1s 6d + RBI.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — so option **(3)** is correct.
1 is correct: its **central bank** recommendation led to the **RBI (1935)**.
2 is wrong: it fixed the rupee at **1s 6d** (**18 pence**); Indian business wanted **1s 4d**.
3 is correct: it was the **Royal Commission on Indian Currency and Finance**.
xa: **Purshottamdas Thakurdas** led Indian business opposition to the higher ratio.
The higher ratio made British imports cheaper and hurt Indian exporters.
⚠ Hilton Young = **1s 6d**; Indian demand = **1s 4d**.

176.s:
Assertion (A): The higher rupee-sterling ratio hurt Indian exporters.
Reason (R): The higher ratio made British imports cheaper in India.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
176.x: Both statements are true, but R does not explain A. A higher rupee-sterling ratio (1s 6d rather than the 1s 4d Indian business wanted) made Indian goods dearer abroad, and that is what hurt exporters. Cheaper British imports were a separate effect that hurt Indian producers in the home market.
176.tq: Test whether the economic consequence in the Reason explains the currency-policy criticism in the Assertion.
xs: **Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A** — option **(2)**.
The notes list both as separate effects of the higher ratio: it **made British imports cheaper** and it **hurt Indian exporters**.
Cheaper British imports is a parallel effect, not the reason exporters suffered.
xa: Hilton Young (**1926**) fixed **1s 6d**; Indian business wanted **1s 4d**.
The Commission also led to the **RBI (1935)**.

176.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the relationship between agriculture and GDP in India on the eve of independence?
o: Over 75% of the workforce was in agriculture, which contributed about 50% of GDP.
Agriculture employed less than 25% of the workforce but contributed about 50% of GDP.
About 50% of the workforce was in agriculture, which contributed over 75% of GDP.
Agriculture employed over 75% of the workforce and contributed over 75% of GDP.
176.x: More than 75 percent of the workforce depended on agriculture, but the sector contributed only about 50 percent of GDP, indicating low productivity and disguised unemployment.
176.tq: Match the workforce share with the corresponding GDP share.
xs: In **1947**, **over 75%** of the workforce was in agriculture, which gave only about **50% of GDP** — option **(1)**.
This meant **disguised unemployment** and low productivity.
xa: Per-capita income: **Rs 265** a year (~**$60**).
Life expectancy **32 years**; literacy **under 16%** (female under **9%**).

176.s:
Consider the following statements about Indian industry on the eve of independence:
1. Indian-owned cotton mills were concentrated in Maharashtra and Gujarat, and foreign-owned jute mills in Bengal.
2. India had a strong capital-goods base.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
176.x: Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is wrong: there was no capital-goods base; basic and capital goods were only about one-fourth of industrial output. So 1 only.
176.tq: Cotton Indian-owned, jute foreign-owned; no capital goods.
xs: Only statement **1** is correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
1 is correct: Indian-owned **cotton mills** in **Maharashtra** and **Gujarat**; foreign-owned **jute mills** in **Bengal**.
2 is wrong: there was **no capital-goods base**; basic/capital goods were only **one-fourth** of industrial output.
xa: In **1947**: per-capita income **Rs 265**; life expectancy **32 years**; literacy **under 16%**.
Over **75%** of the workforce was in agriculture, giving only about **50% of GDP**.
**Angus Maddison**: world income share fell from **27% (1700) to 3% (1950)** (APPSC-GS **2024**).

176.s:
Which of the following statements correctly describes deindustrialisation in colonial India?
1. British policy contributed to the decline of Indian industry.
2. Indian industry lost markets.
3. Agriculture remained stagnant with low productivity.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
176.x: All three statements are correct. British policy contributed to deindustrialisation, industry declined through loss of markets and agriculture remained stagnant with low productivity.
176.tq: Test the linked features of deindustrialisation and agrarian stagnation together.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** (APPSC **2023** keys).
**Deindustrialisation** came by British policy; industry declined from **loss of markets**.
Agriculture stayed **stagnant with low productivity**.
xa: India had a **strong industrial base** before British rule.
The economy was **agrarian**.

176.s: On the eve of independence, which one of the following combinations is correct regarding India’s socio-economic conditions?
o: Per capita income about Rs 1,000, life expectancy 50 years and literacy above 30%
Per capita income about Rs 265, life expectancy 50 years and literacy above 25%
Per capita income about Rs 500, life expectancy 32 years and literacy above 30%
Per capita income about Rs 265, life expectancy 32 years and literacy below 16%
176.x: Per capita income was approximately Rs 265, life expectancy was 32 years and literacy was below 16% on the eve of independence.
176.tq: Test the complete data combination rather than an isolated indicator.
xs: In **1947**: per-capita income about **Rs 265**, life expectancy **32 years**, literacy **below 16%** — option **(4)**.
Life expectancy was not **50**, and literacy was not above **25%** or **30%**.
xa: Female literacy was under **9%**.
Per-capita income ~**$60** a year.

176.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Basic and capital goods — approximately one-fourth of industrial output
Suez Canal — tightened British control over trade
Public sector before independence — steel, automobiles and aviation as its principal areas
176.x: Before independence, the public sector was limited mainly to railways, power, communications and ports. It did not principally cover all the industries listed in option d.
176.tq: Find the option that extends a limited colonial public sector beyond its stated scope.
xs: **Public sector — steel, automobiles and aviation** is wrongly matched — option **(4)**.
The public sector was **limited to railways, power, communications, ports**.
Capital goods ~**one-fourth** of output, **TISCO 1907** and the **Suez Canal (1869)** are correct.
xa: Before **1914** about **97%** of British capital went to government projects, plantations and finance houses.
⚠ **Cotton mills** = Indian-owned; **jute mills** = foreign-owned.

176.s: Which of the following received top priority in the First Plan in response to the immediate economic challenges after independence?
o: Heavy engineering, automobiles and export subsidies
176.x: Large foodgrain imports and inflation led the First Plan to give top priority to agriculture, irrigation and power. Post-partition stabilisation was another immediate challenge.
176.tq: Link the policy priority with the immediate food and inflation problem.
xs: The **First Plan** gave top priority to **agriculture, irrigation, power** — option **(4)**.
This answered **large foodgrain imports and inflation**.
xa: Other challenge: **post-partition stabilisation**.
Agriculture had **over 75%** of the workforce but only about **50%** of GDP.

176.s: According to Angus Maddison, India's share of world income changed from about ______ in 1700 to about ______ in 1950.
176.x: Maddison's estimate (APPSC-GS 2024 key) is that India's share of world income fell from about 27% in 1700 to about 3% in 1950, reflecting deindustrialisation and drain. The reversed pair (3% to 27%) is wrong, and 50%/10% and 15%/7% are not the cited figures.
176.tq: Maddison PYQ pair: 27% (1700) -> 3% (1950).
xs: Maddison: India's world income share fell from **27 per cent** (**1700**) to **3 per cent** (**1950**) — option **(1)** (APPSC-GS **2024** key).
Option 2 reverses the pair; learn the PYQ pair for MCQs.
xa: Some notes give world GDP share **22.6% (1700) to 3.8% (1952)**.
The **1700** figure was almost Europe's **23.3%**.

176.s: Which statement best expresses the economic transformation of India under colonial rule?
o: India retained its position as an autonomous industrial exporter throughout colonial rule.
India changed from a raw-material supplier into the leading exporter of manufactures.
India changed from a leading exporter of manufactures into a supplier of raw materials.
India became exclusively a financial centre without agricultural exports.
176.x: Colonial economic change involved the decline of India's manufacturing export position and its transformation into a supplier of raw materials.
176.tq: Test the direction of structural change; reversed comparisons are the principal distractor.
xs: India changed **from a leading exporter of manufactures into a supplier of raw materials** — option **(3)**.
Option 2 reverses the direction.
xa: APPSC **2023** key: India had a **strong industrial base** before British rule.
Maddison: world income share **27% (1700) to 3% (1950)**.

176.s: The economic critique of colonialism made by the Moderates became an important base for:
o: The Swadeshi movement and early nationalism
The expansion of Company trade monopoly
176.x: The drain theory and the wider economic critique were major contributions of the Moderates and helped provide the basis for Swadeshi and early nationalism.
176.tq: Trace the political consequence of an economic critique rather than selecting an administrative reform.
xs: The Moderates' economic critique was a base for **Swadeshi** and **early nationalism** — option **(1)**.
Drain theory = the Moderates' **greatest contribution**.
xa: **Naoroji** popularised it; **R.C. Dutt** and **Ranade** expanded it.
The **Famine Code (1883)** came from the Strachey report, not from the Moderates.

176.s:
Assertion (A): Colonial railways and ports had a dual economic character.
Reason (R): They served military mobility and raw-material extraction, while also integrating the Indian economy.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
176.x: Both statements are true. The infrastructure served colonial military and extractive purposes but also produced the unintended effect of integrating the economy.
176.tq: Recognise a balanced historical assessment instead of treating the infrastructure as wholly beneficial or wholly destructive.
xs: **Both A and R are true** and R is the **correct explanation** of A — option **(1)**.
Railways and ports were built for **military mobility** and **raw-material extraction**, yet **integrated the economy**.
xa: Railways gave a **guaranteed 5%** to British investors.
Andhra's first railway: **Puttur-Renigunta (1862)**.

177.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Orissa Famine — West and central India, 1899–1900
177.x: The Chalisa famine of 1783-84 struck North India (Delhi, Awadh, Punjab). The other pairs are wrong: Doji Bara was 1791-92 in the Deccan, Hyderabad and the Northern Circars (Bengal 1770 is the Great Bengal Famine); the 1943 Bengal famine is not the 'Great Famine' (that name belongs to 1876-78 and 1896-97); and the Orissa famine was 1865-66 (1899-1900 hit west and central India).
177.tq: Use the year-region pair to eliminate swapped famine locations.
xs: **Chalisa Famine — North India, 1783-84** is correctly matched — option **(1)**.
**Doji Bara** was **1791-92** in the Deccan, Hyderabad and Northern Circars, not Bengal 1770.
The **1943** famine was the **Bengal Famine**; the Great Famine was **1876-78**; the **1899-1900** famine (West and central India) was not the Orissa famine.
xa: Chalisa hit **Delhi, Awadh, Punjab**; it is named after **Vikram Samvat 1840**.
⚠ **Chalisa** = North India (**1783-84**); **Doji Bara** = skull famine (**1791-92**).
The **Orissa** famine was **1865-66**.

177.s: The Orissa and Ganjam famine of 1865–66 led to the appointment of which commission?
177.x: The Orissa and Ganjam famine of 1865–66 led to the Campbell Commission.
177.tq: Link a famine directly with the commission appointed after it.
xs: The **Orissa and Ganjam famine (1865-66)** led to the **Campbell Commission** — option **(1)**.
Campbell (**1866**) was under Viceroy **John Lawrence** — the **first famine commission**.
xa: **MacDonnell** (**1901**, Curzon) followed the **1899-1900** famine.
**Lyall** followed the **1896-97** famine (**Elgin II**).
Last colonial commission: **Woodhead (1944)**.

177.s: Which of the following statements regarding the Great Famine of 1876–78 is correct?
o: It was confined to the Northern Circars under Cartier.
It occurred in West and Central India under Curzon.
It affected Madras, Mysore, Hyderabad and Bombay under Lytton.
It affected only Bengal and Bihar under Elgin II.
177.x: The Great Famine of 1876–78 affected Madras, Mysore, Hyderabad and Bombay and occurred during Lytton’s tenure. It also devastated Rayalaseema and coastal Andhra.
177.tq: Discriminate a famine by combining its year, affected regions and contemporary Viceroy.
xs: The **Great Famine of 1876-78** hit **Madras, Mysore, Hyderabad and Bombay** under **Lytton** — option **(3)**.
**Cartier** was the **1770** Bengal famine; **Curzon** the **1899-1900** famine; **Elgin II** the **1896-97** famine.
xa: It devastated **Rayalaseema** and coastal Andhra.
The **Strachey Commission (1880)** followed, leading to the **Famine Code, 1883**.
**Sir Richard Temple** fixed the **Temple wage** in the **1877 Madras famine**.

177.s:
Arrange the following famines in chronological order:
A. Great Bengal Famine
B. Doji Bara Famine
C. Orissa and Ganjam Famine
D. Great Famine of 1876–78
177.x: The correct sequence is Great Bengal Famine (1770), Doji Bara (1791–92), Orissa and Ganjam (1865–66), and Great Famine (1876–78).
177.tq: Fix the earliest and latest events first, then place the middle famines by year.
xs: Order: **Great Bengal (1770)** → **Doji Bara (1791-92)** → **Orissa and Ganjam (1865-66)** → **Great Famine (1876-78)** — option **(1) A, B, C, D**.
The **1770** famine came under **Cartier**; the **1876-78** famine under **Lytton**.
xa: **Chalisa** (**1783-84**) falls between the first two.
**Guntur** (**1832-33**) falls between Doji Bara and Orissa.

177.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Bengal Famine of 1943 — Bengal — Linlithgow and Wavell years
Great Famine of 1896–97 — Many parts of India — Elgin II
Great Bengal Famine of 1770 — Bengal — Lytton
Famine of 1899–1900 — West and Central India — Curzon
177.x: The Great Bengal Famine of 1770 occurred under Cartier, not Lytton. The other pairs are correctly matched.
177.tq: Find the swapped administrator in an otherwise familiar famine association.
xs: **Great Bengal Famine of 1770 — Lytton** is wrongly matched — option **(3)**; it was under **Cartier**.
**Lytton** belongs to the **1876-78** Great Famine.
**1943**–Linlithgow and Wavell, **1896-97**–Elgin II and **1899-1900**–Curzon are correct.
xa: In **1770** about **two million** died; the Company **kept collecting revenue**.
**Woodhead (1944)** under **Wavell** followed the **Bengal Famine 1943**.

177.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Commission)
(a) Campbell
(b) Strachey
(c) Lyall
(d) MacDonnell

List-II (Viceroy)
(i) Curzon
(ii) Elgin II
(iii) John Lawrence
(iv) Lytton

Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
177.x: Campbell was associated with John Lawrence, Strachey with Lytton, Lyall with Elgin II and MacDonnell with Curzon.
177.tq: Start from the sure commission–Viceroy pair and complete the code.
xs: **Campbell–John Lawrence, Strachey–Lytton, Lyall–Elgin II, MacDonnell–Curzon** — option **(1) a–iii, b–iv, c–ii, d–i**.
Campbell (**1866**) for Orissa; Strachey (**1880**) after the **1876-78** Great Famine.
Lyall after **1896-97**; MacDonnell (**1901**) after **1899-1900**.
xa: **Woodhead (1944)** came under **Wavell**.
The **Famine Code (1883)** was framed on Strachey's recommendations.

177.s: Which commission assessed the causes of famine and recommended measures against future famines?
